pros: When you leave Citi, other roles where you get treated like human and appreciated for what you do (at least on the face of it) are incredibly nice. You'll learn appreciation from that perspective.
cons:
Incredibly toxic work environment, at most levels. 

In no particular order, these are some of the negatives I witnessed/experienced whilst working at Citibank: 

- It is normal to send out an email and get berated and belittled in a chain for doing nothing more than sending out a template you were requested to. Management often justify this with "oh, ignore [them], they're like that!" Why should this be tolerated anywhere? 

- It is normal to be expected to work well outside your core hours, with no sympathy from management, no recognition of it, or even an extension of help for late work coming in that has to be completed due to regulatory deadlines. I was once met with (from my own manager) "Is this your first time staying on late? Well, you should be so lucky." 

- Some people want to help resolve work-related issues, but they are few and far between. It is largely a culture of palming work off to another team with no effort to try and get it resolved- until it eventually comes back around to you for the 5th time. 

- The culture of stepping over anyone and everyone possible in order to get to the "top" is very much alive and well. What I assume would be otherwise nice people (in some instances) treat you incredibly poorly as a result of this. 

- Despite being in a team, you can expect to be somewhat isolated, as work is rarely ever a collaborative effort. 

- Expect no training of any kind. I didn't mind being thrown in the deep end, but I can imagine it could cause what might be otherwise fine employees to fail. 

- People with no emotional intelligence can get into positions that should require at least a modicum of it. 

I could go on. Everyone's experience is different. However, given the size of Citi's employment pool in Belfast, I'm willing to bet if you speak to enough people you will eventually hear incredibly similar points as those I have made above.

Also, the pay isn't very competitive compared to other, smaller tech/FinTech companies.

pros: Benefits packages are good - lots to choose from Belfast office has a good subsidised canteen available Reduced parking rates for nearby car parks
cons: On boarding process at the start is very long and unnecessary. It took 3 months from job offer to start date Training is all completed with a fellow coworker who simply does not have the time or resource to complete this properly Your day to day work will be very heavy in terms of workload. At one point, I was covering 3 people's roles due to sickness. They will still expect the quality of work to be high and additional tasks/goals to be completed but it is simply not doable. The fact I was doing 3 people's roles (these were assigned to me) did not seem to be taken into account when doing any appraisals Those who seem to be getting promotions are those who are on overly friendly terms with their manager or belong to a certain "clique". It doesn't seem to be based on actual work merit and decisions by managers don't seem to be challenged by higher management when they should be Support while in your role will be minimal. I received around 3 one to one in the space of almost a year. No guidance on how to forward your career etc for those who are not friendly or in the management "clique". Those who seem to moan and stress on the job, seem to get further than those who put their heads down Incredibly long hours at times, you will not be paid for any additional hours The salary for the amount of work expected in this role is simply not up to market standard these days. Entry level in other banks seem to pay more than intermediate/senior levels at Citi As an experienced employee, you will soon become disillusioned when others are hired on higher levels than you, yet have no experience of finance, you end up training them and they still cannot perform adequately. You will wonder why you are picking up slack for considerably less money. Look after your existing staff before new hires

3,756,845 one to ones and team meetings a year (I'm exaggerating) won't make your staff think they are being heard if you don't follow through with what you say/ if you don't follow up with what staff raise as an issue.

Due to the 'wait it out' culture, management and team leaders aren't the most suited to their positions.  It always appeared to me that perhaps the decent staff got bored of hard work not being recognised and therefore left the company/moved jobs, meaning that those still there with long tenure were the ones that were content to just bide their time. 
Salaries aren't competitive.  They have gotten better (early 2017) but still not competitive for the Belfast market; Citi seems to have missed the fact that they don't have a monopoly on the legal market in Belfast anymore.

advice: You're losing a lot of talent (and money and time invested in training said talent) to more flexible areas of finance, such as FinTech, by remaining inflexible despite workplaces and ways of working rapidly evolving elsewhere. WFH should be an option, particularly during quiet times of the year; or the option to work from a Citi office in another location, making it easier to spend time with family. A strong personal support network of friends and family is essential to maintain the stamina required for a successful banking career, so helping to facilitate seeing friends and family outside of work should be higher on the priorities list (ie, working from another Citi location around Christmas holiday time, protecting holidays of longer than one week, and providing a laptop to analysts so they can WFH during quiet seasons).   I never leave these sort of reviews, but I know Citi can do better; it certainly has the resources to implement the above initiatives, but I feel it will take more of a cultural shift, particularly from senior bankers who  peddle the sentiment "If I had to sleep under my desk as an analyst, then so should you".  Finally, I'd like to optimistically assume it's been rectified, but the vermin problem in the office was downright disgusting and unacceptable for an employer of this calibre.
pros: The work was, for the most part, interesting. My team were generally welcoming and supportive, I also really enjoyed the analyst training program on offer and learnt a huge amount in my time there, from excel modelling to credit analysis. Citi offers opportunities to relocate to other locations or partake in secondments and rotations in different product teams; resulting in a well-rounded appreciation for the capabilities and services offered by such a global bank. We had a limited amount of team events, and a function-wide Christmas and Summer party - all of which were fairly enjoyable. Salary and bonus are good and in line with the hours that are expected. Citi prides itself on inclusivity and diversity, and I definitely saw and felt these values at play. It was incredible to work with such a diverse bunch of people from all over the globe - finance in London can typically be dominated to the male, pale and stale brigade, but this definitely wasn't my experience of Citi.
cons: Corporate banking is a lifestyle choice. This should be made glaringly obvious upon application.  The hours are long - expect to finish at 9pm on average, increasing to around midnight during crunch times, and roughly 2 Sundays per month - and there is a fair amount of pressure. The nature of the job essentially means you are permanently 'on call', so expect to check emails during holidays and weekends, and expect that you could be asked to come into work at the drop of a hat - I had colleagues who had to reschedule holidays and I cancelled many of my own weekend plans to work on last minute deals. This can take a toll on your mental and physical health, so make sure you are mentally prepared for these hours before you apply. A culture of 'face time' also still exists, which can be quite frustrating from time to time. Internal credit systems were cumbersome, slow and generally very boring and time-consuming to work with; flicking between PDF risk guides, antiquated web-based platforms and excel templates prone to glitches - the whole credit infrastructure could do with a well needed makeover.

summary: Technology Development - worthwhile if you choose carefully
pros:
Well resourced, mature organisation that invests in its staff development, training, infrastructure. Particularly strong on leadership development and graduate programmes, and has been improving on technical leadership with an ongoing multi-year culture change programme ("Engineering Excellence").

Good mobility opportunities due to the size, scale and franchise - for example career pathways from tech into trading are possible.

Plenty of interesting technology projects to get involved in, if you know what to look for - good combination of technical challenge and business problem solving. If you're interested in the business domain, this will give you an advantage in one of the many business-facing roles, for example front office trading technology.

Has many high calibre employees, focused on delivery and execution excellence rather than politics and self promotion. In the right areas there's a culture of 'common good', helping each other and enhancing the outcomes for all (for example, a genuine desire and drive to improve engineering standards and tooling, led by empowered engineers).

Good pay and benefits, including non-financial aspects such as career growth opportunities. Strong focus on diversity and inclusion.
cons:
Size of the organisation can make it unwieldy; some technology projects overlap or duplicate effort needlessly, due to divisional management boundaries and challenges of working across teams, regions and sub-units.

Bureaucratic of course, given it's scale, but needs to pay a lot more attention to productivity metrics to make it's bureaucracy lean and efficient. Major recent focus on risk and controls has probably made this worse.

The work environment won't suit everyone - development environments are heavily controlled/restricted, processes can be slow, inflexible and opaque, there's some significant barriers to adopting or evaluating new technologies, and endless mandatory training due to heavy regulatory context. Same is true even in Innovation Lab team/projects. Easy to get frustrated when what should be a simple task becomes mired in bureaucratic complexity.

summary: Citi UK - culture & opportunities are top notch!
pros: The inclusive culture at Citi UK is amazing, there are various groups that cater to almost everything there from sports to religion to volunteering. And there are always opportunities within if you can be flexible enough. You also get to learn a lot in whatever role you take in (more so if you are proactive about it).
cons: While there are numerous opportunities, Citi (as with other major financial services companies of late) is building up headcount and manpower in low cost locations. Some of these locations may not be easily accessible nor familiar to you, but as mentioned, if you are flexible enough, then the world is your oyster.

advice: Remove the vested interest of those who have been at the institution for too long, and the people who lack the academic as well as professional background/mentality/work ethic that banks have strived to garner in the last few decades.
pros: It is a great place to work.  It will provide opportunities for a successful career to anyone with the desire and drive to do so.  A vast global network with numerous opportunities, always willing to provide those that want it with assistance to grow professionally.
cons: Can be political at times, but this will depend on who your boss and peers are.

summary: A bit big for its own good.
advice: Work on the cons. Size is not an excuse for lethargy or replacing strategy with process. Cut top heavy management and pay up for young talent. Measure actual value (rather than cost) of offshoring and apply this selectively.
pros: Global network means lots of opportunity to relocate and try different teams. There are smart people in the organisation if you look but you won't be stumbling over them. Very good people are generally recognised but an awful lot of average gets swept up the ladder too.
cons: Size makes it very process heavy.  Too many people promoted by reaching certain age/weight rather than on merit. Very US centric in outlook. Top heavy.

advice: Management should be encouraged to forecast their budgets more than 2 years when employing new members of staff to ensure they can cover the staff costs - and reduce possible redundancy of staff, If necessary employ on contract basis.
pros:
Large Global Company - experience of large scale global project opportunities.
Good facilities and wide range of work within Investment Banking.
Salary and benefits as you would expect of such a company.
cons:
process improvement / projects hindered by red tape.
Only investment banking business , so scope of project ventures limited.
Project work and team allocation driven by budget and you could find yourself in a team, with reduced budget and at risk.

summary: Good company to work for, with very good opportunities, but sometime daunted by its own internal political problems.
advice:
Cut down on spin and motivation speaches and accept the difficult time the company is having.
Do something to reduce the empire building activities, expecially in IT.
pros: Big company with a number of internal opportunity; also a company able to trade in large sizes and therefore with the possibility to trade any type of instrument. Mostly friendly attitude and balanced life/work environment.
cons:
A company currently in search of directions, and unclear who is steering it (whether the US government or the CEO). 

A lot of red tapes and inefficient comunication between the business and the infinitely many IT (sub)systems.

advice: Focus more on people development so people don't leave and providing structured training so people are more equipped to do their jobs more effectively
pros: Good benefits, pension, BUPA, maternity and internal gym. Great company culture, good for working mums.A little behind on effective processes/systems. However have made progression in the 9years I have been working at Citi
cons: Hard work is not always recognised and long hours expected at times. Promotion/ progression don't always go to the people who deserve it. Clear variation of pay within the same team and internal pay increases are not great. Training of new staff is not structured.

advice: Let people work according to their style, and give some of the perks that other tech companies have.  Reduce some of the bureaucracy around releasing code, it doesn't have the intended effect.
pros: A decent salary, experience working in a large financial institution, and a not too pressured working environment are all good reasons to work for Citi.  There are also good career options with internal mobility.
cons: The technology is not always the latest and greatest; there are some exceptions and teams doing really good work, but there are also some legacy systems.  In such a large company it is also possible for mediocracy to survive.

summary: Good company but experiences can vary
advice:
Please review recruitment process - takes too long.
Please provide equipment or vouchers for staff to purchase equipment to work from home - laptops as a minimum should be provided.
Not enough females being promoted above VP level outside Legal and HR.
pros:
Variety of work, global presence, working with good people.
Opportunities to rotate and move to new roles internally.
Good additional benefits - annual bonus, pension, BUPA private health
cons:
Lip service to work / life balance and promoting females to senior positions in certain teams. 
No financial support or equipment provided to work from home during covid - not even a laptop.
Recruitment process both externally and internally can be painfully long

advice:
-Increase accountability through out the organization.
-Performance should be judged on objective criteria rather than politics
pros: Citis rotational program offers excellent flexibility, great work life balance. I really feel as through I can gain whatever skills and experience I need during the program. Its a highly respected program with in the organization and I also get a sense that graduates of the program do excel if they focus.
cons: Like working at any other global bank, there is too much red tape. You need to obtain approvals for many minute details and overall accountability through out the organization is low. If you have an overall mentality of "lets get things done" it can be difficult.

advice: Keep doing what you are doing as I did feel that there was an all inclusive environment.  It was hard to accept the statement 'looking after our talent' when the business continues making a lot of redundancies and the talent walks out of the door.
pros: 1. Culturally diverse creating an all inclusive environment.  2. Exposure to a Global Banking organisation represented in over 100 countries. 3. The company truly believes in the concept of work life balance.
cons: Career advancement can prove difficult as whatever role you are taken on to do, some find it very difficult to move to a different part of the business.

advice: I believe that some jobs at Citi are being promoted in a way in which is misleading, in terms of what it is you will actually be doing, I was disappointed as I came to think of it as more of a call centre than anything.
pros: I found the staff very friendly and helpful, they took their time to train me and any queries I had they were more than happy to sit down and explain what I needed to know
cons: Long hours, you only get paid by contract but are expected to work at least an hour extra a day which you do not get paid for.

summary: IBD in UK. Great experiences with individual people, lots of very smart, driven employees.  But bureaucratic..
pros: Truly global organisation with networks anywhere you could imagine doing business.  Compared to other monoline investment banks the breadth of product offerings helps differentiate Citi.  Lots of very smart, driven people which makes it a fulfilling place to work.
cons: Very bureaucratic organisation.  I'm sure other large investment banks aren't dis-similar in this regard, the key difference being when you need to cut through the red tape to get something done for a client at Citi you aren't able to- which I don't think is the case at GS, JPM, etc.

advice: Reward your top performers accordingly and let go of the people that don't add any value
pros: Citi has a lot to offer to those who go out and get what they want and don't sit and wait to be given everything on a plate. Development opportunities, travel, good teams and great people to work with.
cons: Trying to get a better pay without getting an outside offer is almost impossible. The salaries in finance remain very low and even if you are rated at the top of your peers it is unlikely to get any substantial pay increase so at some point it becomes very demotivating.

pros: Global teams and coverage, loads of responsibilities from the start, decent and growing external research credibility. The 'Citi velocity' platform is one of the better ones from the bulges for communication and info dissemination.
cons: When I left, there were many juniors who also left at the same time. That year they had hired a lot of Ds/MDs so the bonus pool was dramatically cut for the juniors, which was sad. It was a strange exodus of sorts. One young female analyst became pregnant and when she returned early they still didn't give her old job back, she had to start covering another sector. Also, I left just after MiFID2 started to ramp up, I heard there is a lot more admin to do now, to justify the salaries of research folk. Sadly a lot of people I knew at Citi were just fired after I left, so I know only a handful of people who are still there.

advice: Communicate, communicate, communicate.
pros: I have found that Cit has an extensive global foot print which provides great carrer opportunities especially for somecone who wants to be in emerging markets. THe brand has taken a beating, but the poeple remaining in the IBD team are top notch and the deal exposure is great as a junior banker.
cons: current turmoil has hit the bank harder than at other banks. THer is unertaiity on long-term prospects and i believe this is impacting the volume of business coming through the door. Wise to stay put at he moment through this cycle and seee what heppens in 2 years time.

advice: Make the things you talk about a reality; simplify your processes; eliminate your long hours culture.
pros: Good basic salary; decent annual bonus on top if you perform well; very good overall benefit package; flexibility to work from home regularly
cons: Long hours culture - no matter what they say about work life balance, there is none. Long hours are simply expected. Plus you’ll have at least enough work for 2 very high performing employees to do, plus they’ll keep adding to your responsibilities, so working long hours is the only way to even try and survive it. That sadly has the result of reducing the overall value of your package. But they pay enough that looking to move to another NI based company realistically means taking a bit of a pay cut. So people get trapped on the eternal Citi hamster wheel.

advice: Employees value true transparency, not a transparency front, and then you see back door deals
pros: Allows working from home, and flexible working policies which means many stay for many many years.   Work is dependent on teams, but can be varied and interesting in the right place
cons:
Salary is well below market rate, if you want to retain employees, ensure that salary raises are benchmarked against the market rather than give what you can get away with.  Good people will stay if rewarded well.

Also, too many clicks within management.  You cannot progress unless you know people rather than through meritocracy

advice:
Look at your turnover rate and ask yourselves WHY and what exactly can be done to prevent it. The answers come from having frank and honestly discussion with your staff.

Pay people for the overtime they do. At the same time, overtime shouldn't be expected.

More fun in the office and team building.
pros:
Plenty of additional benefits to choose from 
Subsidised canteen
cons:
Office environment 
Truly awful. You walk in and its deathly quiet. Nobody will speak to you, not even your manager. You stand no chance of making any "friends" whilst here.

Work life balance
Its non existent. You will be expected to work around 5-10 hours additional each work at least and not be paid for it. You needn't have a partner or any children because your relationship with them will be severely affected because you will never get to see them. The only faces you'll see all week are the dreary zombies sitting amongst you.

Managers
Absolutely zero people skills. They promote people who are good at the analytical work but not necessarily managerial work. They cannot motivate staff. They will constantly tell you about the high turnover whilst offering no solutions and expect their existing staff to work themselves to the ground. They won't ask their staff how they can make anything better because they can't or they genuinely don't care. You can go weeks with your manager not even so much as saying hello to you. 

The work
Repetitive and boring. You will spend your days doing the same thing day in day out to the point its almost robotic. Your work load will be about what is expected from 4 employees in different companies. Mistakes are made because the staff are too overstretched yet you will be fully blamed. You are made to complete additional "goals" which coinicentally is presentational work that should be completed by managers, leaving staff to concentrate on the already high work load they have on their plates. You are told its for your "progression" yet not many promotions actually come up. When they do come up, it seems to be those who stay all hours of the night to work get promoted rather than the efficient workers who attempt to have a half decent social life.

Overall, if you work here, you will be overworked, stressed and fed up. You will more than likely end up on anti depressants and sitting like a zombie within 6 months.

summary: Capable colleagues. Size of organisation is challenging to manage
advice: In reality Citi is a tech company that has a long history and knowledge of banking and finance. In my experience it's managed as if it's a banking and finance company from a bygone age that has reluctantly had to build some technology systems. The latter is command and control with senior MDs seemingly more interested in clipping the next coupon than making the changes necessary for it to succeed into the future ie overly conservatively.
pros: Good quality capable colleagues and a myriad of different possibilities for future job roles and locations. Evidence of increasing sanity of senior mgt team.
cons: It's a very big organisation which makes it tough to find the right people quickly to understand or get things done. Citi is far from unique in this respect, but big banks still trying to manage by command and control type management which is demotivating and ineffective.

summary: Great in the past not so great now
advice: Take a look at long time staff who are leaving and understand why that is.
pros: Its a huge company so you get lots of mobility.  The company has one of the most diverse workforce's in the world. Whilst base is generally under market they can flex the bonus pot to your advantage to ensure overall comp keeps up (in a good year)
cons: VERY Long hours. overall performance of the firm really impacts comp. HR dept is poor in supporting staff. If you have Lehman's on your CV you seem to do well at the expense of harder working employees.  Very much a blame culture and not very collaborative to get the job done. Its all about dodging the buses people are trying to throw each other under.

advice: Not everyone should be a manager, no adult should every be micromanaged
pros: Easy to get promoted, just find a new job (although it may take 20 interviews if you dont have a back), apply, you get a higher rank and more money. Everyone at Citi is a VP, it is not comparable with other companies. Majority of VPs provide very low-quality work
cons: Everything is bad, from IT, through HR to line managers..You deal with constant pressure (and chaos), unfriendly and competitive (not team-players) colleagues and micromanaging LMs. This is the only bank that requires employees to come 3days/week during pandemic to the office, my manager has no mercy to allow to come to the office after 9am ("our MD wants to see us working") despite not facing clients, and HR does not care if you have any issues (they reply after 10-20 days). People who stay here for years have never worked at any other bank and do not appreciate creative ideas. My advice is - stay away from this bank. I am trying to get out, hopefully soon...

summary: Waste of time if your are in the wrong team
advice: Get the training right, get your procedures in order, pay your staff for the work they do and really learn to appreciate them.
pros: The benefits aren't too bad, health, good pension match, life assurance, gadget insurance, emergency child care,
cons: Long hours, low morale, training is awful, no progression prospects, managers talk about career progression but really just mean their own, supervisors do not complete maker/checkers which causes trouble (and they push back saying it should have been done correctly the first time, but ummm, aren't you supposed to check it?) Procedures are literally there as a piece of paper to meet compliance/regulations. They have very little to do with the actually job you will be doing. This is Operations, I think the tech side is much better

summary: Potential to be a great place to work
advice: Address the huge attrition issue that the Belfast CSC is currently facing. Don't bury your head in the sand and take some hard decisions to revert the problem.
pros:
Great employee benefits including enhanced pension and private medical. 
Great people in general to work with. 
Global employer so great opportunity to get exposure to a vast organisation and how it operates.
cons: Impossible to influence anything as the organisation is so smothered in red tape and needless bureaucracy. Opportunities for growth in Belfast are limited as the senior roles are retained in the big cities.

summary: Very fast-paced environment without guarantee of support or training
advice: Rigidly enforce duties while holding employees (no matter how senior) accountable to realistic considered timeframes. Develop a workflow team to make the completion of mundane tasks more efficient and more systematic.  Develop mechanisms for improving processes that rely on gathering feedback from staff that are working the processes. Stop wasting resources on getting yet another project management team to replace a less recently developed process with a more recent half-baked one.
pros: Salary, Depth of Experience gained, Highly Intelligent Colleagues
cons: Some employees are able to justify managing global complex relationships between stakeholders by obstructing internal communication and insulating themselves into work silos where the same work is likely to be completed by multiple people multiple times, while other employees are expected to provide constant updates of imminent progress. This progress often depends on approval from some employees who are causing the obstructions so that they handle less work.

advice: Sack all the Directors who are in London they are many useless guys on the top, worst part of my life is with Citi 2012 to 2016 , please shutdown this bank operations in Belfast and move to London or else just shutdown Citi operations in UK ,Citi sucks.
pros: nothing much really I totally wasted my 4 years of my time (2012 to 2016) , I still regret why I signed the offer back in 2012, Directors are blind and dont give ... about their staff , nothing Positive to talk about really ...
cons: worst company to work for ,low wages,0% bonus for my entire period (4 Years 2012 to 2016) ,0% pay hike for my entire period ( 4 years 2012 to 2016) , management dont want developers moving from Belfast o London (High Paying Place),Tier 2 employers are treated like slaves.technology is ... just application support really not much innovation, if you are young and dynamic stay away from Citi Belfast , try to get into Citi London at least you will be on the high end salary.

summary: Not a bad company for Belfast.
advice:
- Start in should not be about money/cost - a 'cheap' employer can cause havoc within a team.
- Listen to your employees when they raise concerns
pros:
- Networking opportunities
- Everyone deals with the same Citi wide issues so you tend to bond quite quickly with colleagues
- Salary good for Belfast
- Having Citi on your CV will always stand you in good stead and will give you plenty of opportunities for being headhunted.
cons:
- Long hours expected
- Belfast based teams seem to pick up a lot of other regions work due to inability to complete but yet be kept in more junior C levels.
- Most teams are very slow to replace attrician leavers resulting in understanding and more work for remaining employees
- Inability to discuss salary with colleagues in order to obtain a benchmark/expectancy

summary: Poor management and HR.  Unwelcoming staff and poor career opportunitries - NOT recommended
advice:
I found the organisation to be horrendous for its size - I was treated very poorly by both managment and fellow staff.  Very unwelcoming and poor communications between departments.  Too much beauroracy and politics.    I was never given a proper induction by HR - for a company of this size it is essential that this takes place.  Staff were particularly unwelcoming and unfriendly towards me - I felt I was being victimised and belittled by staff who had been there for many years.  
Senior Management were poor communicators and were "yes men" to their seniors, not telling the real truth about particuloar matters.  Poor decisions were being made about IT and technology engineering that have contributed to the poor financial results of the company.  I would never recommend this company to anyone who wants a proper career.
pros: Scale of the organisation - otherwise none
cons: Extremely poor management - unfriendly staff, no HR induction - unhelpfull people in all departments.  Backstabbing

summary: Too big to truly bother with the individual
advice: Get real!
pros: Nice office, flexible working (from home) widely applied and works well in practice although the long hours and 'being on' at all times is almost expected at every level which affects work/life balance
cons: A lot of senior managers rule by fear - and are allowed to by a HR team that seems to want to please (management) more than anything else.  The culture is basically 'fit in or ship out' and you really only get one chance....if you don't manage to impress the right people you are very quickly on a sticky path!  This seems to be the same across all levels so there is little 'firm' strategy and longer term goals. Communication becomes ambiguous because everyone leaves room to change their minds or claim that what they originally said meant something else, to cover their own backside.

advice: Keep it up.
pros:
Where do I start? 
I loved working for this organisation. They knew how to support their staff in everything. Training, development,  opportunities, career progression and so on.
The whole operation was ran effectively, professionally and efficiently. 
I worked as a Vendor Manager and loved every second.  Loved my vendors, loved the team I worked with, loved every day and I miss this place so dearly.
I would have stayed until I retired, if they had let me but unfortunately the location of office I worked was winding down  and therefore I was made redundant. But even up to my last day, they were amazing. Kept me informed at every step of this process regardless of whether it indirectly affected me or not. 
As I said "I miss this place so much"
cons: Absolutely nothing. They were amazing and I wished I remained working for them.

advice: Compensate your staff fairly, keep a work life balance in mind and also dont go easy on people that slack and make others pick up their work
pros: enjoy the people at Citi, I have also progressed rather quickly which has also been a pro and had 2 promotions within 2 years at the firm
cons: work life balance can struggle at certain times of the year, I dont believe the pay is up to standard for an investment bank, even if Belfast is a 'low cost' area.

summary: Not bad for an investment bank!
advice: Think outside the North America box a bit more!
pros: Global. Generally a good culture. Lots of forward thinking strategy, with pockets of excellence.  Good diversity resources, including flexible working, if you work for an area in the business that values this!
cons: Below market on salary. Internal mobility can be difficult. New York focused so many opportunities come up there, which is frustrating if based in other regions! Not all business areas embrace flexible working etc. as the company suggests they should!

advice: Better team events, less admin more tangible work
pros:
Global platform and culture, it's not easy but possible to change jobs and locations.
Bright people who are the nicest of an Investment Bank
Goal to help the less fortunate and caring for the community and planet.
cons:
Long hours, bureaucratic maize at times.
Hard to decipher who does what in the organisation
Work is not overly intellectually demanding, and it is harder to see the tangible benefits for the wider world

summary: Still in Probation Period and I'm Looking to Leave

- Great training and extra events - if only you had the time to attend them
cons:

- Terrible communications: 100+ emails a day but no regular team meetings. No-one spoke to me on my first day. Never had a 1-2-1 meeting with my manager in 5 months
- No training for role, but a million banking regulation trainings you have to complete. No time to do any extra learning/training
- People work loads of extra hours and login and respond to emails when they're on holiday
- Incompetent management, constantly firefighting, total chaos

advice:
Continue to grow Belfast as a hub for Citi Development.
It is good to see so many jobs coming into Northern Ireland
pros:
Everything is always very clean cut no grey areas, and politically correct
Lots of outside activitites to get involved in
You get out what you put in
Get to work on wiode range of technologues depending on what team your in, C++, C, Java, Linux, Windows, bash, perl, ruby
cons: Sometimes the amount of red tape as a developer is particulary frustrating

summary: Too big to fail, but also to truly succeed
advice: Stop off-sourcing, breaking good teams into delocalised service centre until nobody understands anymore what is the goal they are trying to achieve and why.
pros:
Large company with many internal opportunities for personal development
For a bank a tolerable work/life balance
Inclusive culture
cons:
One reached post VP levels (SVP, Directors, MD) the politics starts to become oppressive and to some aspects toxic.
Great company so easy to end up facing a glass ceiling one arrived to VP level

advice:
More actual strategic management and les micromanagement and monitoring - team is mature and professional.
More flexibility organising time off and rota.
pros: Salary is fairly good for the job you do. Environment quite relaxed bearing in mind it is corporate a reception you work at. Showing personality is encouraged, however have to remain profesional
cons: Reception team outsourced for contacting company and employees ar treated as rest of the contractors as cleaners, builders and security including use separate entrance with security searches.

summary: A true career, within a global company
advice: Encourage the team to work through the processes, and simplify - not just to work around!
pros: You name it, you can do it as a career, within the vast company.  There is a true sense of value of all staff, and generally, management are supportive
cons: Finance is fickle, and the market changes frequently.  The blinkered need to achieve a (say) 10% cut again... coupled with frustrating bureaucracy... can make it hard work to simply raise a purchase order!

advice: Programme is very good in it's current state, keep up the good work. Slight improvements can be made to efficiency with mark-ups and feedback,
pros: Great environment with great people. Lot's of support available at all stages of the internship. No knowledge is taken for granted so those studying non-finance related subjects have nothing to worry about.
cons: Overall work environment is very slow and inefficient. You will find yourself waiting for hours on someone without having anything to do.

summary: A good place to work for tough people who can stand a high frustration level
advice: Hopeless to advice anything to these lost in space people. Therefore, Go home all of you !!! , take your clueless "club" members with you and come never back again. Ah yes, and pay your bonuses of the last 5 years back as a minimum compensation for what you have done to my company and the lower rank people !
pros: Depending for what department and what organisation within Citi you are working, it is a good place to work. Compensation packages have been above banking average, company offers excellent internal and external training possibilities for beginners and skilled staff as well, strong commitment to diversity, interesting travel possibilities if working for a global or regional organisation, good possibility to learn how a world wide operating enterprise is organised and working, good place to learn how to read and listen "between the lines", good place to learn the importency of politics and that being in the right "Club" will help to survive, good place to learn something about the cultural differences of how some work task are understood and worked.
cons: To much to write here. Citi has a horrifying week Senior Management, with no Leadership, No truth, No trust anymore. Speaking about my experiences, to much and permanent reorganisations, producing confusion and frustration for staff and customers. If you join Citi in EMEA you have to know the right people, and being located in London is as well a big advantage for your career. Anyway, if you do not belong to the right "Club" you will never be promoted at all, regardless of your location or if you are working you ass off. Promotions are usually based on politics not on skills or performance. As a result you will find many nope heads within leading positions only because they belong to the right inner circle, to the right "Club". To many managers listen to the wrong people and wasting the companies money with ridiculous strategic decisions based on wrong assumptions given by clueless nope heads. You will find a world full of fear, where the few good people left have to be very quite to avoid to get there heads cut off in the next "right placement" round. High skilled people and teams, capable to manage issues quick and efficient have been fired. Their core knowledge is wasted and gone, their responsibilities have been moved to so called "low cost" locations. As a result, customer dissatisfaction has been increased, service levels have gone down. If you don't care about the company you work for, if you could talk the talk, if you like to play dirty political games, if you already know the right people to avoid a "right placement", Welcome to join the madhouse !. But if pointless processes, permanent reorganisations and obviously wrong strategic decisions might frustrate you easily, if you like to work customer orientated, quick and efficient, if you easily might loose you politeness on phone, because you have to talk again with a clueless peanuts paid "low cost" location monkey, then stay out of Citi, this is not the right place for you.

advice: Review and promote on merit.  Offer staff the opportunity for 360 degree feedback so everyone that works with someone has the chance to review their performance.
pros: The global exposure Citibank has provides many opportunities and a wide network.  You will have the chance to work with many exceptional people.
cons: Citi has a habit of 'playing favorites'. Although there are many exceptional people at Citi, there are many who are not there on their own merits, and will continue to get promoted and be protected for all the wrong reasons.  Citi is not very good at rewarding on merit alone.

advice:
-Invest in better technology (project managed by people who care about end user experience!)
-Improve information- availability and quality.
-Understand that not everything can be solved by outsourcing!
pros:
- Typical bulge bracket environment
- Entrepeuneurial spirit

- The resources are out there.....
cons:
.... It is just very difficult to track them down..

summary: Everything is done with a shoestring budget, also potential unpaid work during unsociable hours
advice: Budgets for teams working on crucial applications needs to be increased, at least to the point where developers are able to develop productivity instead of having to deal with painfully slow and sometimes broken processes. Also, I would recommend hiring dedicated testers and spend time improving build processes. Try to emulate what pure software companies are doing. Also, for those in technical roles who don't have heavy technical experience - these people need to be supported with more training and guidance.
pros: Work hours are totally flexible and it's possible for most developers to work from home. Unlimited hot beverages are available and there are good efforts in organising social events. Also, there is an enormous library of online training available and some on-site training also. The 'Citi collaborate' work social networking tool is also an excellent source of resources and a great way to network with people outside your department - and so it's easy to network with people working with similar technologies or with similar interests. There are many clubs/societies organised within Citi covering a wide spectrum of interests and sports. Citi donates 1 day of every employees time to take part in a volunteering activity within the community. Desks are big enough and chairs are suitable.
cons: Everything is done with a minimum of resources. Teams are running complex applications without proper processes and methodologies. The business just doesn't seem to understand what is actually needed to make software. Teams don't have proper build or test processes, and many developers don't even have some of the most basic developer tools and hardware. Most of the developer machines are very low-spec, and can be painfully slow when dealing with some development work. Also, my department seems to have a gigantic budget shortfall, and they've dealt with this by forcefully relocating people to cheaper locations and by getting rid of many contractors (and not replacing them). Additionally, many developers have to work unsociable hours for weekend releases, and they are not paid for their troubles, and even getting the time off in lieu wasn't easy. Also, making requests for basic software, hardware and configurations is a painful and extremely slow process. I don't see any of these things improving any time soon. It's actually difficult to be productive at Citi, there are many obstacles, and not just because of strict banking regulations. Also, there is little cohesion within the department.

summary: A year of my life I'll never get back
advice: Two things.  First: train your managers.  Don't assume being a good developer makes you a good manager, because it doesn't.  Second: if you invest heavily in making developers' lives difficult, and go skint on making developers' lives easier, then don't expect your good developers to stay.
pros: Most of my colleagues were nice people.  That's about all I got.
cons: Management haven't been taught how to manage, and when things go wrong, they're more interested in finding a direction to point their finger than getting things back on track.  You constantly have to break company policy in order to get anything done.  People get excited about "innovative" ideas that other companies have been doing for over a decade.  People care more about doing things quickly, not doing things right.

summary: Very Unethical, A playground for complacency and incompetence.
advice: Stop allowing the employment of incompetent people just because they are friends of friends, and ensure rewarding the best individuals to retain talent. Set a clear career path, and make sure goals are fair and attainable, and not used to hold individuals back.
pros: Great exposure to projects and software systems if you are willing to sacrifice your life.
cons: Very little opportunity for reward or recognition if you are not part of the "clique". Suggest avoiding like the plague. Senior Management lack direction, and your peers are likely to kick back and watch you do all the work and then take credit for it.

summary: You are just a very small cog in a large machine and they can always replace you with a cheaper off-shore alternative.
advice: Middle management need to treat their staff as individuals.  Break the company up, Citi is too big.
pros: Getting time off at short notice is never a problem.  Being able to work from home when unable to get to the office or having an appointment (doctors, dentist, etc).
cons: No loyalty between management and staff.  The feeling that you could be made redundant at any time.  The total lack of recognition for a job well-done.  Jobs for the boys.  You are just a number, one of the headcount.

summary: Laid back work life balance.  Definitely some "lifers" there as long as you can avoid the chop!
advice: Since senior management change was as a result of major investment falings (end 2008), nothing else needs to be said about the highly publicised fall from grace of the company
pros:
Flexible working culture
Generally Easy-going
Good Project Management Method
Competent people are allowed to do what they do best and flourish
Senior management very supportive of staff
cons:
Like other investment banks, it's controlled by regulatory requirements, thus can be stifling & frustrating.  Learn to handle this and things become alot easier
Only 23 days leave
Slight culture of nepotism.  People advanced on length of service rather than competence
SOX!

summary: New product development, Institutional Clients Group
advice: None. The issues are systemic, even management can’t do anything about it.
pros: Good pay & benefits for the role.
cons:
- Crazy amount of politics to contend with.
- Fear based culture.
- The company is too big, struggles to do new things as a result.
- New product approval is overly bureaucratic, and absurdly lengthy, even for a regulated industry.
- Tech & tools available for you to use are comically outdated.
- Severely hampered by legacy constraints both practical and cultural.

If you want to join a company to develop new products and have a sense of achievement and enjoyment in doing so, avoid this place like the plague.

advice: There is a lot of talk about being heathy at Citi, work life balance, be the best you can be, voice of employee, however in reality it feels like marketing gimmiks or lip service but not something Citi is serious about (at least not in my department).
pros: Good place to learn eveything there is to know about Cash Implementations, great location (Canary Wharf), good benefits (maternity leave, option to buy holidays)
cons: No work life balance. Working excessive hours becomes the norm and is seen as normal. Just being good at your job does not get you promoted. Anybody wanting a promotion is expected to put in extra and beyond.

advice:
Give the staff a pat on the back for a job well done at the very least and make sure that if there are any rewards the message is passed down to all the staff and not just the level of management below you.
Channels of communication are still unclear.
pros: to learn processes and how to manipulate people with the aim to eventually becoming a senior manager
cons: Any technical skills you go in with wil be lost or become redundant unless you revisit them yourself regularly.

advice: Ensure next level down are held accountable for cascading organisational change initiatives - you'll never change if they don't
pros: Internal mobility opportunities, learning and development agenda is strong, work/life balance good if you have boundaries, flexible working, benefits, challenging  and interesting work, truly regional and global work,
cons: Too much focus on revenue generating and not enough on behaviours, poor leadership and manager capability due to promotion of specialists into managerial roles instead of people with actual leader experience and/or aptitude - place is full of individual contributors

advice: You need to focus on culture. You need to train your staff well and focus on well being of your staff as it is not a priority.
pros: Salary is good. That is all.
cons:
-They don’t provide you with the tools to do the job ie laptop. You buy your own. 
-Working 11 hr shifts for the last 3 months, 7 days a week and told (not asked) to opt out of the working hours directive. 
- Team spilt between different time zones so expect 10pm meetings. 
- Training is below standard with trainers flying through screens and not explaining. 
- No video calls so if you are new don’t expect to know what your team look like.

advice: corporate values and outstanding company culture has to filter down to all divisions, including retail branches
pros: Great support network, strong and well recognised brand worldwide, consumer products  are very competitive and reasonably priced, aspiration and huge effort to maintain clients` trust and constantly improve client satisfaction, market leading solutions for international business traveller clients, generous employee benefits package, good career oportunities for the most talented employees
cons: Bureaucracy, lack of empowerment, incompetent managers on low levels, political approach preferred, lack of education support

summary: Good experience but not the best place
pros: Global, challenging and high visibility projects. Good reputation for your CV. Innovative solutions to have a good balance between professional and personal life (home office). Great perks for full time employees.
cons: Operations & Technology is not seen as investment, it is seen as expense. Too many controls and procedures, slow pace, some bureaucracy, personal growth based more in relations -due to power niche- and not in personal performance at all.

summary: More Finance/Admin than IT Type Work
pros:
Good benefits - pension, annual leave, sick pay
Ability to work from home when required
Some flexibility around working hours
cons:
IT project work is mainly off-shore. Belfast office only seems to get some code updates to work on. Not good if you want to have a career or progress a career in IT.
Poor management
Long and late hours expected to get work done - but no compensation for this
Sterile workplace - factory feel
People quite tense and under stress and pressure

summary: Terrific co-workers and managers, but lots of bureaucracy and legacy systems
advice:
Streamline procedures
Give the employees more options to change and progress
pros:
Good working environment
Managers tend to trust their employees 
There are good programs for in-house training, in several fields, mostly business-related
Sober and friendly mood
Good work-life balance
cons:
Too much bureaucracy
Slow career path
Lots of legacy web applications to use for doing anything useful
Not much visibility about other deparments and projects
Recent tendency to centralize most interesting stuff (projects, training) in NY, rather than London

advice: Support the ones who work for their roles and not give it to the ones who can only know the talk and bring nothing new to the table.
pros: Good company benefits.  But don't all companies!!
cons: Promise the world and get none of it.  Office politics is always there and favouritism too.  They are happy to have high turnover and loose quality professionals, in order to keep the favourites.    Systems are backward, they are in the ancient times honestly.  DO NOT BOTHER!!!

summary: Great learning experience, but lacks clear program for developing bankers.
advice: Have a clear plan for developing talent. Too many people I've worked with have left simply out of not being satisfied with client exposure / development.
pros: You work with hard working, dedicated people who, in my experience, are always willing to help. Great cohesion between various teams. Broad geographic reach gives rotation opportunities, but they are hard to get.
cons: Seniors don't take juniors to pitches enough. Lack of structured program to develop juniors into strong bankers.

advice: Hire the right amount of good candidates. Lot of the teams are understaffed and lead by people who are keen to achieve their personal bonus/promotion targets but deliver sub standard deliverables.
pros: You work on every thing from A - Z in the project, so you get a lot of confidence and experience on a range of things in the tech world.
cons: Largely depends on the team you work. Poor management , lack of planning, favouritism. Very poor work life balance.

pros: In the past great place to work, easy to move around and expand your skill set. Supported development by leaders.
cons: Now the banking environment has become more difficult to operate in this has translated into a less pleasant atmosphere in most departments. Redundancies happen on a regular basis several times every year. Performance is not rewarded as it once was. The environment in banks generally has become more strained as people try to work under heavy amounts of regulation.

advice: Given the investment in analyst/associate training, some MD's should take better care of junior resource rather than accept that the best move on to other places
pros: Lots of training across multiple jurisdictions,  wide alumni network that comes in handy at later stages in a career, exposure to multiple bank verticals
cons:
Reviews skewed towards views of immediate line managers rather than true 360 
views (which at times is great but at others can damage juniors), highly bureaucratic

advice: Recognise the wealth of talent you have and please break down some of the overbearing governance to allow innovation to thrive.
pros: Mostly great people, nice to work with professionals
cons: There is just way to much work. The work is constrained by so many processes there’s no room to use any outside experience or talent to get things done. So somehow it’s stressful because of the volume of work and governance yet boring because it’s just delivery without creativity.

advice: Focusing on offshoring just creates an unstable working environment. Local talent could be procured onshore which would make the whole operation a lot smoother. But as always, nobody will listen ...
pros:
Flexible work pattern
Salary level reasonably competent
Prestigious office if that is your thing
Employee walfare is ok
Good facilities
cons:
Senior Management seem to "manage up"
No regard for a job well done
You will feel like a cog in a machine
Will get rid of people without regard once the going gets tough
Poor at resourcing projects
Are in love with offshoring

advice: very efficient and effective. the morning meeting can tell you what you need to do today. and the closing meeting can sum what you have done today.
pros: high salary, approachable colleagues, great location and office. challenging tasks and projects every week and huge travel compensation
cons:
Long hours, usually 9 am to 9 pm, Saturday is working day. 
A lot of repetitive works. too many men, a few women workers

advice: Continue to communicate and deliver the results which will in turn deliver a change in perception
pros: Stimulating enviroment which despite the public set backs still has enormous franchise power.  The PR is probably 6 months behind the business at the moment
cons: Biggest challenge is to overcome the brand damage.  In investment banking the client has to feel that they are getting the best, blowing up your own balance sheet is not a good start

summary: Assistant vice president - Senior support Analyst
advice: Break done some of the process barriers and embrace 21st century software practices.  Skillset in Belfast is there for the taking
pros: Good opportunities for advancement. Investment in Belfast is high, so job security is number one here.  Some great opportunities for improvements to outdated processes
cons: Bureaucracy standing in the way of real work.  In order to get sudo or production access this take many levels of approval for a brief period

advice: Targets and bonuses lead to poor behaviour. Try and manage people rather than spreadsheets. It is not a factory.
pros: Working twice your contracted hours help you learn the role quicker. It's easier to understand how the financial crash happened after working there. Some good people worked there.
cons: Poor pay, haphazard management. Financial regulations were seen as a nuisance to get around and it was more important to be seen to be working than actually achieving anything of note.

advice:

pros:

Great leadership.
Great benefits.
Good salary.
cons:
Outdated infrastructure. 
Slow to upgrade infrastructure.
Short staffed teams is common.

summary: Too Many Cooks (and not enough of them!)
advice: Pay more attention to your staff.  We do an annual review/survey, and every year the same results are mentioned, maybe there's a reason for this.   If you don't train your staff properly, then don't be surprised when errors occur.

It's a job in a tight job market.
I get overtime
Easy to dodge blame
cons:
Easy to dodge blame.
Pay/benefits don't compare well against rivals.
Long working hours
Poor prospects (unless your someone's friend)

advice: I applied through global something program which they offer to college seniors and we were selected randomly by each department so I did not have an option to apply to where I wanted to. Even though we could write down first and second choice, it did not really mean anything
pros: good opportunity to get a peak into the industry. I worked for corporate finance and ended up getting practical advice from other bankers about banking
cons: Cannot really think of one. Work life balance could be one of the cons.. other than that, it was a good experience overall.

advice: Stop talking about leadership, you are good managers, leadership is about people. When selecting to reduce workforce, why is the top layer always protected from being put on the risk list. Managers need to get closer to the coal face of what people do. Yes, data tells only one story, but won't tell you the part of the story, as in people.
pros: Lots of good stuff you can get into. You make your career, if you look around..Great benefits, and people who want to get things done. Brand and global experiance
cons:
In Tech, its starting to fall behind the bell curve on tech solutions, its clear its focus is on business and not tech.  Im not so sure it can keep up the pace and is already showing cracks on its tech platforms and solutions.  
Not such a great career for Tech people, limited I would say. You only realise once you leave just how far behind in Tech it really is. But still thankful for the opportunities it can provide.
Work life balance is difficult, and you will work long hours and be expected to take on more and more responsibilities as it continues to reduce its Tech workforce, the work does not disappear. Retention has been dropping through the floor due to this "suck it up attitude" from leadership. Most certainly not your 9 to 5 job, expect to do 10hr days, not much opportunity for training and development, and if you are remotely managed, you will tend to be forgotten about to an extent. Collaboration is a word picked out of the dictionary, and the silo mentally is still strong in many places. 
Remember, this firm is about $$ and not about the people. Have that mindset and you will do just fine and properly get a promotion on the back of it.
(this review is related to technology and not the rest of the firm, which I'm sure is all ok)

summary: Good pay, nice building and the hot salad is not too bad either for £3.75, however...
advice: Trust your employees. Perhaps it would be better to do this after you get rid of some of them, but in my opinion, splitting tasks into so many parts in order to prevent somebody from screwing up is not a very efficient way of working; if you are worried about this, why did you hire them? It is no use E-mailling employees to tell them to feel empowered when you don't actually trust what they are doing.
pros: Citigroup is a large, well known company, so it is good to have something like this on your CV. Also, compared to other places where a programmer may work, Citi pays quite well and the work hours are not particularly demanding either; usually the floor I work on is empty around 5.30pm.
cons:
Things happen very slowly! There is a Virtual Request system which every process goes through, it is painfully slow, involves too many departments and requires too many signatures. The problem is there are too many steps required to do something small, and the departments which carry out these steps are sometimes very short of staff or short of staff who are actually able to do what is required.

This is perhaps a problem which affects many other companies, but basically, there are too many workers who are incompetent in their current roles accompanied by even worse managers who seem to think their department is a separate company and thus do not cooperate very well with other departments.

Also, remember that this is a bank, if you are looking for a challenging role which involves the implementation of some fairly new technology (as advertised by HR), look elsewhere. It can be a relaxing place to work, however, after a while, relaxing becomes boring and you may find yourself watching pointless training videos about Microsoft Office to pass the time.

pros: Very good pay, never met more friendly and helpful people in my life. I have never been happier and more valued as I am right now. Furthemore, I am only an intern, but given more responsiblity than normal employees. Citi is a place I can feel included and honored to be a part of!
cons: Only thing I would say is the hours. Obviously it is the part of the grind.

pros:
It is a truly global organisation so there are genuine opportunities to move departments and/or location.

I thought their systems were antiquated, but now I am working at a much smaller bank I realise Citi are pretty cutting edge in comparison (but definitely not perfect!)
cons:
A large amount of red tape, sometimes making it difficult to get your job done.

Salary package behind market rate.

Some departments within the bank are very "corporate" others are more relaxed, it's a lottery

Off shoring of many back office processes makes it difficult to get things done.

advice: Listen to staff and do not ignore members who would contribute significantly to team efforts, this may help in retaining staff.

Below par salary for graduates
