Overall toxic work environment that will make you evaluate the industry you are in and will not take responsibility for this

advice: listen to the needs of your employees. more parking options required at belfast location. career and goal tracking should be implemented more effectively with entry level employees.
pros: plenty of opportunities happening in belfast, hard work goes a long way and doesn't go unnoticed.  end of year bonus also a plus
cons: peak seasons means long hours, but if you're a hard worker you won't mint too much. belfast is a low cost location so salaries can be on the lower end, but if you have enough gumption to ask for more you'll get it!

advice: moving in the right direction. keep making sure all employees understand strategy of the bank. make feedback more frequent and specific on performance
pros: Global bank, opportunities to move internally, strong platform across numerous productions. good colleagues. strong industry experience in sector i work in - oil and gas
cons: pay is below street for my product. size leads to internal beurocracy, hard to get deals done sometimes. reputation remains tarnished.

summary:
Mix of Good and bad team, corporate banking is overworked and unsupported.
room to grow but a difficult road
advice: add TTS to corporate and get better trade people.
pros: Fairly good salary, global prospects but not easy to move between countries and roles ,global company with clear order
cons: Blackberry day and night, work not spread correctly , defentions of work and tasks between product and corporate banking unclear. no union, HR outsource for the higher end jobs

advice: Do not promote work/life balance and flexible working arrangements if managers are not willing to support.
pros: Great exposure on a global scale to a wide range of roles. Opportunity to develop understanding of an institutional bank based in Belfast.
cons: Long work hours, limited work/ life balance despite big promotion on flexibility. Depending on team / departure can be operating in silo, limited ability to move into other areas or gain promotion. Planning new initiatives don’t always appear to have taken into account implementation and change management strategies.

summary: Just another employee number lost in a sea of the brainwashed
advice: The rest of the world does not have the same working culture as the USA. Ensure your IT managers have a basic understanding of IT. Allow more flexible working, especially in virtual teams. Listen to your staff. If a whole team is complaining about a manger you MUST act. Not all good managers are good with people. This must be addressed
pros: Big firm, lots of great benefits, friendly staff, good social committee, free parking, good location, salary is competitive.
cons:
No matter what your position in the firm, you are just another employee, one of thousands across several regions. There is so much red tape and bureaucracy - more than any firm I've ever worked in previously. You need to raise requests to do absolutely everything / anything. 

Most of the Americans staff are always online and I get the impression that a lot of them have no life outside of work. Some of the management that I came across really are on a different level and have zero in common with their staff. They seem to be almost brain washed, constantly speaking in corporate language, and clinical to the last with the most tedious task or request. These managers also do very little to improve that situation with employees and some do not possess any interpersonal skills whatsoever. 

There was also zero training. We were given a booklet when I worked there to select training courses from and then informed 1 week later that there was nothing left in the budget! Then there’s e-mails. You will get 100’s if not 1000‘s per day. The Americans and especially the Indian employees love to e-mail constantly and keep you informed of things which don’t concern you, your team, or your region. This means every morning you spend 30+ minutes sorting (deleting) all of the rubbish e-mails. I think these e-mail offenders want to be seen to be doing something so constantly e-mailing is one way of doing that. Some of them even e-mail to tell you their daily schedule or to tell you that they will be back in 10 minutes as they have to go pick up the kids! – thanks for letting the 500+ people on all of those distribution lists know!  

You are also forced to go to regular town hall meetings where some big whig will fly in to give updates. I found this very frustrating as I was always busy and when I went to these town halls I was coming back to even more work as my entire team had to attend. The updates were normally extremely boring and most people spent the hour or hour and a half texting / surfing on their phones (if you were lucky to be sitting at the back) or staring into space. And guess who were the only ones to ask Qs?.... yup, other managers / senior managers.

My job description didn’t match the day to day aspects of the role itself and it was nowhere near as hands on as I was lead to believe at interview. The job was extremely silo’d and you find yourself doing the same thing day in, day out. Some people don’t mind this but it wasn’t for me. In some cases you are expected to be at your manager’s beck and call 24/7. In IT, On Call is often a requirement though this was not stressed to me at interview. On call payment was also not as much as promised.

My ex-boss was a real piece of work and no one in the team liked her at all, in fact 6 of us have left since January this year and most of the rest are looking for jobs at present. I don't think she ever smiled, she had a permanent scoul on her face, and if she passed you in the corridor she would never acknowledge you unless you were another senior manager or higher. She very rarely let us work from home - even though it was sold to us at interview how flexible Citi were and that working for a virtual team enabled us to WFH was available whenever we wanted. Not a chance. You were always quizzed why you wanted to excuse yourself for an hour to go to the doctors / dentist / personal issue and asked could you not reschedule outside working hours or at the weekend. It got to the stage where we just didn't tell her that we needed to leave for appointments, and we covered for each other if she came looking. She also wanted 1 on 1's every week. Mine was on the same day as our team meeting and a day after our wider team meeting, so I was regurgitating the same updates 3 times in just over 24 hours!. When I rescheduled my 1 on 1's to bi-weekly she marked me down in my appraisal for this even though it was 30 minutes wasted where I would be better working. She was rarely reachable as she would go to the opening of an envelope if it involved any possibility of networking in Citi. On MIM (Major Incident) calls she would dial in to announce her arrival, and then drop off and leave us to sort out the issue, taking all the glory afterwards and not handing out praise awards which every other manager seemed to do for any piece of work you completed. After my child was born she would not let me change my shift from 9-5 to 8-4 for a few weeks to help out at home with the new arrival despite the fact that there were other guys in the team who could adequately cover for each other. I think the quote was ‘I’ve no business need for anyone in the team to be in here at 8am’. She advised an ex colleague not to apply for an internal job at a higher salary grade as he wouldn’t get it – he applied and got it. She was the worst 'manager' I have ever had the misfortune of working for and anyone you ask about her, cannot stand her. 

A lot of jobs there in IT are now being out sourced to India but they are constantly hiring. You have to ask why there is such a high staff turnover. Citi to me was like being back at school and I could not wait to leave. I’ve also never met as many people who absolutely hate their jobs / managers, but still stay there. This is possibly due to the higher salaries that they pay.

This firm is a walking talking cliché of 'the office' and corporate culture that you will either love and thrive on, or detest and squirm in. Avoid.

advice: You are doing a great job by continually telling people it will get better, I dont envy you as the jobs you’re asking people to do are so grim.
pros: Excellent co-workers, my mangers were very understanding
cons:
Quite demoralising work, fairly average pay but not what I had applied for. Was reassured during recruitment process it would not be transactional, but thats all it was. Very long hours, equating to less than min wage. Not quite sure why anyone stays, labour turnover close to 30%, other teams higher. 
The jobs are just beyond what they are currently able to automate. 
Pay rises are minimal, promotions are total BS, given a worthless title and way more work - think 30 AVP’s on one floor, laughable really.

advice: Keep doing what you are doing.
pros: The global team spirit amazing. It feels like a small company, but works like the largest and most complex. Citi Never Sleeps, and with so much to do, we just don't want to. Love Mondays.
cons: Relatively speaking, I can't think of one. If there are any, they are the same as any global bank with a large audit department going through change, which is a constant.

advice: Take steps to understand what really drives the success of great teams, particularly with regards to employee self-empowerment and self ownership.
pros: Good offices, generally good compensation and benefits, good ethical standards with respect to diversity.  Good opportunities for internal mobility.
cons: Some upheaval with teams being reorganised too frequently.  Over-focus on metrics, which can cause teams to lose sight of potentially higher priorities that are less easily measurable.  Having to contact teams by raising ticketed requests, whereas you may just want to have a discussion before you figure out how to raise a relevant ticket.

advice: Need multicultural talents in middle eastern region as opposed to more of one particular type of employees hired over the years.
pros: International brand and a great group to be a part of.  Great internal training and certification programs provided for employees to take advantage of. Top management was accessible.
cons: Long working hours in my case. There are not many other cons that I can think of. I resigned due to family reasons.

advice: Keep linking overall company imperatives to individual team members goals, and reinforce communications about the connection to make everyone in the bank understand how they are supporting the overall company.
pros: Fantastic organisation and institution.  Dynamic.  Competitive compensation.  Fabulous career opportunities.  An intelligent culture and one that is positively challenging.
cons: Being such a large, global company one drawback for some will be the need to work remotely with colleagues around the world, often in a matrix structure.  However, many see this as an opportunity and enjoy this aspect of the environment.

advice: Improve on career path for employee
pros: Some groups are really good at technical stuff but many around are just very bad. Overall architecture of the Risk platform is going though sea changes so one might get good opportunity of working in C# and few other technologies.
cons: Pay is not at par with market, Some managers are absolutely non-technical and weak. Career growth is not enough for average employee apatite

summary: Complex structure with lots of overhead
pros: Coverage has an innate ability to sniff out new opportunities within the Citi footprint and client base. Aggressive when it comes to growing revenues and cutting costs. Good graduate programs, people generally make time to speak to each other.
cons: It is a massive bank and their matrix reporting creates a lot of layering, with many grey areas. It is a foundation for political games and manipulative people excel well. My department is not diverse and the culture is very much South Asian. MD in team cannot spell or make logical arguments.

summary: lots of knowledge gained in Citi
pros: you can learn a lot in citi. It has presence in 100+ countries and you can enrich your knowledge & experience. Very few banks have a global reach like Citi
cons: At present, Citi is in cost cutting mode and has reduced drastically its budget. So always there is a crunch about funding and there is no major investment spend for new projects apart from regulatory ones.

advice: No particular advice. It was a great experience, the training and talks were very insightful. I recommend the company to anyone who is interesting in the banking industry
pros: They really make you feel you are part of the company and they have a great company culture. They also organize nice summer events
cons: There were no particular downside. I guess it depends on the team and the people you are working for

summary: Double check to make sure that this is what you want...
advice: Treat your employees like human beings and not canon fodder...
pros:
- The presence of this company in Northern Ireland has definitely contributed to the economy.

- When you join as a graduate there are many young people at your level so there is good potential to make friends and join clubs (Gaelic Football and Toast Masters)

- If you join as a graduate they do have a good technology academy teaching you coding fundamentals and an overview of the various areas of the investment bank sector.
cons:
- Management had created a culture of blame amongst the teams, very often I would be on call with the team from Belfast and then another team off site. It was quite common for me to witness a snarling match between the two teams and just generally poor attitudes.

- I will say also that communication between teams was generally poor. There was never a sense of greater collaboration with the other sites. Everything seemed hostile all the time. 

- The managers in my team were very poor communicating or checking up on newly joined graduates in the team. Very rarely got a hello or a greeting out of any of them - was a "cold" environment to work in.

- Within my team there were a lot of blame games going on as well. No one was willing to show true leadership and take responsibility for when things went wrong.

- My experience at this organisation in general was that you were just a number for management. There was no sense of a team who wanted to achieve something together, was more like a team of managers trying to push their own agendas.

 - I will say also that due to the sure size of Citi and the many business sections it is divided into, you will feel like a very very small cog in a behemoth of a machine. You will probably specialise in a very small area, where you will tend to do the same repetitive task day in and day out. Flexibility to move across the organisation is possible but for me was restricted. You would probably have a chance to share and implement your ideas instead of obediently following one manager unchallenged.

- There was nearly nothing that was inspiring working in my team or this organisation. The most inspiring day for me was when I handed in my resignation and walked out the front door.

Note to potential applicant for Citi Belfast*
I am summing up my experience at Citi the best way that I can. As you can probably tell I do not think very highly of this organisation. I have heard other people enjoy it here but for the most part this company has a reputation for being a meat grinder (certainly during my time). If you do choose to apply for a role here I wish you all the best and pray that you do not have the same experience that I had. Good luck in your career and whatever path you choose.

Equipment
I was provided with a sub standard Chrome OS PC that wasn't fit for purpose so had to buy my own laptop which I received no reimbursement for. 

Team Structure
Again, working from home during a pandemic has its limitations for team building/co-operation however my experience at Citi was that teams were very disjointed with little crossover. There was no real efforts to keep the team in touch and team meetings were a rarity. 

Work/Life Balance
There was definitely a culture of not being away from your computer at all during the hours of work which was only exacerbated by having to message when you left the desk/went for lunch. Felt almost like you were back in school having to ask permission to leave your desk.

Management
From speaking to people in other teams at Citi, along with my own experience, it seems like managers at Citi are told to manage through thinly veiled threats and aggression. I found that my manager was as nice as nice when talking directly, full of praise and advice, however when there was any official requirements such as probation the story was very different. summary: So incredibly disappointed-hoping things take a turn
advice:
-Stop having the blind leading the blind
-Encourage a culture of support, instead of cut throat competition and CYA
-DO NOT put a person new to Citi in a subgroup responsible for a major project before you onboard them and they have a sense of stability.
-Be mindful that the first few months of starting at a new company are the most critical, this is where first impressions are formed and turnover happens. With that being said, you should not allow someone's initial opinion/experience upon starting to be silo'd within a team who could not give a ** about you or your success and will use you until it no longer benefits them
-Make psychological safety real, otherwise, it's just non performative which is worse than not having a policy on it at all
-If you could only have one subject in onboarding, it should be helping people navigate the networks within the organization and understand how the company works, what to expect and 100% clarity on role.
pros:
-Fast and efficient recruiting cycle-keep it moving quickly
-Excellent benefits
-WFH flexibility
-Decent starting pay
cons:
Non-existent onboarding-I was assigned 35-40 trainings on mostly things I had no context for. 
No orientation to Citi or the culture or any HR related things, had to figure everything out for myself-no-one seems to have the answer. 
The benefits center and IT are so incredibly inefficient; after months of trying to resolve a mistake the Benefits Center made, I gave up and just ate it.
Within my first couple of days, before I even had a chance to settle in and understand my role or establish a relationship with my manager, I was immediately thrown into a 3 person sub-team, which is largely what I am basing my review on. I realized how cut throat and bureaucratic it is. 
Instead of being supported and encouraged by the lead on the project, I had administrative tasks barked at me and things indirectly blamed on me-one of the worst examples of leadership I have ever witnessed!!! There were no intentions of guiding me or supporting me; instead this person set me up for failure and made sure they shifted blame when it was convenient. It became real clear that you have to over document and over communicate to protect yourself. 
I was made to feel incompetent for asking clarifying questions, I was accountable for things I had no control over, like getting executives to review and approve something before the deadline. Im trying to chase people that have never heard of me when my lead has been here over 20 years and can only tell me that they know just as much as I do. Its truly discouraging 
Every day feels like a corporate day labor job, no real role or identity, just an SOEID #.  In my short experience, I learned that people are not interested in your success at all, it’s 100% self preservation. I do not feel like I belong and I certainly do not feel psychologically safe and secure.
 
Additionally, the people I was assigned to work with have no idea about my skills and background, nor do they care. I've been a senior executive for a long time in other industries, but a VP at Citi is way different from a VP in other organizations. Here I am treated like a clerk... unless its a huge project, then I am solely responsible for its success, without having any real authority or decision making ability. I still don’t know what my job is but I do know they are not maximizing my skillset.
Every day, I feel insecure and the worst part is that the work itself is not challenging, in fact, I am capable of much more; it's the people and the way Citi operates that makes it difficult to work there. I haven't been a part of many companies where the culture and ways of working would be the number one reason for failure, not incompetence our unqualified people. I have actually came across a lot of smart people that are too stressed or busy to effectively transfer knowledge to new people. 

This experience has evoked a lot of negative emotions, but I am hopeful that things will change, provided I’m not stuck in this sub-team forever. I would really like to be successful here

advice: Streamline system or directory is needed that lets an employee know who to talk to / who is an SME POC for certain systems/tasks/processes. pros: Promotion opportunities are there but you have to have been in your current role for at least 1 year, Great management communication. I have been huge fans of all of my managers. Not much micromanagement, assuming you get done what needs to be done. Overtime is always available on my team, which is the ONLY reason the pay is competitive; without overtime, the turnover would be far higher than it already is. If we were limited to only our base pay and ~3% yearly raises, the average analyst could not keep up with inflation and COLA increases & would consistently look to move to firms with higher salaries. The overtime availability is the main anchor keeping the tip of the spear analysts in place. Work life balance is excellent, especially at Tampa due to having more employees than we can fit at the site. Tampa is only 2x/wk in office requirements whereas firmwide in NAM is 3x/wk. Jane Fraser is a cutting edge CEO and seems to realize that among the Big 5 Investment Banks, the firm with the most flexible work requirements will attract and keep the best talent. The flexible work requirements are another offset to Citi offering a lower base pay than competing firms; a vast majority of millennials would take a drastic pay cut at a firm with hybrid requirements over a firm offering a higher salary but a full RTO mandate
cons: Onboarding process takes a long time from when you get first interview to starting your first day. Have to be in your current role for at least 1 year to be eligible for promotion which has lead to very qualified team members not be able to get openings they deserved & were more experienced/qualified than outside hires who filled the positions. Base pay is lower than competing investment banks but at least on my team this is offset by overtime availability. Oftentimes it is challenging to find the right team that will have the right access to complete certain tasks; workaround processes are common. Some systems and standard operating procedures are antiquated and very manual, opening up higher possibliities for errors. Citi had/has to layoff 20k team members by 2026, that has to be a con although a solid portion of that figure is not filling open positions from natural attrition

Directors often cannot be trusted either, as the ones who survive are usually the "yes men/women" whose only concerns are staying off the list themselves or getting promoted at other's expense. It is one of the most toxic cultures I have ever witnessed at the workplace.

-There are ample opportunities for skill enhancement and career advancement within the team. Regular training sessions, skill-building workshops, and project involvement contribute to continuous learning and professional growth.

-The company acknowledges the importance of work-life balance and offers a flexible work schedule. This flexibility allows employees to manage their time effectively, accommodating personal commitments without compromising productivity. It fosters a sense of trust and autonomy among the team members, leading to higher job satisfaction and overall well-being.
cons:
-One of the significant drawbacks is the apparent disconnect between the higher management and the rest of the organization. Important decisions are sometimes made without considering the input or feedback from employees at lower levels. This lack of communication and alignment can lead to confusion and frustration among the workforce.

-While Citi offers a hybrid work model, mandating three days in the office can be restrictive for some employees. It may not align with everyone's preferences or individual circumstances, particularly those who thrive in a fully remote setup. More flexibility in this regard would accommodate diverse working styles and preferences.

-The office (Marynarska Office) infrastructure and amenities are somewhat lacking compared to industry standards. While the workspace is functional, it lacks certain modern facilities and comforts that could enhance the overall working environment. Investing in better facilities and amenities would improve employee satisfaction and well-being.

advice: Complete an ACTUAL pay equity review and invest in existing employees to ensure alignment with their correct compensation tertile to improve morale and reduce turnover. Offer internal employees comparable salaries to external candidates for promotional opportunities - and even lateral opportunities. Increase accountability of HRAs to HRBPS and HRDPs. The dynamic between the HRAs and HRBPs and HRDPs is elitist as it is currently designed, and I'm confident that won't be changed by senior management for many reasons. However, at least make it APPEAR as if the HRBPs and HRDPs have equal seats at the table and are not assistants to to the HRAs.
pros: Flexible work schedule, supportive coworkers
cons:
During my tenure, I encountered situations where I was increasingly tasked with justifying decisions made by upper management that posed ethical challenges and were difficult to explain, often without prior briefing. There was notable inconsistency between the messaging conveyed to employees and the realities unfolding behind the scenes. Furthermore, it was apparent that the internal advancement process adversely impacted existing employees, as they often required many years in-seat to reach even the mid to advanced tiers of their salary ranges, whereas new external hires were often approved to join at significantly higher salaries than their experienced veteran counterparts. The pay equity reviews conducted *almost* yearly often did not detect MAJOR discrepancies in pay for alarming disparities, and as such adequate funding was not received to properly remedy them. Kindly note I left Citi in summer 2024.
The work environment also saw a concerning number of employees taking leaves of absence due to mental health issues induced by work-related stress. My confidence in the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) program was completely undermined when the CEO and Chief DEI Officer failed to even mention the word 'Palestine' in internal communications, although had no issue mentioning the word 'Israel'. A firm cannot claim inclusivity when it effectively disregards the existence and rights of indigenous peoples.
Unless you are applying for a very senior management role externally, I would caution against considering employment at Citi.

summary: Dynamic place to work but stress
pros:
High chance that you will be working with colleagues coming from different parts of the globe fostering a diverse and dynamic environment. Work culture is very Western-oriented which means there is little chance of micromanaging (depending on the manager). 

You will gain exposure to many aspects of the bank, and the bank encourages you to pursue broad variety of career paths but you must meet high standards and expectations. Always put your best foot forward.
cons:
Poor support for work-life balance. While management makes an effort to reduce workload, this does not come to fruition, and burdensome/complicated policies/processes change often which adds stress. Given this, rendering overtime is the norm even without additional compensation for this.

Work culture can also get competitive and deadlines, assignments, and commitments are very strict. If you are not a fast-paced worker then you will likely be frowned upon.

There is mentorship but not as strong as I expected. Trainings are helpful but it does not really get you far ahead in your role as most of it will be learned through experience. To add, managers are often busy (in meetings) so you are expected to work (and figure things out) independently most of the time, which is suitbale for people who prefer to be individual contributors.

cons: Workload and Pressure: Like many other banks, Citibank's work environment can be demanding, especially in certain roles or during peak periods, leading to high levels of stress. Bureaucracy: Being a large organization, Citibank may have bureaucratic processes that can slow down decision-making and hinder efficiency in certain cases. Long Working Hours: Some positions at Citibank may require long working hours, which could impact work-life balance. Job Insecurity: The financial industry can be unpredictable, and Citibank, like any other bank, may face economic challenges leading to job uncertainties or restructuring. summary: Mediocre Experience at Citi: A Detailed Review
advice:
Grant HR Autonomy: Provide HR professionals with the authority and autonomy to address instances of workplace politics and favoritism impartially, ensuring that fair and equitable practices are upheld throughout the organization.

Implement Anti-Bias Training: Offer comprehensive training programs to HR personnel to equip them with the skills and knowledge necessary to identify and address biases effectively, fostering a culture of fairness and transparency.

Establish Clear Criteria for Recognition: Develop transparent criteria and mechanisms for attributing work credit, ensuring that individuals who consistently contribute to the company's success are duly recognized and rewarded for their efforts.

Foster Accountability: Hold managers and supervisors accountable for their decisions regarding work credit allocation, promoting a culture of accountability and fairness in performance evaluation processes.

Encourage Open Communication: Create avenues for employees to provide feedback and raise concerns related to work credit allocation and workplace politics, fostering a culture of openness and transparency within the organization.

By empowering HR professionals to address workplace politics and ensuring that work credit is attributed based on merit, companies like Citi can cultivate a more inclusive and supportive work environment where employees are motivated to give their best and contribute to the company's success.
pros: Thriving in Challenge: Embracing Quality Work Culture and New Tech Stack
cons:
"Cultivating a Dismal Experience: A Reflection on My Tenure at Citi"

Throughout my tenure at Citi, I encountered persistent challenges that significantly detracted from the overall experience. Despite dedicating considerable effort and contributing to the company, it became apparent that one's contributions did not directly correlate with financial benefits. Instead, it seemed that success was contingent upon ingratiating oneself with senior management, fostering a culture of favoritism and undermining meritocracy.

The toxic atmosphere within the Institutional Clients Group (ICG) fostered feelings of despondency and disillusionment among employees. This pervasive sense of negativity hindered productivity and led to a lack of focus on work tasks. The absence of motivation, particularly regarding gender diversity initiatives, compensation structures, and encouragement, further exacerbated these sentiments.

Efforts to address concerns and seek resolution proved futile, as avenues for communication and feedback appeared rigid and unyielding. Despite attempts to engage with relevant stakeholders, including HR business partners, the lack of receptiveness and flexibility within the management structure stifled progress. HR can't do anything if management is not supportive. Moreover, instances of credit misattribution and the appropriation of one's work for the advancement of others underscored systemic issues within the organization.

Regrettably, the absence of support and responsiveness from management eroded confidence in the efficacy of organizational processes and channels for recourse. Consequently, I would caution prospective employees to exercise thorough consideration and scrutiny before committing to joining the organization.

In light of these experiences, I advocate for a comprehensive evaluation of the organizational culture and practices within Citi to address systemic deficiencies and foster a more inclusive and supportive work environment.

advice: meet and talk with the teams under you. Citi has so many layers of management and it should not be that hard to do (to get the message upstream, VOE is a joke....). No one is happy here except senior VP's and directors because they get paid a lot and don't have to be a leader, they delegate everything and offer 0 leadership. No one likes to speak up and there is so much unhappiness! As I mentioned, I left on my own accord and was able to land a much higher paying role within weeks of looking. This was because I was treated poorly and I felt there was no impactful value coming form my isolated area of work. I brought this up multiple times only to be lied to. Is that really how you treat employees? wow.
pros: I would say there is some autonomy, the benefits are decent and everyone has a job title that sounds really great. In reality, there are really not many "pros" to working here after the honeymoon period is over.
cons:
1. culture is terrible, alienating and discriminating.
2. really horrible and rather lazy people are the ones you have to depend on for everything from on boarding to daily career tasks. There is no direction and no guidance on anything. Its a "throw it in your lap and figure it out" culture and if you cant figure it out then you have no value. You will have no resources that are dependable and people will literally not respond to emails or requests that imply any type of assistance.
3. Probably the most disappointing aspect: your manager or director will might have basic management skills but absolutely no leadership skills. This refers to the context of any type of crucial conversation to resolve any roadblocks that may occur. 
4. they will lie to you and blame someone else or hr. This happened to me when I requested to move teams three times.
5. they will move you without asking you and to a team that requires a different skill-set than you offer which ultimately sets you up to fail. Hence the lying part previously. This happened two times to me before I finally left to get a better and much higher paying job.
6. yearly salary increase was 1.25% for 2023/24. If that's not insulting, I don't know what is.
7. you will not get the opportunity to be involved in big projects and this impacts your performance score which impacts your compensation. I never scored low but all 3's which is average, any professional with 10+ years exp and a graduate degree is not average but does not get opportunity or inspiration to tap any potential.
8. I would not work here as you will not be nurtured by a good leader to grow professionally (and personally) unless you are in the "in crowd". If you are the type that puts your head down and does your work, you will get all 3's and a 1.25% raise yearly. Go somewhere else get treated better. Anywhere will treat you better than than this place.

advice: My advice for management would be in your collections department. If you see somebody who seems to be struggling emotionally like I did you know maybe try to be a little bit more aware of that. I had never worked in collections before I worked for Citi and I had no idea what to expect. And although the managers were more than understanding, and the company was great, and took care of me with FMLA and I was able to continue working there for the time I was until I found other employment I didn’t want to leave, but the job itself was just too taxing on me. If I had known, my medical conditions had developed because of the job itself it might’ve been different today been able to talk to somebody and deal with it the way in similar positions where people deal in high stress with other peoples pain whether it’s emotional or physical have to speak to therapy on a regular basis to see how they’re dealing with it and if they can continue the job. It was compounded because I didn’t know any of this, so on top of dealing with all of this I actually thought I was dying of something horrible like a brain tumor.  That part of it can be almost when you look back on it in the moment when I wake up at home and the last thing I remember is leaving for lunch and my wife is freaking out because it’s 11 o’clock at night but I got off work at 4 PM And management told her I left for lunch at 11 AM and I have no idea where I’ve been for last 12 hours. The kind of thing can really have a negative effect on all aspects of your life and I think in the situation if I’d been aware of the effects this kind of job can have on you like 911 operators and other people in positions that deal with people in turmoil I could’ve avoided a lot  of unnecessary doctors appointments and MRIs and CT scans if I had just known and been able to talk to somebody about it .
pros: Unlike a lot of companies who say they give a lot of care concerned towards their employees city really did stand up to the expectation they didn’t just say it because not long after starting my employment, there, I started to develop some sudden frightening medical conditions that caused a negative affect not just at home but my entire life including work and they were more than understanding. They helped me get on FLMA and most companies don’t even consider that for you within the first year and this was in the first few months, and after everything when I had to leave due to my medical conditions they were over understanding wanted me to stay and said I was always welcome to come back. They try to accommodate me in every way possible and it wasn’t their fault that they couldn’t accommodate me in a way that I can continue working with what was going on with me medically. As far as the managers and coworkers I have no complaints. I was lucky I had a great staff that I worked with my managers seemed genuinely concerned when I started to get sick and city is very good at giving praise and reward for good work so I got lots of certificates of awards for outstanding work performed, and that motivated me.
cons: As it turned out, although they tried in every way to accommodate my medical conditions, I started to develop once I started working there and we’re unable to part of the reason why was because it was the job that was causing my medical condition. I was working in collections And it is very hard when you care about every single person you are talking about to either have them attacking you and calling you a vulture or listening to people, screaming and crying constantly about their lives falling apart and they have no money and it breaks your heart. After a bit of time of literally hundreds of these kinds of calls a day and still trying to have to get money out of these people because I worked in the part of collections where they were 90 days or more past due. It was very very taxing on my emotional status and a part of that caused my Brain to put up a defense mechanism that caused sudden unpredictable, blackouts and loss of time. Which itself was terrifying. So what I initially feared was something horrible like a brain tumor simply turned out to be extreme over stress from not dealing with the constant either berating I got from the past due customers or the embassy I felt for way they were suffering. Especially from the ones who would do both scream at me and call me all the most horrible things in the world and then turn around and cry on the phone about all the horrible things that were going on in their lives and they didn’t have any money and it was hard enough. It’s hard to be a human being and hear that every five minutes 100 times a day and feel nothing. My advice for anybody who goes for any collections job make sure it is a company who cares about their employees like Citi does but if you are like me and you are very empathetic, it might not be the kind of position you want to do because you still have to get results to keep your job and I didn’t get awards because I didn’t get payments but the ones I did get came out a price that my body started to pay my mind and brain started to pay for it wasn’t worth it. If you do take this kind of position and you are on sensitive side to other peoples concerns, and suffering at the very least, seek some sort of therapy where you can talk to somebody talk through. There’s a lot of jobs where you have to deal with people and their personal problems and at the worst times in our life and it’s hard to deal with the only way to get through all that is to talk to somebody about it and find a way to compartmentalize all these people suffering. I hear it happens a lot with people in the medical industry or 911 operators and stuff like that you don’t think about that when you go into collections you think it’s just money but when you’re hearing it on the receiving end 100 times a day it’s a lot to take in and you realize this is not just about money. This is about peoples lives .

advice: Stop using sentiment as a metric. Sentiment is not supposed to be used that way - it’s intended to identify pain points in calls so that you can adjust your guidelines/policies, fix your website, fix your phone tree, etc - it’s not meant to be used for you to judge your employees because their clients are upset that certain areas of your company are faulty. In the same tangent about using sentiment as a metric, you’re discriminating against representatives that may be depressed or sad, or simply have deep/low/quiet voices naturally. Choose better applications to facilitate account management instead of (probably) cutting corners and saving every penny you can while making your agents suffer by using Sawgrass (an application that breaks all the time and/or doesn’t provide necessary info). Train management to identify the ACTUAL reason(s) agents are doing poorly instead of having them guess and provide incorrect feedback which results in zero improvement. Overhaul the Fraud department so customer service agents don’t get hung up on or hear silence when we call to warm transfer.
pros: Good amount of vacation/sick time. Offers remote work.
cons: Metrics are near impossible to meet - almost everybody on my team is constantly in the red(negative) for metrics, which affects potential raises, time off, etc. I personally know that some metrics are reported incorrectly because the automated metric capturing/reporting system will have errors intermittently which affects us regardless of whether it’s our fault or not. Managers are quick to blame us for shortcomings but unwilling to show us how to improve because there’s no time for coaching or meetings. Managers are not fully trained to tell us why we’re falling short - I was told, for months, that I was failing in a specific category because my call time was long, but, when my call time decreased enormously, my score in the aforementioned category did not improve, so I’m left clueless and punished because my manager can’t tell me what I actually need to improve on. The applications we rely on crash/break constantly. Teams/personnel are unaware, not fully educated on company policies, not trained correctly. Fraud department is unwilling to do their job. Metric capturing is used incorrectly so certain agents are discriminated against.

Hire some specialists!  Some tasks that should have dedicated, centralized focused staff are being outsourced to the same group of employees who are tapped to do EVERYTHING. So, superstars are getting burnt out and are leaving while some other employees get to coast.

Favoritism abounds and sucks - so many managing up suck at managing across, down, or with customers. Stop ranking employees against each other - especially when they do very different things. It's unfair and disheartening to learn that someone else of the same title and productivity level gets 3 times the bonus you do because their role is more central to that division.

summary: Sr. Data Analyst at Review: Unveiling Exceptional Insights and Analytical Excellence
pros: The remuneration package is notably favorable, reflective of industry standards and commensurate with the level of responsibility assumed. The workload is characterized by a manageable cadence, affording ample opportunity for meticulous attention to detail and comprehensive analysis. The spectrum of Associate Vice President positions is underscored by a discernible flexibility, enabling strategic maneuvering in alignment with individual career trajectories. Engaging with an expansive cohort of senior personnel augments a robust vantage point, fostering a panoramic understanding of the broader team dynamics at elevated echelons. Intervals of respite are inherently unmonitored, cultivating an atmosphere of autonomy and trust that valorizes one's self-regulation and well-being. The absence of temporal demarcations for ingress and egress engenders an environment that privileges productivity predicated on deliverables over strict temporal parameters.
cons: Depending on the composition of the team, the manager's demeanor can be egregiously unpleasant, manifesting a disposition that verges on the abhorrent. Despite committing substantial temporal resources and exerting oneself into the late hours, a disconcerting propensity exists for the manager to unearth perceived inadequacies, thereby rendering even diligent efforts inconsequential. Navigating the stratified hierarchy with circumspect discernment is imperative, as individuals at elevated echelons might camouflage their true intentions, adeptly manipulating unsuspecting colleagues for the surreptitious acquisition of information that could subsequently be wielded as a weapon of subjugation. Exercising vigilance is paramount, given the regrettable vulnerability that comes from naivety – a pitfall I encountered firsthand. The laptops supplied, regrettably, perform in a manner redolent of excrement, delivering a user experience characterized by unmitigated frustration. The paramount emphasis on security, while laudable in intent, begets a technological environment so constrictive that it precipitates a conspicuous deceleration in laptop functionality. Furthermore, the stringent security protocols preclude the concurrent use of multiple websites, culminating in a stifling user experience. The absence of extracurricular diversions within the professional domain engenders a state of perpetual ennui, ensuring that tedium pervades the entirety of the calendar year. For non-Polish speakers amidst a Polish-speaking cohort, anticipate pervasive exclusion from critical exchanges, thereby exacerbating a sense of isolation. This language barrier invariably becomes a crucible for Machiavellian office politics, wherein intrigues revolve unabashedly around linguistic disparities – a lamentable testament to the depths of interpersonal maneuvering.

summary: An almost OK place to work and learn
advice: Be fare with the team. If you get an HR complaint take them seriously rather than using HR as your pawns. Do a better job at recruiting/look for ways to have a diverse team without hiring based solely on race/sex. Retaining good minority employees is key, but don't keep the slackers/bad co workers. Each branch is different and has different niches so don't focus on doing the same thing just because you are told to. Voice of Employee Survey is done every year and they consistently fail to make changes based on it- their only goal is to have 100% participation.
pros: Citi is big so there are opportunities to transfer to different positions and locations. Good Rewards system in banking and credit cards. Nice incentive awards trips for top sales people, but now it changed to popularity contest after the Wells Fargo fiasco. Very good at promoting minorities If you want a salary increase then leave for a year and come back like I did. The base pay is better than 90% of the banks. If you get a good location you can coast easier. I learned a great deal about banking and sales I learned how to be more political
cons: Senior leaders have HR working as their puppets for retail banking. If you file a complaint it will get brushed under the rug. Back in the 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s Citi did a poor job promoting minorities. So now they hire based on race/ gender in order to meet a quota and pass up on much better candidates. The computer systems are antiquated. Wire transfers sent using a DOS based system. The computer systems often crash and are slow. They patched multiple systems together. I worked at Chase and it's so much easier to use. Audits are a nightmare and they come into a branch and can always find a reason to fail someone. Certain managers get preferential treatment where 1 manager gets promoted the other gets put on corrective action for the same situation. Citi has multiple silos where it's hard to transfer to different departments and managers don't often support moves. branch model is where private bankers and investment advisors and give little help to the team. They only hire members of wealth management team from outside banks (except the secretary role). Managers aren't eligible for overtime so they often get stuck doing the banker or teller job when short staffed. Senior leaders lead with fear. The stock hasn't bounced back since the 2008 bailout.

advice: Clean up communication. Overcommunicating isn't the fix all you think it is. Be clear, direct, and effective with your communication. Enforce it as a core value. Respect your employee's time. Stop scheduling meetings 6:30 or 7:00 am CST when you know the majority of people you mandate attendance from are in TX. If you're going to set monthly metrics, enforce them across departments. Don't enforce it for one when you know they depend on the work from another who doesn't have it enforced. On that note, stop moving the goal post and the measurements of success. 1 review takes more than 2 hours to complete and you'd know that if you spent 1 day in the shoes of those below you. Treat employees with respect. If an employee created a useful tool, don't take the work for it and assign to someone else. It breeds resentment and shows you play favorites On that note, stop with the nepotism. It is completely out of hand and you're about to lose so many good workers because of it. Training new people is expensive. Keep the ones you have by treating them with respect

Department head seems out of touch with the day to day, so much so, her monthly meetings are scheduled prior to regular working hours for 75% of those required to attend. They push for sustainability when the foundation is rocky at best . QC is under immense pressure to meet certain weekly/monthly goals but transaction management isn't and much of the time isn't helpful. Reviews will sit with them for weeks and when complaints are made, it's QC's fault for not sending follow up emails. The double standard is so bad, I'm routinely scared of losing my job on a whim. I wouldn't recommend the job to others and am actively trying to leave. It's not worth the mental health issues.

summary: Great place to learn and grow
advice: Citi can improve on providing new hires or colleagues who are transitioning to a new role a proper training or induction. Managers can also improve by encouraging employees in their team to collaborate with each other and to set up sessions where colleagues can teach their skills (or hacks) to others. Since the bank environment is so rigid, innovation and adaptation of new ideas can be challenging and often overlooked.
pros: Citi is a Global Bank. The Service Officer role allows you to meet colleagues from around the world virtually. You act as a liaison, between the banking team and the backoffice teams. You are in close contact to Investment Counselors, Bankers and Banker Associates. In this role you are able to learn about different financial products and how to implement them. If you are keen on learning about finance and banking, Citi has great specialists that are willing to share their knowledge. The role of a Service Officer requires a lot of organization skills. If you enjoy client facing roles, this is the job for you. You are in contact with Citi clients everyday. This job gives you the opportunity to showcase creative solutions to client's requests or issues. It is a well-payed job in the industry (at least for Mexico).
cons: The bank, as of today, is subject to Controls in several jurisdictions (US + Mexico). It is as bureaucratic as any bank. Employee development within a role is fast, but the possibility to change roles in a little amount of years are scarce. Normally another colleague has to change roles or leave the bank in order for new vacancies in the team to be available. The job involves high levels of stress (one has to find ways to manage this, outside of the workplace). Since the institution is so big, there are a lot of existing silos. There is no Onboarding Training in place for most of the new hires. You have to be proactive. The training each employee acquires is different; since you have to be self-taught. Or you have to look for mentors to teach you in their spare time (which can be difficult). As an employee, you are required to take a lot of trainings during your day (but you have to find the time to take them while multitasking).

summary: CPWM - We Turn Business Away At Any And All Cost!
advice: All of these problems I listed have created a terrible client experince. I honestly don't know why people would give us money with how long everything takes to get done here. At Citi, the company comes first, not the clients. I would suggest that all of upper management take a day to work as a CSA. After about an hour, they will realize a technological overhaul is the most important. It feels like Citi is so concerned with breaking rules that they are willing to turn business away. Our numbers were embarrassing this year and it's no surprise that there was such high advisor turn over. Update Netx360, concierge, eclipse and Salesforce to synergize. Get faster servers, allow for banking/brokerage systems to speak with each other. Automate account openings, less manual reviews and put more trust in sales.
pros: 1. Work-life balance 2. Compensation 3. Benefits 4. Brand name
cons: Citi Personal Wealth Management is a runaway train heading in the wrong direction with no conductor - disaster is imminent. In the CSA role, I was told I would be a "sales assistant." The interviewers made it sound similar to the responsibilities of an Internal Wholesaler for insurance carriers I.E. talking to potential clients on the phone, creating proposals, sending out marketing material, ETC... WRONG. In reality, CSA's are responsible for maneuvering Citi's endless interdepartmental bureaucracy on behalf of financial advisors. It is 100 percent an administrative role. You will be a workhorse to complete administrative tasks for up to 4 financial advisors that you may or may not ever meet in person. You won't have a clue how to do anything. Your middle-level manager may or may not ever learn your name. You will be dependent on a severely underqualified and understaffed Field Services team to support you. At this point, I rarely call them because 90 percent of the time they are wrong or don't follow through on the requested task at hand. Speaking of unhelpful departments, Supervisory (OSJ and RSO) completely run the show at Citi and I strongly believe their entire function is to turn business away at any and all cost. They make even the most basic task, such as a wire transfer or account maintenance, feel like you're running an uphill marathon. They are zero help. For example, say you're missing something in a complex account corporate account opening, instead of pointing out what you are missing - they will leave a note that says "call field services." Out of spite, I call them directly. Speaking of automation, there is absolutely zero at Citi. All reviews are done manually. Further - there's no kind of notification system for when a review is complete. You have to manually check everything. What year is it again? The technology in general is about 25 years behind our competitors. We use four different CRM systems that don't communicate with each other. They are all clunky and are about as user-friendly as a broken computer. Get used to frequent software crashes because Citi only pays for the minimal amount of bandwidth to keep servers operational. The most disheartening thing to me is that every employee, management included, is well aware of this laundry list of problems, and they just accept it. "Welcome to Citi," they say.

pros:
* great atmosphere, positive people all around, from top management down to the last person I’ve met (and I met hundreds, literally)

* amazingly complex and such a mess in many ways that it’s a challenge for me to always learn more and see more stuff that we could fix by using technology 

* if I come with an idea, most likely I’d be told to go for it and give it a try. I was never told “no!” which is quite surprising for such an American Corporate 

* great work-life balance. And generally speaking - what you give is what you get. You can “fade out” and just do your job, and that would be alright, but you can also go full-in and come with tons of drive and energy and do amazingly crazy stuff - up to you
cons:
* as said, American Corporate. And a financial one. Sometimes it seems not like red tape but red concrete. And the amount of training you got to complete (especially after initial onboarding) is crazy. But you get used to it and take it as part of life, just like dentist :)

* inability to use 3rd party tools in general and specifically cloud-based stuff, so say goodbye to hotjar, Slack, mixpanel, Google-everything (Gmail, Calendar, Mapd, etc.). This is due to security stuff but it makes the life of a product manager more challenging and sometimes damn frustrating.

It's because the NY'ers are afraid of losing their jobs so they keep job security by hoarding a lot of projects and promoting people differently. summary: Great People, Questionable Practices by Corporate
advice: Get rid of Jane Fraser, she is a former business consultant following the tradition of gutting businesses, cutting costs, underpaying employees, and sacrificing product quality in favor of stock price.
pros:
Excellent manager and coworkers, and largely everyone working in our area in branches were pleasant, hard-working people who cared genuinely about helping clients
Great first experience in banking, and the concierge position empowered me and gave me a clear path to how I could become a Personal Banker in the future
cons:
(As a pre-word, many of these points likely apply to many of the other major banking institutions in the US as well)
Corporate obviously cuts costs at every opportunity, and the current CEO's changes have driven many people, including senior employees with decades of experience at Citi, to other institutions. Branch employees were expected to work during the pandemic, often without a branch manager, but without pay increases, either to adjust for the risk of in-person work or even just an adjustment for overall inflation during COVID.
Cost cutting means that clients have seemed to not always come first in terms of corporate's priorities. The systems are heavily unreliable, with lots of incompatible technology that seldom seems to work. Corporate says the solution to everything is usually in the Source, which is the database referenced when helping customers. Often, the solution is not in the Source, and clients end up frustrated without many answers.
Citi Customer Service was always sending clients into the branch, saying that we could help them with things we had no control over. This is probably a result of miscommunication to the customer service representatives.
The customer satisfaction surveys don't make any sense. Employees are held to a standard based on "Net Promoters", which refers to people who score the service as a 10/10, or 100%. Each survey that is 9 or below counts as a 0% score, with 0 resulting in a negative percentage. Branches were judged based on the monthly average, but this would often not reflect our actual performance because lots of people just don't give 10s on principle. What this means is we provide great service, get recognized for our competence in the client's review in word, but a score of 9 counts as a 0 and we are punished (usually in the form of a negligible annual pay raise, with the justification of being an "under-performing" branch.

pros: The salary is decent that's all. No weekends no holidays.
cons: Their downfall is they don't train you properly and they expect you to pretty much take initiative in training yourself by asking questions etc. There isn't no real training. All teams do what they want. So you may get on a team that's real relaxed and allow you to do half a days even though there may be said to come in to office 3 days a week. Then another manager on another team may not be as relaxed they may say no you have to come in 3 days a week full office days. Also there training and what they want you to do is all over the place. Pretty your manager runs the show on your team. So what you see what everyone else do doesn't mean you will be allowed to do the same. They are a lil relaxed as far as time off kind of. If you are ok with being chained to a desk and figuring out how you make the rich even more richer than this the job for you. But to me the stress isn't worth the headache of staying. If you can find something else use this as a stepping stone and move on. But for some people it's the dream job. Also you have to use your own PTO to pay yourself on a holiday when we are off that's should be a company paid holiday smh. That chips away from our vacation PTO. My only real complaint is they don't prepare you for your job. You are winging it. And they get mad when you arent ahead like you should be because their training structure sucks. Also covid numbers is COVID rising and they still want us in office 3 days a week. And ppl are coming in office and getting sick. Also they dont pay you when your sick with covid. You have to pay yourself outta your pto. Most workers just work from home when they have covid even if you have symptoms! Which is crazy but ok.

summary: Citi can be a stable and comfortable place to work once you are there for a while.  But its soul is dead.
pros: There is a culture of mediocrity, bureaucracy and indifference at Citi.  That can mean a comfortable and somewhat relaxed work environment.  If one has some degree of competence and had a moderate amount of integrity about the work they do, they will be valued at Citi and their jobs will be quiet safe, routine and comfortable.  Many people love that, set their life priorities to be outside of the workplace and simply earn a living at Citi.  At Citi you don't rock the boat, you go with the flow, hunker down and do what you are told.  Very slowly but surely, if you are good at this, you will ascend up the command chain.  At times it gets very hectic, there are many "emergencies" to deal with whenever anything has to actually get done with expedience.  But in the end, I've never seen a missed deadline actually matter in my 6.5 years there.
cons: Compensation is mediocre at best.  Bonuses are nonexistent if your job doesn't bring actual profit to the firm in a direct way (trading, sales, etc).  Quality of benefits has dropped like a rock since 2007.  A lot of mediocre people at the firm, especially in middle management.  Can be very frustrating.  Very silo'ed, segregated environment.  People and groups first look at whether they can legitimately transfer work onto somebody else or have it not get done before looking at how to serve the client or project.  NOT A MERITOCRACY by any stretch of the imagination.  The best and brightest do NOT get ahead at Citi.

summary: Has been a great company to work for and hoping it will continue to be.
advice: Clean up the old stuff left undone all over the country and get out of the businesses that do not make sense.  Subprime is an area this company never should have gotten into so deeply.  Realize that the "one stop shop" is not what consumers want.  This has failed multiple times over the past 5-6 years.  Also, stop with the quirky ads and slogans.  "Citi Never Sleeps" describes the state of the company for sure.  We are acting like we are sleep deprived and unable to come up with, much less execute a cohesive strategy.  Stop the multiple layers of management reporting (having 2-3 matrix bosses).   Too many masters to serve with too many conflicting agendas.
pros: Has been very good for my personal growth as well as helping me reach goals I did not think possible professionally and financially.  They pay very well with a generous bonus program.  Benefits are top notch.
cons: Duplication of efforts across several areas within the businesses and technology.  Too many offices of 25 or less folks scattered across the country.  They have never completed many of the acquisitions they have made over the years.  This lead to many little "kingdoms" running on thier own with the title of "Citigroup" in name only.  I encounter different groups that were acquired years ago, but still consider Citigroup to be "them".   Conversely, there are several of the old school corporate types that still refer to the company as "The Bank" or "Citicorp".   News flash, this company is no longer just a bank nor is it Citicorp.

advice: You ask for ideas and what can make the job better or easier, then 99% of the time just say "We can't do that" (when it's obvious you could if you wanted to), or "That's not how we do things", which is the whole point of change anyway. Read the dozens of business articles out there on how micromanaging your employees creates a toxic work environment.
pros: Very good work-life balance. Mangers have little to no say in when you take time off. It's submitted to an entirely different department. If not to many people already requested time off, you get it. Benefits are great. Love the team I work with. Benefits are excellent.
cons: At least in this department. It's a swinging pendulum between "Get your production score up!" and "Slow down and get your quality score up!" Documentation on how to do your job is confusing and lacking, and changes regularly. Many times new policy procedures are mentioned in passing in the team Skype chat you must always have up or you will miss something. You must keep track of your time to the minute in 3 separate programs. One tracks your productivity time, one you have to manually enter start and stop times for anything and everything you do, 3rd one is for payroll purposes. If being micromanaged is your ideal work environment, this position is for you. Change is constant. Too much of "Oops! We told you to do it this way, but it was wrong. Do it this other way now, and redo everything you have already done. They constantly promote "Diversity and Inclusion", but only as it pertains to the latest buzz-trends. If you are of certain races or sexes, you aren't included in the "Support Communities."

pros: Good company.  Well compensated with great time-off and other benifits.  Work/Life balance seems to be important to the management and is greatly appreciated by the employees.  If you are looking for a place to settle in for a long career and are flexiable with switching groups from time to time, it can be a great place to work.   Other perks include a casual enviornment, and flexiable hours and the ability to work from home if necessary.  Most managers take the stance of as long as the work gets done, that's all that matters, so clock-watching by the managers isn't a big problem.
cons: Company is large to the point where it is sometimes hard to be noticed outside of 1 or 2 levels above your level.  Information regarding changes in the orginization or similar happenings are often poorly communicated to the employees.  It can be easy to get stuck in your current position and be overlooked for promotions and raises.  Ratings are given on a curve so this further inhibits the ability to get a raise or promotion unless you force their hand.  Obviously at this point in time (Feb 2009) it can be somewhat nerve-racking when your company is in the news every day, but I think if you are in the right group, there is a long term future at the company.

As far as the rest of this Citi site (I was promoted to this credit position, and was at Citi for a total of three years) there is an open floor plan, kind of a "good ol' boy" environment - so it was not welcoming to an introvert like me. Jobs (mostly back office) were moved from NYC to this location outside of Buffalo, then some of those jobs moved to India so there is always a feeling of "how long will my job actually be here?" (in other words, questionable job security - but this may be a Buffalo/Rust Belt thing more than anything else: the fear of losing a job). Beyond the VP level the % of women in leadership is <5%  (opportunities for women on the business side is better).  Also many departments are run by foreign nationals who mostly/only hire from their own ethnic group.  

Many ineffective managers continue to get promoted up the food chain.  Extremely political at the expense of good technology, best practises, and most efficient use of resources.

As company centralizes the technology and processes (a good thing) more and more scope and responsibilities are falling on the same shoulders--although has not been a significant pay increase or bonus in years. advice: Invest in your top people and foster growth in their career.
pros: Work-life balance is one of the best aspects of working for Citi, as they allow you to work from home and will work with you to adjust your hours if you have to deal with family commitments (depending on the team).  Working for a global bank is a good learning experience, and there are opportunities to interact with people from multiple continents on certain projects.  In technology, vendors know Citi is a huge contract, so you can get wined and dined, if you can make it through their sales pitch.  There is a 6% 401k match and the health plans are good, though a bit more expensive in recent years.
cons: Ever since the financial crash there has been a huge emphasis on expense reduction, which means employees (aside from the top echelon of management) are hard pressed to get travel reimbursement, or training approved.  In corporate, the annual adjustments and bonuses have been poor, and many see nothing come year end.  If you are an old timer who made your money in the good times, you can hang around and lead a relatively stress free existence collecting a fat check.  If you are younger and work at Citi for a while, you will have a hard time keeping up with inflation. cons: You're pretty much chained to your desk while on the clock.  They strictly monitor your time off the phone so don't get up to use the bathroom much.  The management doesn't have a clue as to what their employees are doing nor do they know correct procedure.  They monitor about 5 of your 2000+ calls each month so there is little feedback from them on what can be improved.  A lot of them also do not know bank policies.  I myself had a question about a particular policy which I took to my manager.  He gave me what he said was "the correct procedure".  I was discharged by his manager two weeks later.  My ex manager still has his job so incorrect procedure is still coming down the chain.  The turnover rate is also insane because people hate the job so much.  I went through 3 departments in training classes of 20 people.  Each training class I was in had about 2-3 survivors after one year on the job.

Regarding performance reviews... If you are working with people outside of Atlanta, these people have no input to how you are reviewed. Only people in Atlanta have input.

summary: It is a really big bank that values policy and procedure more than doing what is right for the client.
advice: Business Banking performance is driven by the need to book loans and win new clients. The credit culture at Citibank has to change to improve turnaround, get local credit authority, and demonstrate a commitment to the market.  For years the competition has used our inability to get anything done on a timely basis against us- and it is getting worse.  When you have employees who have been here for 20+ years saying that they have never seen it so bad- you have problems.
pros: Everyone is nice and there is opportunity for good training if you are interested in Commercial Credit and the analytical side. Best to get your training and some seasoning at Citibank and then leave to actually be able to put your skills to use.
cons:
Massive bureaucracy that drives the business. I would guess for every revenue producer there are 10 people who provide support.

Business Banking has an unyielding, unwavering , uncreative credit team that lives by it's rote interpretation of credit policy and target market restrictions. Morale in this segment is now worse than the dark days of the single digit stock price.  Highly rated performers are leaving in droves as they are unable to book loans- which is the primary driver of performance ratings. Can't book a loan- you go on performance plan. Nice way to motivate a team

pros: Benefits are relatively decent depending upon one's position. Middle-level jobs commonly offer better benefits than entry-level jobs, but this may be expected across competitors.
cons: Very minimal training for entry-level and mid-level positions. High stress environment and language barrier among peers makes the job tedious. Dealing with frustrated customers is possibly the worst element of working in the student loans customer service field for this particular company. (For example, it is impossible to truthfully promote CitiAssist student loans based upon Citi's poor business practices and policies. (i.e.: unemployed students - and there are plenty of them - receive little to no options for postponing and/or reducing payments immediately after graduation and while searching for employment). Dealing with frustrated consumers on an hourly basis is not for the weak of heart, or for those who understand the client perspective. Citibank expects loan reps to be cordial and remain calm and collected during these heated interactions. Management is not supportive of employees during this process, and simply fails to follow through on notifying the powers that be of consumer complaints. I was instructed to "ignore" angry consumers' complaints on numerous occasions but would go home to the family each night feeling like a snake and scoundrel for not offering consumers options, or at the very least sharing their true perspectives, requests, complaints, and suggestions with upper level management. Very challenging issues with poor, misguided management. Pay rate and annual compensation not worth the headache, in my personal opinion. Thick-skinned individuals seem to manage better, but I could only tolerate (and sleep peacefully at night) after a few months working here. Outsourcing of jobs a common complaint, also.

pros: Diversity and globality.  It is a business that is far reaching that allows one to explore a number of different businesses under one roof. cons: It is way too large.  As much as diversity and globality is a strength it is also a weakness. Micro-management is prevalent in some businesses. Some colleagues are amazing, others just don't care, and still others used to care but don't anymore. Massive layoffs the past few years have been terrible for morale. There's an underlying feeling that some of the goals in certain businesses are purposefully inflated so few can meet goal, let alone exceed goal, so then bonuses won't have to be paid. I've heard this from veteran sales people who were very successful for many years, but are suddenly "not making goal" anymore and placed on final notice. Strangely, there are also some people who do very little and get away with high compensation and outright laziness. Absolutely confounding.

summary: Citi is changing, cost cutting and has problems with employee moral.

However, there is no formal process in place to identify talent and groom it for future leadership roles with more responsibility.  This contributes to the generally low morale and high turnover.
