advice:
Quality of work should almost always be the primary focus for a company.

I had a coworker who was tasked with maybe two projects and when he couldn't do anything else he literally slept at his desk. Management was blind to it for years. He's actually fairly skilled and reliable but he slept or twiddled his thumbs because management just wanted him to occupy a seat for 8 hours a day. Ridiculous! Of course if I was him I'd seek out work when I'm caught up with my projects, but it can be tough because management never had a steady stream of projects. But they sure as heck wanted you to warm a seat in the meantime. How that makes any sense is beyond me. I understand being available for when people need you, but it's called being on call. 

Also there were times I had to remote in to my computer when out of state. Remoting requires updated Java, which is impossible to do on most public computers (library, hotels, etc) without an administrator password. On top of that most browsers are changing their defaults to disable Java and/or ActiveX. In other words, make sure you bring a laptop and test connecting ahead of time before considering working while away.

Also please consider updating your websites and applications to support newer browsers. Windows 10 is shipping with Edge now and I believe they no longer ship with even IE 11 installed. Which means any sites and apps which require them (most that I'm aware of) will not function in the future.

Consider using server blades to run virtual desktops for even your on site staff to cut down costs and make it easier to maintain. I swear half my coworkers are trading out parts on a quarterly basis.

Also thin apps may cut down on licensing costs. It will also allow even cheap laptops to run expensive processes off more than powerful enough servers.

Quit screen scraping! What a ridiculous process. Very error prone and inefficient. Start working with teams to pull data from files and datasets that are on mainframes. On that note, start giving your transactions IDs so when you submit washes and credits you can link it to the corresponding debit.

Seriously consider the benefits of switching to multithreaded applications and normalizing databases. There are so many inefficient processes and database designs that could be exponentially improved by a programmer who knows what they are doing.

advice: You need a separate quality department who's sole job is to score calls, or you need to have supervisors from another site score calls to eliminate the favoritism factor.  Rethink the "four principles" and come up with a call model that fits collections instead of making the same call model fit all lines of business.  Improve communication so that your employees can stay in compliance with state and federal laws.  Try hiring a competent IT department or at least staff them fully so they can keep equipment functioning.
pros:
Decent sick/vacation time
Casual office environment
Good coworkers.
Good work/life balance
Schedule flexibility
Plenty of job openings to move into advanced positions (to a point)
cons:
Communication in the company is non-existent.  There may be a change but we won't hear about it until a week later.  The company does not provide email or instant messaging, meaning all communication is by mouth.  Tech support is non-existent taking months to repair a small problem with a computer.   The new dialer system used is buggy and half the features do not work requiring extensive workarounds.  

In collections, they have a unrealistic call model that frustrates customers as they are asked why they are late every time they are contacted (every 3 days), as well as about a million other questions.  The emphasis is no longer on money collected but is now on call quality, which would be fine if the calls were not scored where even a small mistake completely fails you.   There is no translation line meaning customers who do not speak english or spanish are out of luck.

Supervisors say they will be "working closely with you" then will meet with you once during the month.  There is a great difference in the amount of support and motivation depending on who your supervisor is.  When you find out the name of your supervisor and the other sup's say "I'm sorry" there is a problem.  You will find random things on your score card that are not relevant or are completely false.

If I ever worked overtime it was indeed to stay on par with my case load, but after some time on the floor, I stopped working overtime.  Not because I couldn't, but because I didn't need to.  They're some analysts that work overtime, but that's because they're not very good or because they're how I was starting out; they want to better themselves.  Also, I'm not sure where people are getting off by stating we don't get overtime?? I got paid time and a half for ALL overtime I worked.  I actually loved those weeks when I worked overtime because my paychecks were so huge come the following week.  It baffles me at how many negative reviews people have left, which ultimately scare people away from the job, or frighten people new to the job. I love my job and glad that I ignored all the terrible other reviews that are on this website.  The negative reviews are probably from people who only give 50% effort or were just terrible at their job.  Just remember, anything worth doing is worth overdoing.

summary: Play their game... or get out!
advice:
Upper management- make sure that the reps are the #1 value of the business. If reps are #1 then they will feel better about the company they work for and that will show in the calls. We want to feel valued.
Reps- make your customers #1
Get rid of the WWW score card in collections- it's great for customer service but doesn't work for collections.  Pushing reps to go through this score card is outragious. 
Increasing the requirements to bonus while reps are not meeting all standards currently is just wrong. Stop making it harder in effort to save money by removing the incentive to the rep. We have families and bills and we rely on our incentive.  
Never again change the incentive metric without making sure the system is calulating correctly 100% of the time.
pros:
Great people, very friendly place to work. 
Vacation and personal time bank is well above other companies. 
Benefits are great and include short term disability paid at 100% for some time (depending on seniority). 
Some managers allow you to flex your time to take care of personal issues without using your vacation or sick time.
cons:
Working for this call center is like high school, you get promoted for knowing and being friends with managers. Tons of favortism. You can bypass this by applying for a TAP position which is a training program for those wanting to be managers. I believe its a 2 year program. 

Bonus/incentive is iffy. They allow managers to have disgretion if you get your bonus- even if you met all standards and were a top performer. They can take it away for petty things like a disagreement with your manager earlier in the month. 

Citi has an unrealistic expectation of how collectors talk to customers and has a very confusing scoring card for the call. There is no script to go by. You have to ask many many questions about what happened to them financially to get them behind, where are they now financially, and when do they think the situation will change and include dates. Since we call the same customer every 4 days, these same questions have to be asked again, even if we know and can see the answers from the last call. This just upsets customers and makes our job harder.  

Incentive metrics are always changing and getting harder and harder to make. Unachivable at times for many reps.  

Communication is horrible all around. It is very hard to know what is going on within the site. Some reps don't have emails to get communication. Changes to policies happen without notification/training (many times the communication isn't passed to reps). If a change is made and you are not there that day, you may never know of the change. Sometimes these are big changes that will prevent you from passing your calls- thus leading to your bonus being revoked. 

Training is minimal because there is not a active training system to prepair you for real calls. You don't know what you are doing until you have to hit the floor and have to figure it out on your own. Training for calls consists of powerpoint slide shows, not an active training system. You also get to sit and listen to reps but most will not allow you to touch the system because it will effect their stats. Thankfully, reps understand this because they have been there, and are always willing to help out the new hire once they get to the floor.    

Lots of FDCPA violations all around because the auto dialing system doesn't work very well. Making changes to make sure we are in compliance has taken years (3+ at this site).  They are still working on fixing it!!! Changes like this take forever and as a rep I really can not understand why. 

HR (on site) is substandard. They refer you to a 1 800 # for everything and can not explain to you issues about benefits, pay, leave, or anything else for that matter. They are there for hiring, firing, and investigating personel issues. When you work in a call center the last thing you want to do is call another call center. LOL

You may not be passionate about the work you're asked to do, but in my opinion Citi DOES take care of their employees and do hire people who are friendly, caring, and enjoy helping others. Their pay may not be the best, but you get benefits from day 1, overtime is readily available, and you get a lot of time off, as well as bonuses for working nights or on weekends, full meals for working holidays, etc. I think they make up for it.
cons: It is a financial institution, so you constantly have to make decisions that are unfair for the client to benefit the business and some information you are asked to give can be misleading, especially when you are asked to cover up flaws in Citi policy and put the fault on someone else. Many times a client will be impacted due to a bank error and we will do nothing to fix it. We manage risk in my department, so closing accounts and decreasing credit. We don't take the customer's situation into account at all - it's purely numbers, and little sympathy is given. summary: Bureaucratic Beast of Company Which Does Not Value Employees
advice: I don't know what to say to upper management. The best manager I've ever worked for was a senior manager but I'm quite sad to say they were the exception rather than the rule. Citi needs not more managers... but of the managers they have (they could probably do with fewer) they need to be insistent upon the managers walking the walk, instead of merely talking the talk. In many ways dealing with management is like dealing with politicians, all of them saying what they think people want to hear, but few of them meaning it.
pros: If you are someone who can "work" the system. If you are a younger worker, if you are a man, if you are not a minority, if you are not disabled, you /might/ be able to work your way up to a more or less livable wage.
cons: Very poor work-life balance.  In the almost 9 years I worked for a Citi site  /no/ women were promoted to higher management positions... none. Although men with less experience, less education, who fell into the magical zone of 25-35 years of age, white, adhering overwhelmingly to a particular religious preference were promoted and mentored. The HR department saw employee concerns as bothersome (with some notable exceptions). Senior management excelled at talking the talk, few actually walked the walk (with a few exceptional and notable examples... of whom there has been no equal).  Merit pay is really not merit pay. Senior management decides based upon budget how many can receive top evaluations that merit pay increases. In a department that employs say 100 people this can mean that only a handful can obtain a score to merit an increase, regardless of whether their performance merits one or not. They start with what the department will receive in terms of budget and then they work their numbers from there. One poor manager can truly mess up an employee's life. Senior managers express the view that employee benefits are "given" to employees rather than earned compensation. Bureaucracy is be all, end all, to the point where attempts at quality control reviews earned violation warnings retroactive to the employees being notified of policy changes on call handling, and even created a circumstance where employees could be coached on a "high risk" call, but the employees were told they had to sign they had reviewed the call handling with their manager, but they were not permitted to see or to understand what the high-risk factor was, to listen to the call, or to know any of the reasons why (or to even be able to review what was written on the reverse side of the document presented for their signature). If an employee balked or raised questions about these sorts of practices, they risked being labeled as "difficult." Older and longer term employees would have goal posts for performance changed in apparent move by management to rid the company of more highly compensated longer term employees in favor of younger, newer hires (even giving newer hires different performance goals to meet for call handling).

advice: Make sure to hire people who don't just bluff their way through an interview, but are actually competent (for example, as BI project leaders, they should have at least a general idea of the basic components of a BI project). summary: Great company to build out your career - but a legacy institution.
advice:
Let go off some control: Empower your people: top-down decision making is killing this amazing company. You will not be able to move fast enough to keep up (much less outpace) the more nimble competitors in the market. 

Be transparent. Most people can get on board with big change if you would be more transparent and admit when things aren’t working - such as when you bring a senior leader on board who clearly isn’t what the bank needs, or when a major project becomes irrelevant. Don’t fear failure - people respect you more when you embrace errors and take a ‘test and learn’ strategy.

Get bad managers out. Stop promoting people into management who have zero interest in developing others. Throughout my career across various products here (and in my previous company), I continuously saw bad managers staying in their seat, mostly not because they were bad people (quite the contrary), but because they did not have real managerial skills (and no interest in developing others), so they created toxic environments for their teams. I don’t think manager training is effective if people you are promoting don’t want to be managers - try selecting good managers instead.
pros:
-The people. Some of the smartest, most driven individuals who care deeply about the work, and the culture is quite open: people seldom turn down a request for a personal meeting and they are generous with opening up the network to you. So this makes a huge company feel like a small place, which is amazing. Also, people are genuinely kind and empathetic as part of our culture, compared to a place like GS.
-The work. Complex, rich challenges to tackle in all areas from talent to new product development to client experience and innovation, and really smart people you can tap to address those challenges - if you’re bored here, you’re not pushing yourself and you’re probably in your personal ‘comfort zone’. Great intellectual stimulation for those seeking that, and I found that in spades in the business.
-The global reach. Citi has been in many countries for 100+ years, so the relationships with global partners run deep. Few companies can match that know how and this global connectivity is an undeniable competitive advantage vis-à-vis our competitors.
-Benefits. Citi doesn’t pay at top of the market, but the other benefits are very competitive - including paid paternity leave, mental health benefits, and a variety of employee support programs.
-Culture. Always depends on your manager and where in the business you work, but generally trends towards more family orientation and flexibility and work life balance. With new push to the “CitiWorks” model (no one has offices, open floor plan seating, etc.), more people work from home at least 1x week, which means company is moving in the right direction. Also, a massive focus on pay equity, diversity, etc. are huge plus.
cons:
-Culture. Yes, there is a less bright side: While people are open, there is  poor change management capability (especially at the senior exec levels) so constant change by mandate is the norm - re-org after re-org and relentless cost-cutting measures and lay offs are the BAU... the result is heavy attrition of talented people and burnout for those who stay.
-Internal mobility. While Citi historically prides itself as a great place to build global talent, the internal recruiting and mobility process is currently broken at best. Jobs often don’t go to most qualified candidates (it’s who you know - the employee engagement survey points to this), the process of applying for a new job internally usually takes several months (and there is lack of transparency/feedback in process, etc.) and if you have aspirations to move internationally, you’re pretty much on your own moving yourself/figuring it out unless you are an MD.
-Slow to change. It’s a 200 year old bank, and the resistance to change runs deep. It is frustrating to see so many people with great ideas and those ideas getting dying in the vine constantly because: 1) key decisions are almost always made by senior leaders (meaning change leaders lower in the hierarchy are disempowered) , 2) company lacks the infrastructure to drive change: poor technology/productivity platforms, procurement processes are impossibly slow, etc. and 3) fear of failure - lots of saving face goes on, creating an environment where failure and experimentation are not welcome, therefore - innovation is stunted.

cons:
Business/Market State:

I worked at Citi Commercial for 4 years it was truly a growing experience and showed me the true nature of massive corporate environments. I wouldn't take it back but there are some fatal business faults that this company gets away with due to the monopolistic nature of this department. Innovation, Competition, and Product investment are "too much cost and effort" Likely due to Citi commanding complete market share control compared to other banks. The technology stack suffers and is trapped in a Pre-Y2K mindset.

MASSIVE TECH DEBT. 

Workforce Labor Relations:

If I had a dollar for every gifted mind I met at this company that's talents were squandered I would be rich. This company sets you up for failure bluntly you have to be a strong person to be able to handle the rampant understaffing and soul-crushing lack of morale. The management in my experience is robotic and only worries about their bottom line. When I was on the phones producing 10% of the SLA I was a favorite. The second I became a squeaky wheel revealing the massive technical debt they had I needed to be eliminated. 

Group cohesion is not cultivated and there is no sense of teamwork. You will get blamed for other departments' problems and people's mistakes. There is a huge throw-them under-the-bus/fall guy mentality. If you use HR that's it your done. IF managers spent half the time they did on cracking down on workers, building team morale and motivation maybe their products wouldn't suffer so greatly. Write-ups are for arbitrary made-up reasons involving 5 min breaks  running their shop like Bezos warehouses, instead of actually getting issues resolved. Stop fighting with your workers do your job and fix the platform.

After you fix 75% of their issues, carrying a dead website so much that the tech teams want to hire you they will use office politics and a general disdain to kill your career. 

Citi employees need to stand up together and reject these toxic relations with management. 

Management & Outlook:

Ive stated the problems above. If management doesnt get with the times I can't say I have a positive outlook. It seems like no matter what they default back to their same problem state. HIRE PEOPLE. There are smaller shops with a bigger staff. The levels you staff at are insane. Stop doing the bare minimum.

advice: Train your managers. Cut out the cancers. There is no opportunity for advancement. Managers only care about their bonuses and will lie and manipulate metrics so they get their's but staff get nothing. Racism, misogyny and ageism are rampant. I sat right next to my manager's office and could hear every conversation that took place. I once heard her tell another manager that a high-performing person on our team would never be promoted because "there's too many blacks already." Cliques abound. As an older employee, I especially felt the brunt of ageism and was told by my manager I would never progress because I was considered old. My manager once mocked me and said I was "older than (her) grandpa." Your big mistake. As a former C-suite executive who needed a health plan and wanted to continue to grow retirement savings, I was more than happy to work hard and contribute above and beyond. I could have brought so much more to the table but your imbedded biases, unrealistic work expectations (metrics and no PTO) made me give up.

cons: There is so much wrong with Citi at the customer service level it would take a book to tell it all. PTO is never approved - I went more than a year with only three days off and then lost 12 PTO days under "use it or lose it." Management only cares about themselves and their bonuses. Bonuses for regular reps are almost impossible to achieve. You always "just missed" meeting bonus metrics. My personal manager openly mocked team members in team meetings for their single parent status, illness or older age. Manager often would mock what we were paid by saying fast food workers made more than we did and then ask what we thought about that and would wait for a response. I once received an annual raise of 7 cents per hour following an annual review where I was rated as exceeds expectations. When I expressed very polite astonishment at such a small increase, my manager told me I was ungrateful and unprofessional. This was my final job in a 45-year career, including part time jobs in high school and college. This job was the worst job I ever held considering I previously had jobs in HS and college like busboy, pizza maker, parking lot attendant and cold calling sales. Citi has a new CEO and was forced by covid to reevaluate its pay and treatment of employees. Former coworkers tell me it has improved and the company did ask me to return but I do not trust them based on my four-year experience with them.

summary: Stimulating, High-Paced, Dedicated Employees Driven Primarily By Fear
advice: You are extremely shrewd and calculating in understanding that the current economic environment gives you the latitude to be hard on employees and not compensate them - particularly in the O&T side of the business.  2012 will be the year of "Client Excellence".  But what will you do to foster employee excellence?  How well do you expect an atmosphere of fear to drive positive behaviors with clients?
pros:
-Number of vacation days.  It's how they compensate for poor compensation, but if you take all of the time you are allowed you will be buried in work and buried by your peers.  In effect, you pay for taking time off.
-Strong institutional industry knowledge in older colleagues who have stayed with the company because they are vested in the old corporate pension plan most of us do not have.
-TARP funds are now paid back to the US Treasury - with interest.
-Great place to build foundational experience, then export.
-Global presence allows you to network around the world.
cons:
-Terrible pay relative to the industry and marketplace.  HR and corporate execs just flat-out lie about performing "extensive market analysis" to determine pay, and "driving a culture of meritocracy" and 'equitable pay practices".  They don't even believe their own lies, as it is common place for managers to apologize to their employees at year-end compensation and performance review discussions for the compensation decisions that they themselves are not even allowed to make.  Managers are "coached" to not do this, but they do it anyway because they're human beings and feel ashamed of what they are handing the employee after driving them so hard in an environment of constant fear.  Worse, with the miracle of social networking they can't even hide the lies anymore.  You can see instant (and constant) up-to-date picture proof of how well your even lower performing peers live, party, vacation, and spend.  Yes, these are the very same lower-performing peers who constantly post status updates to their Facebook page while everyone else is working.   The company just can't lie anymore and have us believe it.  But, the compensation decisions are being made by people so detached from technology and social media, that they have no clue that everyone is proclaiming:  "The Emperor Has No Clothes".  So, how does the company respond?  Coming in late 2011-2012:  The Corporate Social Media Policy.   Control the message.   
 
-The company severely cut back recognition programs in the economic downturn.  Responding to negative internal feedback from employees, they've now announced that you can print your own service anniversary certificates.   Now everyone can recognize themselves on their own company anniversary date by walking over to the printer to retrieve their reward.  You seriously could not make this up...even if you were a writer on "The Office" writing staff.  A complete disconnect between the employees, and the well compensated and highly rewarded executives who approved the program.

-The system of force ranking employees top to bottom pits employees against each other and drives all of the wrong behaviors at a time the company desperately needs people to work together.

-The company, through executive and PAC contributions, has historically supported politicians that turn around and do everything in their power to regulate and destroy our industry once elected.  The 2012 election cycle will allow us to see if they have learned their lesson.

summary: Good place to work but might not have enough challenges

Great place to start a career. Good regular 40-hour work weeks.

Some days seemed really long and just sat at my computer not doing anything.

pros: If you're willing to put the work in, you have endless opportunity. summary: Massive scale, enormous business opportunities, mired in mediocrity.

advice: Make your employees feel appreciated by giving them at least a cost of living wage increase each year. Frozen salaries just don't cut it. Don't take your employees for granted. pros: Good people, decent salary, decent benefits. Ability to work remotely occasionaly. On site gym, ATM, cafeteria.
cons: Frozen salary for 2 years. Huge benefit cost increase. Overtime occasionaly required, but that is the norm for any IT job.

advice: You have some incredibly valuable talent  in your numbers, and with the proper dedication to nurturing the fullest growth of your rank-and-file today, you stand a great chance of securing a brighter tomorrow.

cons: In the conflict between build the bank and run the bank, which should really be no conflict at all, thought leadership on running the bank often stands in peril of taking a back seat.

Mobility

summary: Learned a lot - would recommend the Investment Banking Analyst program

summary: Great stepping stone to where you really want to end up
advice:
-Improve your systems (Taking pride in 200 years of service, but having nothing to show for it is sad)
-Redesign / Rebrand products and services to be more competitive with those across the street
pros:
Great initial salary, training was very professional and pretty accurate in terms of what's faced in the field.  Benefits are very quality, and most coverage kicks in on day 1 of work which is nice.  Management is easy to talk to, and work with and have been very supportive since day 1 as well.

-Looks great on a resume.  Use it to your advantage.  I was able to get a better / more quality job that I enjoy going to.
cons:
-Computer systems are ancient (slow).
-What I thought was an international bank is so segmented and cutoff that it seems like many different companies strung together.  There is really no communication between the different countries, and even worse, the different markets within the United States sometimes.  
-Also, it's very hard to get ahold of departments such as our Credit Card department, which is one of the biggest reasons customers choose to walk in the door.  Very embarrassing to get transferred to 4 different departments around the world, just to find out something simple about a credit card for a customer.  
-Incentive / bonus plan is well thought out, but not very attainable.

-PRODUCTS- Warning :  (You will feel like a used car salesman working here) 

-Unfortunately, the products offered (other than some of the credit cards) are not very competitive to what's offered across the street.  This makes the sales process that much harder when you know it's not the best for the customer. 

-Goals-

I understand there will always be a goal required in a sales based environment, but when I'm asked to call my friends and family in order to get accounts to meet a certain deadline, that's just wrong.  I wouldn't push my friends and family to get involved with a bank that cares more about numbers than it does quality.  If they were able to rebrand and redesign some of our products, we could have people walking in rather than us dragging people in.  

In closing, this is a great job to use as a stepping stone to something more beneficial.  The growth as a personal banker will just lead to more headaches if you're going towards the manager role.

summary: It was a call center, what more is there to say?
advice: Management was actually pretty great, you were able to view them/talk to them like normal people.
pros: There is opportunity to "climb the ladder".  Pay, benefits, and perks were pretty good.  I was also able to network & meet a lot of new people.
cons: Citi is big on laying off entire departments, then moving that department to another location where they can hire all new people to do the same job for less.  Make sense financially, but what a horrible way to treat your employees.

advice:
There would be no harm at all in having two days off together, as an available shift option.  One day need not be a weekend day.  I've worked where people could have Tues-Wed off, etc.  You would have fewer sicknesses and burn out if this was implemented.  

Center supervisors need to be aware of the particular practices and rules of their manager staff, and take complaints seriously, especially from diligent, experienced workers.  

Scoring of calls must be of "real world" substantial points.   Agents should not be abusive to callers, but a successful call is one that leaves the client willing to talk with us again, even if they are delinquent, or resolves an issue for either the client or the bank, and follows the legal procedures or bank procedures appropriately.  

Anything that comes between me and my work is a problem for me, and should be a problem for my manager.  Massive, ongoing, constant dialer issues must be addressed.  A manager's "special project" that results in special scheduling or extra work for already-overloaded agents should not be allowed.  Broken computers or programs that freeze should be removed and replaced.

If this has not been done> implement a plan by which time off is accrued per pay period, in addition to a certain number amount sick time off available to start.  Do not punish or accuse workers who try to ration that time by taking half a day off, etc.  This will reward long-time employees and reduce turn-over as they will have a reason to stay longer.  You will not have sick employees dragging around, spreading sickness, at the end of the year when their time is used up, either.

Scoreing l
pros: Most supervisors are paying attention and do their jobs well.  Promotion is possible if you do good work.  Pay is acceptable, we had a pay freeze, then some small incremental raises.  This was after the Crash of 2008.  Training was good.
cons:
No one is allowed two days off together, except supervisors.  Promotion is often the result of kissing butt, resulting in some very poor supervisors.  

Time off can be hard to get approved, and you are given a very small "bank" at the beginning of your hire, and the beginning of the year, from which you are to draw all of your absences and time off.  I would be sick, and come in after half a day off, or leave after a few hours to save my time, and be talked to about how I must not really be sick, if I didn't take a full day.  When I started taking a full day instead, I quickly depleted the bank, so it was a catch-022.  Yet, I was also talked-to about coming to work sick, since I could pass it along, and should stay home if I was ill.

Another issue was the call scoring.  A new metric was introduced that had everyone in the center failing -- literally everyone.  It was, and still may be, very much based in the OPINION of the listener, on such things as, "did you establish a relationship with the caller" and such wishy-washy points that allowed managers to trash the employees they didn't like.  I was an award-winning employee, for my call quality, and could barely pass, occasionally.  Most people in my section had failed, failed failed, despite being conscientious long-term, experienced employees, many who had almost never failed a call scoring.  One was failed for "hitting all the points, but not in the right order." 

The order of the score sheet had never been brought up to anyone else I talked to about her review, and my passing calls were often not "in order" of the score sheet requirements.  Calls just don't flow by script, and in fact, we could be dinged for sounding like we were following a script.  Another catch-22 for her.   I watched people with 12-20 years with Citi quit or retire, because they suddenly could not pass a call, and many were crushed, would be in tears.  I hope this scoring system has been abandoned.

The list of items on the score list was enormous.  One of the agents printed it out as points to follow, on calls, and there were more than 20 items on it.  But calls over 20 minutes long would not be scored (too long for the managers to listen to) and those would of course be the calls that all points could have been met on...

Another supervisor was fired, while I was in that section, for abuse.  However, it had taken a year of complaints by various employees.  Again, I saw employees in tears, and crushed, after being with him, having been called stupid, and verbally berated in an entirely unprofessional and unacceptable way. Such complaints should have been taken seriously much sooner.

Dialer is run out of Kansas City (or was) and often started repeating, or sending us other inappropriate calls.  This was constant and rarely addressed, and on a Saturday, could not be addressed at all.  It is frustrating to re-call people you just talked with, and have to hang up on all of them, because no one in Kansas City worked on Saturday.  This was NOT an uncommon issue.

pros: Been with Citi for over a decade. In that time I've seen my skill set expanded, my responsibilities grow and have met colleagues that have since become friends.
cons: 9 months after being hired, pension was done away with. 3 years in, took a 5% pay cut. 5 years started seeing mass lay offs in the Northeast. Eventually talent and institutional wisdom was lost.

advice: Don't concentrate analytics is one location, listen to employees and get rid of toxic managers.

The incentive pay was adjusted every 12 months , to make it harder to make anything extra . Treat you just like a number .

cons: Only 18 PTO days and not very good benefits. Dental insurance is expensive. Medical insurance has really high deductible and no copay options.

advice: Take care of the employees, give more respect to them
pros: Big bank, always can find some department that you might be interested in working in.Working there used to be about the customers and employees. The merger with Travelers turned it into the mess it is in now. Now it is all about senior management and how much money everyone in the company could make for them. It has become a very cut-throat environment, where the more sadistic you are, the better the rewards. HR was never about protecting the employees from poor management, they were all about protecting themselves.Citibank was a great company to work for. There was a very competitive salary package, first class benefits (I had the highest possible health insurance package 100 deductable for my entire family and was only paying 300 pretax money including vision and dental - the company paid 2600 on my behalf - just for the medical!!) all my benefits alone equaled half my base salary, and they also provided extensive training and licensing for their employees. Within the five years that i worked there I was promoted twice. The management always showed respect to their employees and was very much a sense of family and team spirit in the office. There is really nothing negative to say about this place and I can only hope they make it through this economy as it is still the "home" of hundreds of thousands of employees and I hope I will be able to return to this place one day.
cons: The ONLY thing I can say is the idea of job security in this economy we are in. Other than that I have no complaints. I know a countless number of people who have left the bank thinking they found a sweeter deal elsewhere (mainly meaning higher salary) but they have ALL returned or at least tried to, dependind on how bad they burned their bridges on the way out. The balance of income, benefits, work/life, respect, training and licensing and support from management is second to none. Also as far as the aspect of salary, citibank was by no means giving their money away, but you were WELL compensated for meeting goals and hurdles as well as commision. I knew of several personal bankers who were making over 100,000 in income.

advice: It really does not matter what advise you give. Management has just as much of a turn over rate as the regular employees and are always trying to take departments away from each other. summary: Save in the eye of the storm
advice: Do more in terms of salaries to reward staff who are pulling their weight and beyond. And test new candidates better before employing them. You have a lot of staff who are not pulling their weight but who still complain that they do not earn enough money!
pros: I started in Citi just before the crisis hit and survived in the eye of the storm, still working there today. Good salary, good career opportunities, respectful treatment of staff, good benefits, flexible working hours, great people (in the right department).
cons: Other companies pay higher salaries.

summary: Good company. Depends on the area and management.
advice:
I believe the more someone is prepared and sufficiently trained (within a reasonably short time) , the less corrections there will be in the long run. I know everything can't be learned immediately but, there is a critical baseline that needs to be incorporated (including glitches in the systems). This should be shown to new employees by the best in the group who communicate clearly. Extra incentives for their proficient training for new employees is worth the cost.

Raises basically went away after a couple years except for a select few. It was clear that senior management dictated that the manager would have to choose who would get what little they were allowed to give despite reviews. One manager made it impossible in order to make her budgeted payroll look good (and probably get an incentive). We all knew but were grateful to have or jobs. I have no blame for the managers who had to do what they were required to do.

There were anonymous survey's about what needed to be changed by senior management. Citi was a huge corporation but I think it would've been more productive for senior management to know what's going on in the front lines in order to improve the process, employee moral and feeling valued.
pros:
I generally enjoyed working at Citi. I was in a business casual, semi-relaxed environment. The pay is decent. 
Coworkers on the teams were very helpful. Most of my coworkers worked together toward our goals. There were personal and group incentives. 

I had wonderful managers except one. He eventually was fired for harassment but it took a very long time for the company to have enough evidence (I worked in a few different departments). The other managers were very helpful and supportive but they're under stress too. Orders come down on them from higher ups and then they are the ones who have to implement changes whether they make sense of not. 

There were jeans badges you could purchase each month and the money went to a different charity each month. It was tax deductible, as well.
cons:
The jobs I had were high stress jobs. This was only because of the nature of the work and some of the jobs required being on the phone all day so, the actual work was constantly interrupted. The Ops Support division was the least stressful except for a couple duties I had to manage in addition to my core work.

Managers moved quite a bit and it was good sometimes, and not at other times.

Training (for me) was non-existent. I did a few side by sides and was through out into chaos (beginning of the mortgage meltdown). I realize that no company was ready for the regulations that would be coming down and then constant change. But the actual phone work, systems and other basics weren't covered to my expectations. It was extremely frustrating and actually took longer to grasp the job. Collections schedule was insane. 3 early mornings, 2 late nights and  some Saturdays. Sometimes that day/night shifts were back to back. Yes, it's that way at most collections agencies due to call times allowed by law to contact customers. However, with some simple adjustments, east coast and west coast could have been given to different teams.

pros: Advantage of working in a large investment bank is that you get a lot of feedback for your design, because your application handles hundreds of thousands of orders in an hour before exchange close with each of the order being different from others. A single failure out of all these is highlighted. So you get a lot of feedback about every bad design decision made by you.
cons: Enterprise politics is the worst part of the job. Another problem is low productivity because of spending time in mundane manual tasks to take care of compliance and bureaucracy in the system.

summary: Good place to work if you're willing to move around internally to get higher increment but can run into difficult boss
advice: Keep up the good work in leading the bank in the right direction, adopt security process that makes sense & doesn't sacrifice efficiency, keep diversity in workplace
pros: Internal mobility is supported, lots of learning opportunities, mature bank with processes already in place, lots of nice people to work with, able to quickly recover from global financial crisis in 2008

advice: Management understands that the changing banking landscape is forcing a change in culture. Needs to take Talent Management seriously, not just talk the talk but also walk the walk.

summary: A lot of benefits and cons

summary: Loan Processor Commercial Banking (Non-Mortgage; Up to $250K)
advice: You need a dedicated employee to maintain the policies and procedures to keep them current and up to date.

summary: It is a great company to work for but be sure you know what you are getting in to
advice: To SVPs, stop being afraid of your manager and find your voice. Notice if you have a manager that has never hired anyone that ends up staying as their employee. It could be the problem is not the employees but the manager. Be aware that the culture there is to be afraid of management and to never speak to them. That really should be a red flag to you. Fear and intimidation is no way to manage. Ensure that your management team is not managing by withholding information or playing favorites. Having to re-hire and re-train staff costs the company a fortune in the end.
pros: Great benefits, the company is very open and diverse, they offer "Angel Days" an extra day off a year if you donate an hours pay each pay period. They offer a free day off to allow you to volunteer in a charity. The facility I was in had a world class cafe with chef prepared offerings and a gym for $12 a month on site.
cons: The old saying that your job is only as good as your boss is true. If you don't have a good working relationship with your manager and there is no growth opportunity or transfer opportunity where you work in the company, you are doomed. That was my experience. The entire floor is set up in tiny half walled cubicles. Everyone and I mean everyone (VPs included) were in them. It did not matter how much quiet or concentration your job required or what the stakes were if you made a mistake - you were in a bull pen environment . No one respected your space or need for quiet in that environment. The managers all had conference calls at their desks, meetings at their desks. Parties in other departments on the floor. Citi was also very bad about having "clicks" and the management tended to be hobbled by senior management to the point that they had no real decision making authority. What resulted was a "Stepford" like unit. There was just no escape and no one to tell or who would listen.

summary: Not bad for a big bank
advice: Please reform your hiring process. It is standard at Chase to have new prospects interview with the entire team that they would be working with. A candidate may easily slip through the cracks when only meeting with one interviewer, but meeting multiple people will ensure the hiring of quality people. Additionally, if you want to foster teamwork, the team should have a say to new additions. When you hire people who are essentially dead weight, you place the burden on their peers who have to spend their own time in training them and correcting their mistakes.

Luckily, I work in an area where the area director and district manager make time to meet with staff. If you work hard, communicate well and of course produce, you will be recognized, just don't expect that to happen as fast as it would in a small start up company.
cons:

Company is huge, which causes disconnects between departments
Technology is surprisingly lacking

I am unsure as to what standards they make these decisions on, when someone gets promoted to manage a branch and has no capacity for empathy, and is lacking in people skills. I have also seen the hiring of new staff, who are incapable of reading simple instructions and doing remedial arithmetic.

summary: Great Place for Starting One's Career
advice:
Decisions around goals and tactics to achieve them need to assume a wider perspective and align with broader corporate goals.  Rewards and recognition need to align with those as well.

Innovation and challenging of long held shibboleths need to be encouraged over slavish, unquestioning obedience to management.  The former culture that encouraged challenging of tasks and sparked new and unusual approaches to the industry that catapulted Citi into the forefront of the industry needs to be  actively and seriously pursued within a venue that is both safe for the employee and encourages collaboration.
pros:
Being able to put Citigroup on your resume still has power.  Citi has its feet in a wide range of services in the financial services industry.  One can find an opportunity almost anywhere one's interests lie.  

Citi has a strong culture that encourages diversity at the entry level.  Those with exceptional talents and skills can find opportunity here.
cons:
Citi once had a reputation for innovation and entrepreneurship.  Since the Travelers-Citibank merger that has given way as a different corporate culture emerged from the merger and subsequent challenges.  While Citi still offers a career for those who want to pursue a career in financial services, it is no longer the best place for mid- and upper-management who have built some credibility of their own but want a more aggressive, creative and entrepreneurial work environment.

Decisions made by functional units are often made in a vacuum that supports the unit goals but are often not in sync with wider corporate goals.  Decisions also are slow in coming, and corporate politics, borne of multi-layered bureaucracy, can have greater influence than basic business sense would otherwise allow.

Opportunities for mid- and upper-level managers are questionable unless one is looking only for a relatively stable and safe environment where performance is largely gauged by how well one does what one is told.

Managers who question, are innovative and are constantly looking at the appropriateness of how things are done will probably find the environment stultifying.

summary: Citibank, a great place to start a career in finance
advice: The one thing our Senior Management needs to know is that you force us (the bottom) to explain your poor  decisions.  When Citibank is forced to cut in half my customers Equity Lines, and forced to write-down yet another 10 billion dollars...I have to explain that to the normal consumer...and most of the time...I don't know  how to explain your actions.  Our customers make Citibank successful...not a securities trader with his eye on a fat commission...Greed is not a best way to make a successful company....a successful company works hard at making sure their customers are happy...a loss of confidence in the senior management of Citibank is a common topic of discussion.
pros: It is a great place to learn as much as you want to about the financial markets.  It is also a fantastic place to work to meet business leaders in the community.  The support from Area leadership is good and very helpful and at the Area level there is plenty of opportunity to advance....especially if you are willing to commute a little bit.  Another great reason to work for Citibank is the assurance that you will be paid...granted there are always cuts in the corporate world...at the local level...your job is assured as is your paycheck.  And in a struggling economy, assured paycheck is a good thing.
cons: The one downside to working for Citibank is the simple fact that you are small fish in a huge pond.  With the total employee count for Citigroup in the hundreds of thousands... you have to be really good to make an impression.  Fortunately, it is easy to be noticed because (as I have learned) the corporate world is chock full of mediocre people.  If you are smart, and driven and want to succeed .... Citibank is a great place to be.  On the other side of that coin, there is a lot of competition for the best positions...so you have to know what you want and work hard to get there.

summary: Careful before you jump into this ship.
advice: Take a serious look at the businesses you are in and divest yourself to core services.  You are simply too big to be managed effectively.  You don't have the management skills or the backbone to make the right calls.  This is a company that is worth more broken up than as a single group.  All businesses are not the same and you need to stop trying to shoe horn businesses together.  Their success was uniqueness and ability to deliver services to their customers.  Student Loans and Credit cards are different businesses with different strategies and different services.  Why are they together?  Give it up and break it up.  Do your shareholders some good.  I include myself in that group.
pros: A large company that could present many opportunities to employees.  The benefits are decent.  Vacation starts off at 3 or 4 weeks right way.  Medical is pricey like at all companies.  If you are part of the "in" group, the compensation can be decent.  There are some groups that have very good people who are dedicated and well-intentioned.  There are alot of resources in the company that open doors to this place that can't always happen at other places.  Working remotely or from home was available for some employees.  Paternal leave for fathers was offered (unfortunately after I had my children).
cons: Incompetent Sr. Mgmt.  Citigroup is simply a mass of acquired "little" companies that effectively ran independently.  As the sr. mgmt of the corporation attempted to merge these companies they had no skilled people to do so and ended up breaking a lot of good companies and introducing beauraucracy that has since crippled this place.  The place is full of cronyism.  Promotions and bonuses depend on how well you are liked and if you are "in".  Be very careful who you line your star up with or you will be stuck forever.  Change is like moving a mountain and if it happens it is typically in  the wrong direction.

summary: Big, but not lumbering. Ordered, but not rigid
advice: Like any company, you must always value the input and experience of those who work were the "rubber meets the road"...there are times where there is a gap between very high level corporate directives and how they should actually be implemented. With Citi being so big, this is not surprising, but if there was some kind of system to communicate down and ensure feedback was passed back up, that may make things better.
pros:
There are many diverse projects and technologies, which is understandable given the size of the organization. You can be involved in as many technologies as time and interest permit. Even with the turmoil in the financial sector, Citi appears to be fairly stable internally and there is always enough work to keep you busy and engaged. The organizational structure in the Technology side takes a little bit of work to understand, but does make sense.
As a contractor, Citi is not in the least stingy in the hours they'll let you work. I have also heard that their alternate work location program allows people to not have to work our of a Citi office, I even know people who work remotely full-time.
cons: There's a lot of work, and I mean a lot. This is ok for contractors, but it has to be hard for employees as they usually don't get comp time or overtime for working more than regular hours. The sheer size of  the technology groups can make doing anything seem very slow and like your always getting bogged down in a bureaucracy that  doesn't always make sense. Also, as Citi likes to buy other companies, we are always working on integrating acquisitions, so if you expect either things to stay the same or to be able to do things quickly, you're going to have manage your frustration.

advice: Citi is experiencing a brain drain due employees leaving for better compensation.  Citi needs to retrench and start a compensation plan to minimize talent losses.

Administrative duties such as payroll were expected to be self-completed and off the clock. Constructive feedback and suggestions completely ignored. Once I left, I was offered the full time position I had been waiting 6 months for.  When I first began, there wasn't really any training period, I was thrown into the position.

summary: The good and the BAD of working at Citi
advice: Unless you are trying to get your IT employees to quit, I would think about giving them a little more incentive to stay.
pros:
Pay:
Good pay when first joining company, but if you're in IT, you're in for a big disappointment come raise and bonus time!  See downsides for more...    

Benefits:
Very comparable to a few other companies that I have worked for.  And every company's benefits get cut every year - Citi is no different.

Time off:
Excellent - more vacation than I have ever heard of!  Although sick days are limited, which I don't like.  I still don't use them all - I just don't like that they're limited.  I have never had issues taking unexpected time off, although I pay for it later if there is a lot of work that I miss.

Good name / recognition:
Over the years, people in general have seemed impressed when they hear that I work for Citi.
cons:
Horrible pay increases:
Maybe I'm spoiled, but my performance over the 15 years prior to Citi brought me nothing lower than 6-7% combined raise and bonus between four other companies.  Again, that's not average, that's the lowest I have ever received... prior to Citi.  So what does this type of performance get me at Citi?  Anywhere from 0-2% combined raise and bonus!!  It's not just me - of the six other people in my immediate area that have shared this information with me, none had gotten even 2% combined raise or bonus in years.  I have spoken to only a couple of other people in IT who are not in my immediate area and they both made a 3-4% raise+bonus sound really good, but very hard to get.  I'm sorry, it's not really good nor should it be that hard to get.  Everyone in IT says that the Business side gets all of the money - I have only heard these rumors and can't confirm them.  

Work/Life Balance:
My area preaches no more late hours/weekends, etc., but then turn around and schedule an extra 40-50 hours per month.

Career advancement:
We were told that in order to get promoted, a position at that level has to open up.  I have never heard of this outside of Citi.  Elsewhere, I have been promoted for doing a good job that deserves a promotion, whether there was an opening or not.  I could understand this if you wanted to get into management, but not at any level lower than this.

Competence of Senior management:
Although no different than almost every other bank out there, senior management took on so much risk with their lending the entire world is now suffering!  Banks such as Citi wrote the book on Risk, then decided to throw it away for near-term profits - unbelievable.

summary: Great for self-starters, but very political.
advice: You need to put Citi on the right track asap. As it is now, this monolith is sinking like the Titanic. Employee morale is at an all time low. Now's the time to cut the bureaucracy and right the ship.
pros: Citigroup is a great place to work if you're a self-starter who can manage your own career effectively. You will be given opportunities to advance and grow, and people are generally very helpful and friendly, even if they don't know you/don't work for you. The reasons for this are two-fold: 1- the 360 reviews Citi conducts-- employees can and do review managers and those who are higher in the corporate structure than they are, and those reviews do count. The MDs are approachable and very willing to spare their time, if they have it. 2- Because Citi is so fluid in terms of who does what job, there's constant reorganization going on and you may suddenly find that the person whose phone call you ignored last month is now your boss! So it pays to be helpful and friendly.
cons: Very political. You can easily advance without doing a lot of hard work if you cozy up to the right people. This is by no means typical of most employees, but I've seen it in action and it's frustrating to those of us who work hard, put in long hours, and sacrifice in other ways to keep our careers on track. I also found that some managers can be less than respectful of their employees. I had one manager who would yell at me as if I was a child. Sure, there are rules against this and you can take it up with HR... if you want to kiss your career goodbye. Further, there's not a lot of flexibility if you're sick or if you need to take time off. I asked my manager for a couple of days off since my family was coming in from out of the country and she said No. No reason, just no.

summary: Depends on what you are after
pros: I was at the Blue Ash, OH location.  There is a wonderful group of people at this.  Everyone was very friendly (genuinely friendly!)  I felt welcome from the first minute.  The company also sponsored a lot of activities at the site - annual employee appreciation cookout in the summer, holiday lunch in December, lots of little 'feel good' activities that seem to have disappeared from a lot of companies.  I had a strong sense that the upper management at the site was involved and engaged with the employees and felt that they were approachable if you wanted to talk.
cons: It is a global company with a lot of folks from outside the US working at the site.  As such, there was  a lot of push to attend meetings and calls from 8am in the morning until late at night.  Also a lot of sense that it was expected for you to be in the office during the core hours in addition to participating in those off hours calls.  On top of that, they had what I will call a typical big company sense of being dysfunctional -- i.e. there were always a ton of meetings and very rarely would decisions get made.  Also there was a lot of sense of folks trying to protect their territory even if that meant fighting for a solution/implementation that did not make sense.   I almost don't want to word this as a con as I think some of it has to do with banking regulations and such but for me it was a con in that I frequently felt that I did not have proper access to the things (data and systems) that I needed in order to do my job.  Again, this may be common in financial institutions so it may not be fair to word this as a con, but in the grande scheme it makes for a big headache for an employee who is used to getting things done.

summary: Amazing Career Opportunities and Benefits! Come Find a Career at Citi!
pros:
When you do what you love, you don't work a day in your life. That is how I feel working at Citi. I am grateful to have found a role in the company that suits me, my life and my personality. 

I currently work in a global  role for a Managing Director who I look up to and admire for her leadership qualities, people skills and ability to manage in a manner that exemplifies high standards and integrity. Although, I worked for two less than qualified managers in the past, I found a role within the company that is a better fit. 

Citi is a great company because: 
1. Work- life balance matters
2. Opportunities to change roles and/or grow 
3. Many diversity groups to join. (This is a great working opportunity and it's a great way to showcase talents outside of your business as usual (BAU) work.) 
4. Citi give you 8 hours a year to volunteer. 
5. Excellent internal learning libraries. 
6. Competitive pay. 

I strongly believe that working at Citi isn't just a place to be "employed and get a paycheck." It's a place that has allowed me to do what I love, to grow, continuously learn and establish a long-term career. It's up to you to take advantage of what the company has to offer and I do!
cons: Like with any company, there are some challenges around management. During an interview, ask questions and come prepared. You are in charge of your life and your career. Make sure that you are a right fit and you understand your role before accepting a position to avoid issues later on. Sometimes it is not the job for you or the right team. Find a department that works for you.

Overall, if you're wanting to get started in AML and Citi is hiring, this is a solid place.
cons: During my tenure, there was 1 major layoff which left half the floor without a job. As a monolith, Citi doesn't value the employees in "non-revenue generating" departments and we constantly got the fact that we don't bring in money thrown in our faces when we asked about when contractors would become permanent. Ultimately, the company has a culture problem. The employee engagement events were not accessible to people with food allergies or intolerances, which may seem like a small consideration but it's such a punch to the gut. Citi also has a habit of hiring a whole bunch of temps (sorry, contractors) because they got into a case backlog, then firing them once they're in the clear. This is a terrible business practice and ends up not only harming people but also produces shoddy work that just has to be cleaned up later. Rinse, repeat. For those select few of us who remained, opportunities to move within the company (either in AML or the bank overall) were frozen out. It led people to feeling stuck and angry and unheard. When I left, morale was at an all-time low and the department was hemorrhaging people. Like I said:  rinse, repeat. That's not even touching on the QA process, or how new processes were implemented with seemingly no forethought.

advice: Overall a good company filled with high achievers and good leadership.
pros:
Citi sets very high standards for hiring which is reflected in the quality of people you work with which is exceptional. Colleagues in my immediate group were wonderful which made coming to work each day very enjoyable. They were also a helpful and collaborative group.

The organization touts that it is dedicated to promoting from within and they honor and execute on this. Once you prove yourself you should find ample opportunities to move up, around, or get involved in outside projects to learn new skills. Training is always available and ongoing. There were also a lot of great leaders in the organization to learn from. However, like any large organization it can be highly political and tough to navigate effectively at times but doable. 

The Brandon complex has most things you will need during the day. This includes a dining facility with multiple restaurants and food choices. A banking or ATM machine. An onsite doctor's office was really convenient and a tremendous time saver. There was also an onsite gym with lockers and shower facilities as nice as any top-rated gym in the area. The benefits were also really quite good.

Most of the building/complex was organized or structured as a hoteling setup (call center-like). The space is very attractive. You work in large groups at long tables very close to one another. You are given a small locker to keep your personal items in and can't keep personal items in your workspace. The table chairs and workspace were ergonomic and nice. Finding a quiet place to concentrate was a challenge at times.
cons:
Not a con for everyone. It just did not work for me. 

People work close together and noise levels were significant in my area. I had an auditory processing condition making it difficult to hear people on the phone due to the background noise. I purchased special headphones but they didn't help a great deal. I was not comfortable seeking an accommodation for this.

If privacy or being able to have a personal space is important to you this is could be a negative and worth consideration. Hoteling is not for everyone. At the time working home for Tampa employees was not an option.

Navigating the organization can be challenging and political. Getting things done quickly can be challenging. This includes getting access to resources needed for your job. Speaking up can be tricky and fraught with peril. Be very mindful of who you direct request/s to...and how you make that request. Optics are important.

I worked for Citi during a time of significant departmental change. I really enjoyed the people I worked with outside of the environment.

A company that definitely tries to incorporate diversity and inclusion into it's recruiting culture but still has a way to go in terms of creating an environment that feels like differences are at home.
