Too many, "lifers" (only worked at Citi their entire career) running the bank no new fresh talent/ideas
Horrible vacation packages (2 weeks) most other banks give 3-5 weeks regardless of title
401 K package doesn't make sense to match 1 year after employment other large firms match from first date of employment

summary: It was good until it wasn’t.
pros: Lots of Flexibility when it came to work life balance. The group I supported was a wonderful group who had great ideas.
cons: Direct manager was great. Senior management, not so much. Always looking to save a buck. The team wanted to be innovative but they were always held back because they never got the funding they needed to make changes. When all the offshoring started it never stopped. Too many long tenure people (15, 20+ years) were let go to save money and move jobs to low cost countries.

pros: Vacation time is good and the people there are great. I've learned a lot on the job. The main office that I'm working in is an open floor plan, which is a pain and doesn't give you any downtime, but most employees follow a hybrid model. 2 days in, 3 days out.
cons: I don't have a lot of work experience, so I cannot compare my position at Citi to other corporate offices. I'm not thrilled about the commute but Manhattan is expensive and I signed up for that when I started my position in the main office.

advice: Make sure your recruiters are following up. Citi reached out to me and the role actually seemed interesting and I wanted to learn more, but after being reached out to and then having no response, it came across as disorganized. It wasn’t a good experience.
pros: The company is hiring at a large scale
cons: The recruitment process isn’t good. A recruiter reached out to me via LinkedIn, I responded to learn more and I didn’t hear anything for a month. The same recruiter then came back to my inbox to ask me about another role. Based off the lack of communication in just the recruitment phase, I can only imagine what it would be like as a full-time employee and I respectfully declined any further offers.

advice: Evaluate long term costs and benefits, not just what you can kick up on a spreadsheet and pie chart to the execs.
pros: Options to WFH, decent enough insurance, plenty of opportunity to move around.
cons:
Super "clique-ish". High school 2.0.
Increases and positions are granted based mostly on favoritism and not actual work.
Insane amount of outsourcing. Products and internal tools are developed in one contractor cycle then supported by people who had no hand in the creation.

I left in 2014 and still had a computer with windows xp and office 2007 on it.

Completely disorganized mess.

Insane workload expectations and stress.

advice: Managers pay attention to your tellers and treat them with respect. Excessive unnecessary pressure creates stressful environment which backfires.
pros: The starting hourly pay is decent with commission. Unfortunately, commission is not payed out in timely fashion. The coworkers are friendly
cons: Excessive pressure to cross-sell. Managers with no managing skills and no respect to their employees. Random monthly surveys done based on customer interactions with grades from 0-10. Anything less than 9 equals to zero and the process in which the survey is setup makes it difficult to achieve that 9. Too many monthly surprise visits from the regional manager.

advice: The managers were great guys to get along with and seem very helpful but also serious about their role at the bank. I would just like to feel the genuine interest to help each of their employees succeed
pros: The on boarding process was very well carried and the managers and onboarding staff stay in touch with you the whole way through
cons: Have to wait a while to move up, however if you're confident in your skills you'll be fine. The company likes to make sure you're fully ready before you move forward

advice: Continue to focus on talent and harvest a positive work environment in a lean economy
pros: Large company but community feels small. Great for networking and learning new skills. Company is focused on employee feedback and is making the necessary changes to stay ahead of the company. Vision and strategy for the future is well defined and the right leaders are in place to execute
cons: Salary is not as competitive as others in the industry and benefits are not as great, however there is a lot of focus to lead in this area across the different markets.

advice: The company should be split up.  There is no clear vision of the future.
pros: Large network, global perspective, smart coworkers, large potential impact, the opportunity can be good in the short term if you are in the right role.
cons: Very political, hard to get anything done, spend most of your time justifying your job to management.  The higher you rise in the organization, the more time is spent on political things and the less on actually doing work.  After years of cutbacks, the people that survived are the ones with the sharpest elbows.

advice: Foster a culture that considers new ideal from employees.  I found that anytime I suggested something new I was trounced.  I felt as if I had to be there long enough to learn the politics before I could say anything,
pros: Working with smart colleagues, good compensation, opportunities,  excellent benefits
cons: Too big.  I found that it was more important to know how to work the politics than doing the job and this became more apparent the higher the rank.  Often times jobs are pigeon-holed so that employees can only perform one function.

advice: Provide competitive salaries and please consider doing GC on time.
pros:
Good Benefits like 22 days of vacation.
Flexible working hours.
cons:
They don't care of your work status. Actually it might also depends on the team and manager. my manage is bad at this.
They send back to home country after 6 years of H-1B. 
People look at your title before taking your ideas and respond to email. so your ideas might not be consider even if they are lot better what architects provides.
Very less or negligible bonus and i believe salaries are less compared to other companies.

summary: Breaking the way toward Life-Work Balance
advice: Find opportunities to foster closer relationships amongst sales team...
pros: The benefits package was amazing for a entry level type position, I was able to gain additional training paid for by Citibank while on Co. time that I have been able to take away. Flexible work schedule, amazing facility .
cons: I was on a sales team in the credit card division, the part of being prepared to meet quotas can be stressful, large call center, if part of your desire for work is to build relationships with coworkers this may not be for you.

advice: Pay more attention to your employees - they are overworked, understaffed, and morale is low as a result. The opportunities to use our vacation benefits are few and far between, and working all holidays and weekends is damaging to family and social lives. Also, why are we not allotted an hour lunch like every other salaried position within the company??
pros: Good starting position; nice salary, good benefits, daily interaction with management. Duties as a Workforce Analyst are easy to learn and master. Plenty of career opportunities stem from this role, their only requirement is that you maintain the role for 1 year. Overall the company is fine to work for.
cons:
The company as a whole may be fine to work for, but there are several problems with this position/department:

Work/life balance is skewed in this department - the department is running 24/7 and they have to cover all that time. EX) 1st shift is 0600-1430, 2nd shift is 1330-2200, and 3rd shift is 2130-0600. This is also not a M-F position, most people in the office work on a non standard week, Su-Tr, Tu-Sa, etc. While there is a pay differential for "non-standard hours," it is also extremely difficult to get into a schedule that is considered standard M-F. Taking time off is also extremely difficult, as the entire department is currently understaffed, especially on weekends, and they have a minimum number of staff that they require be there to cover their products. So if you work every Saturday, and want to take a Saturday off less than two months in advance, good luck to you. Oh and the opportunity to take off holidays at the end of the year was gone in the vacation bid at the beginning of 2016, which was based on seniority so most people did not get those days off. Also, if you were awarded a new schedule, be prepared to wait 3 months at a minimum to move into your new schedule as they require that your current shift be filled before you can move. And with how slowly they are hiring, and how quickly we are losing people to other positions or companies, moving shifts is becoming more and more difficult.

For a position that is salaried and is considered an exempt position, there are very little opportunities to take breaks - most analysts do not take lunch every day, and even when you do feel you have the opportunity to take a lunch you are only allowed 30 minutes.

Feedback in this role is also abysmal; the department had a total of 5 managers for a 100 full-time, salaried employees for more than 6 months before filling their management gaps. During that time, year end reviews were held with managers that have very little time to notice you and provide actual constructive feedback. Management consistently speaks of "progress" and making much needed changes to how things are operated, but changes take far too long to be implemented.

The job responsibilities are straightforward, but they oversell the "analyst" portion of the job; currently it is more of a "button-pusher" position. To their credit, they are doing what they can to change that, but they have been working on that change for the better part of 2 years.

pros: There are many good colleagues who are always willing to share the knowledge and help the daily business. If you learn fast, you can have many opportunities to take more tasks and be involved in many new projects.
cons: Supervisors consider "overtime" normal, which means you have to "nearly always" work until very late. There is no work life balance in Citibank. When doing the HR engagement survey, all supervisors will imply or request you to rate them the best, even though you don't think so. Supervisors often call you when you are off the office or on vocations.

summary: Strong Technology Teams But Systemic Issues
advice:
You need to get scheduling for releases correct. I know the business ultimately dictates, but this is for them too. If we see a release is going critical, the answer can't be to just push people harder and cross our fingers every time; it has never worked for a single release I've seen! If we can't support issues, then just be willing to move them out! Plan the release with actual wiggle room for another project or something, don't just stuff it to maximum capacity and then throw another urgent item on last minute and expect things to test green.

Keep up the great work on community and policy culture, though. Citi is terrific in that regard!
pros:
I want to be clear that for all my complaints below, Citi is a great place to work with terrific people. Yes there are problems, but the pros really do outweigh the cons!

Huge company provides tons of opportunity for lots of different roles and they generally encourage you to change positions every 2-3 years if feasible and there is generally room for both lateral and vertical mobility for both individual contributor and manager type roles. There is a ton of variety here and you can work hands deep in code for a team in Hong Kong or stay a mile high working on a project for the offices in New York - and you can frequently do it all from home (depending on the team).

Training and career development are a lifestyle here, with constant offers of paid-for training courses and opportunities to get industry certifications cheap (such as the PMP or others). There is also a lot of internal support structure to provide and receive mentorship.

A huge plus at Citi is the corporately accepting culture of people of "all walks," including people of any gender, sexual orientation, or other social descriptor. The benefits even extend to partners for situations in which states will not recognize a marriage, although I have not tested the efficacy of this myself.
cons:
Benefits provide good coverage but the 401(k) options are surprisingly lack luster for a bank.

Work life balance is usually maintainable (as in, keeping it to 40 hours with minimal overtime), but there is a ton of pressure here to be "always-on," to the point that I know team members who never use all of their vacation days because they are practically afraid to be away from the office lest they fall behind on something.

The flip side is that, as it a huge financial company that impacts a whole mess of people, sometimes you really do have to be there at 11 at night or at 2 in the morning. It's just part of the job, but thankfully not often.

The biggest con is that those huge overtimes should be avoidable but middle managers are all but instructed to squabble and bicker about schedules and who is right about what project being important. I don't think I've ever been on a release where everything that was supposed to go in actually went in on time.

This isn't helped by the IM/Email culture of the workforce either. If you need something from someone at another Citi site, sometimes you can't just call them because they are in meetings all day and you'll go straight to voicemail. So you IM them and send emails and they might respond or they might ignore it because your high priority issue doesn't even register on their radar - to be fair, it may really not be a priority for them, but it causes people to feel frustrated and that can spread over to the other managers and developers unnecessarily.

advice: Promote based on merit, not politics. Cut out levels of management. Get managers that help staff do their jobs and focus on the client, not look good in front of upper management at the expense of staff and morale.
pros: Driven people; outgoing personalities. Colleagues willing to learn from each other. Brand recognition goes far, especially in LatAm region. Many interesting people in the organization.
cons: Office politics and unclear growth path. NOT a meritocracy. Connections more important to advancing career than actual work. Also, too many managers but little management (few people want to take responsibility for important decisions).

summary: Executive turnstile leads to ever changing goals that are never achieved
advice: Set a vision and stick to it for more than 1-2 years.
pros: Generally not a very high stress environment. People tend to be friendly.
cons: The constant leadership churn causes a lot of thrashing. Each new executive cancels that last executives major goals/project. Citi never completely fulfills its promise to shareholders. Promotions are extremely challenging to achieve. Head count and open reqs are constantly frozen or removed. Rarely promoted within your role. To get a promotion you almost always have to take a new position with a new function, business, etc.

advice:
Management needs to work on finding a balance for their team. Favoritism is very common and they only way to get anywhere or anything is being friends with managment. 
Management won't fight for their employees... common excuse "It's out of my hands...It's an HR decision" 
I hated seeing great talent leaving Citi because of pay or unfair evaluations. Just because in an evaluation it states where there is room for improvement, does not mean you should make something up just because you're suppose to put something.  You play with peoples careers.
pros:
Vacation, benefits, work life balance, remote work, great for moms.
 If you're offered a position with Citi make sure you negotiate and ask for more money or they will give you the base, most jobs have a huge range 20-30k to work with and they will offer you the least. Negotiate, Negotiate!!!!
cons:
Compensation is below average,only way to make more money is to leave Citi and come back. It's a running joke... everyone leaves and comes back...but they come back making 20k more.  
Lucky to get a 3% yearly increase. You're treated as person in a seat not as a loyal employee. Turnover is high only because of the pay. I was offered 25k more doing the same job elsewhere. 
Don't expect a bonus, bonus' are given based on mgr discretion, they are given an amount and based on how they want to give it out... hope you're buddy buddy with them or you won't see anything, many years was told they didn't have enough in the budget to give everyone raises, some people in the group were given 10% others nothing.
Management is very poor, you get promoted only if you apply for a higher level. Citi never promotes by rewarding for performance. Example- to go from a JR to Sr level someone must leave the department and the position must be applied for. Never granted based on great work.

advice: Pay attention to your most precious asset, people. Quit trying to build little fiefdoms. Give people the opportunity to grow.
pros: It is a place to coast. There is not strong management oversight. You can find some people working there.
cons: The management setup is a disaster. I had 5 managers in four years. The only constant is change. Change in managers; change in policy. Forget about doing any company travel only upper management gets to go anywhere. There is no training support. There are no annular pay increases. I got one 2% raise in four years.

summary: overall good, but after a while you need to move on
pros:
- great place to start your career as resources available (market information, Mumbai outsourcing, research) are valuable
- market leader in most areas
- diverse people
- good opportunities to network
- good benefits (pension is generous at 7.5% of earnings + 50% match up to 4% of earnings)
cons:
- can be bureaucratic, process-driven
- certain teams can be very narrowly-focused, out of touch with rest of firm
- sometimes slow to react to market opportunities, i.e. creations of new teams can take a long time
- reputation externally has suffered over last six years

advice: I don't think you should fire someone just because their handle time doesn't improve. If someone is really trying and it still isn't improving maybe its not them. Maybe the help they are being given isn't working. You say you are all about creating  a remarkable experience. If that's so, why fire someone if they are providing that experience just in more time than someone else? The customers aren't upset with a long call when they are being helped. Also giving people more schedule options would be nice. When people quit why not offer their schedule to the other co-workers as long as it fits business needs. I also think that giving employees part time options would help people stay. 40 hrs a week of back to back calls burns out your employees. By providing part time, I think the employees there wouldn't get burned out as much,and it would let your employees handle it better. Also back to back calls kill us. HIre more people . you can always give out Vto if its to slow.
pros: overtime available. benefits. If they aren't busy, you can apply for voluntary time off which means they let you go home unpaid if you wish. It isn't guaranteed though. They have a gym and cafeteria. They give you 6 days of sick time, about 12 days of vacation time and they give you holiday time. If they schedule you on a holiday, you get paid double time and a half which is awesome. they also let you use holiday time for days off if you want too. You can choose an hour lunch or 30 min lunch and you get two 15min breaks . co workers are great and the managers do care about you. They have other job opportunities to apply for with in the company.
cons:
training doesn't prepare you for the phones.  My trainer called it survival training which meant you learn about 20 percent of what you need to actually do the job. When you get on the phones, you will feel like you have no idea what you are doing. They do have people there to help but when someone is on the line and you have them waiting it puts a lot of stress on you. After a while you will learn and know what your doing. 
They make it seem like you can change your schedule a lot but you can't. You can change it once a year, and it goes on a seniority basis. Also they have people quit a lot and they don't replace them right after, so in my department we often would get back to back calls which can get really draining. They are really big on meeting handle time goals, quality goals, and other goals there. If you don't improve, they may fire you. There was a girl who had gotten an award for best 1st call resolution rate but yet they fired her shortly after because her handle time was too high. It seems like they focus too much on what you aren't doing right.  As long as you meet your goals you'll be fine though. You may get angry customers, and it can be hard when maybe they got screwed but there is nothing you can do.

advice: Benefit cost increases often out-pace merit increases resulting in compensation going back-wards year-over year.
pros: Good company overall with many really good people working there.
cons: It is often said that the "C" in Citi stands for Change.  To enjoy working at Citi you need to embrace the constant change.  This is not only a result of the changing market conditions but also managements continuously changing priorities.  It can be frustrating at times to work full-throttle on a project to have it set-aside to begin work full-throttle on a new one, until it happens again.

summary: Big money center banks are all pretty much the same
advice:
If there is an open position please find someone within the US to fill it. What does the US government get by way of taxes if the job is offshored?

For a moment, forget about the taxes the US government would get. In what way does a job created in India benefit Citi in the US? If you employ someone in the US, there is a chance, however small it may be, that the person would come back to you for a mortgage loan or a home equity loan or a credit card or a checking / saving account. In a worse case scenario where the US employee does not offer you any business, there is 100% chance that the money earned in the US would at least circulate within the US and help American economy. The job created in India has near zero chance of helping US economy. And remember, when the American consumer rolls, the US banks tend to improve their earnings as well.

One might argue that the employee hired in India generates similar business opportunities as the employee hired in the US. Well, if you have the statistics, please make the numbers public along with the business volume in USD terms.

This problem is not seen just at Citi. This is common place occurrence where short sighted American corporations are shooting themselves in the foot. Wake up !!!
pros:
The company has a global footprint and hence offers plenty of room for career mobility within the company. The company offers comparable 401K and other benefits though there as been some level of reduction in health benefits recently. 

They do believe in meritocracy but occasionally, one does see old boy networks playing their part. This is arguably true for most big money center employers, so one could give them a pass on this one. In short, if one maintains high level of efficiency at work and keep up good relations up the chain, getting a promotion would not be difficult.

Work wise, they do offer a reasonable balance between personal and professional life.
cons: Ease of mobility does not necessarily translate into higher wages. They have been outsourcing a lot of their back office/technology work. This tends to bring down not just the morale but also the compensation levels of the work force in the US. In addition, they have also embarked on re-locating a lot of positions to low cost states such as Texas and Florida. While this may bring in some savings to the employer, it may not always be the right option for people with school going children and working spouses to relocate for example - from New York to TX. So watch out what you are getting into.

summary: It's an ok company. You may have a chance to move up if you know someone.
advice: Take the time to value your existing employees and review the time/effort they put in. I worked at a branch in NY. I was rated satisfactory or better, did all the training to move into the ABM role, went to different branches to help when needed, used workforce to make schedules, reviewed accounts, reviewed teller transactions, cash counts, filled in other roles like customer service when it was a position, went on company interviews/workshops which had all positive results, had a substantial knowledge of internal systems, and even had increased authority in my head teller role. However, when I went to apply internally for ABM positions in which I had completed all the required training, I only received one call back... Ever. And during that interview, the Area Operations Director, had a quite an issue with the distance I lived from the branch I was applying, which she made apparent through our interview. After that, the rest of my applications were never even considered. And I even went on a mock interview in LIC after that. During 2012-2103 I literally applied for every single Assistant Branch Manager position in NY and NJ. I sent out over 20 submissions and did not even receive a response to one. Meanwhile, the company hires inexperienced external candidates and also left various spots unfilled. Ultimately I needed to leave the company because I clearly did not have a chance to advance and a tellers salary was just not substantial enough for my situation anymore. I even wrote in depth about this in my last VOE. In the end, you lost a good employee.You wasted thousands of dollars paying me, sending me to extra training, sending me to career advancement workshops for a new role, for nothing. I would have gone to just about any branch, would have gladly worked overtime, weekends, etc. all for a the chance to have an intensely stressful job, with long hours, and little recognition.
pros: Work-life balance is ok. Not a bad place if your branch staff is competent. Good chance for advancement if you are related to someone.
cons: Concerned about service and operations but doing away with more operations and service positions. Slim chance of moving up unless you know someone. In addition to family, will advance anyone that has amazing sales stats even if you are incompetent. Raises kind of suck

summary: Less qualified people got higher level jobs when site opened a few years ago.
advice:
Talk a close look at how much this company relies on Microsoft Excel to compensate for not addressing key technology needs.  
Implement a central query program that could query multiple databases and link them. 
Listen to employees and set STANDARDS for employee reviews.  
Don't just promote people because they have been there for a long time.
pros:
Clean work environment and new computers/facilities.
Gym and good cafeteria on site.  
People are generally nice.  
Appears to be stable for now.
cons:
When the site opened a few years ago, there were more quality jobs available than supply in the Buffalo labor market.  They naturally decided to fill higher level positions first based on the applicants at that time.  In many cases, these positions were filled with weaker talent.  As better qualified applicants applied to Citi, they were positioned under the weaker talent.  Now there are many people reporting to people who are less capable, have less experience and are less effective than themselves.  

Changing jobs is very difficult.  Recently finance brought in 17 new jobs.  The management positions were filled by simply taking the "next person in line" who fell under the senior manager.  They were not open to current workers on the floor.  

All departments work within silos.  
Communication is minimal.
Morale is weak.
Arrogant Management
In finance, very high workload for experienced non-managers.
Promotions for year-end 2009 appeared to be based on seniority only.  Also, those who complained the most about deserving a promotion got one.  

Organizational structure rolls up through New York separately through each department.  It does not roll up to Senior Management team at site.  

Many departments do employee reviews based on money available for small bonuses and promotions.  They determine these things first and then back value the reviews to fit the budget. 

Very political and bureaucratic.

advice: Better assessment of some of the management that aren't contributors to the organization. Some of them remain in the jobs despite being bad elements to the bank and senior management doesn't take action.
pros: There is good teamwork. I have been provided job growth opportunities along the 9 years I've been with Citi and the positions always have been challenging. Also good mobility opportunities.
cons: After the crisis salaries have been frozen, despite working on the high growth areas that haven't lost money. Bonus compensations have also been affected.

summary: Good opportunity to enter in Financial industry and good scope for growth available here.
advice: Please outline the basis of giving bonus or increment to employess since it does not go inline with perfomance ratings given.
pros: Good scope of growth available in this company. Managers are very much supportive in terms of work and also personal life when it comes to take time off when you need it to support your family.
cons: You get good performance ratings but at times it does not result in good increment or bonus. It hurts when you work hard and don't get rewarded monetarily.

summary: Constant change; feels like running on a treadmill making up time with yet another manager.  Competitive & cutthroat
advice: Seek more employee input prior to rolling out new strategies rather than what appears to be advice from sycophants who are then promoted.
pros: Excellent platform, relative to other large private banks.  There is an ability to change roles if you are early in your career.
cons: Horrible management, constantly changing, lack of focus and poor execution on plans.  Major overhaul of the business by tearing down profitable businesses to build up the investments platform.  Success remains to be seen.

advice: a shred of transprency would have been nice.
pros: more collegial than other investment banks, but still very hierarchical and unnecessarily competitive.  good analyst training program.  tribeca us a great place to work.
cons: very difficult to move internally--extremely political.  HR is a disaster -- beyond unhelpful to the point that they actually made my experience worse.  very little investment in technology -- i fought for years to get a second monitor, but never got one.  lots of red tape everywhere.  layoffs every year continue. long hours, grunt work, but that was to be expected.

summary: If you wanna be stuck in a job with high expectations and no $ , then work here!
advice:
Promote hard working performers.
Get rid of the Manager's with hidden agendas.
Ask for 360 degree feedback from works on their managers, you will be enlightened!
Get training $ to the employees, or you are going to lose some really good IT people like you did ME!
pros:
Telecommute - Many received mandatory 3 days a week work from home due to downsizing of real estate in key states, New York, New Jersey, etc.  Ability to work from home was a benefit to me.
Holiday/Vacation Time off - Received 17 days vacation on hire in, and 12 holidays.  It is probably typical, but was more than I had before.
cons:
Training - They have no money in budget for training.  They will expect you to be CISSP, but getting it approved goes all the way to the top, and then they won't pay for travel.  Any other training you need to stay current on IT will never be approved, and if you had to travel to the class or conference, it will NEVER be approved.  They have high expectations on your IT skill level, but do not send you to any training that's critical for you to stay current!  CAREER SUICIDE!
PAY - Worked there over 5 years, my pay went up 1% or less each year even with great performance reviews.  Citi = no money.
FAVORITISM - People are promoted based on Senior Managers needing head count under them so they look important and don't lose their jobs.  People are promoted not based on experience/skills but on hidden agendas.  Bonuses, training, pay increases come from who you know, not what you know.
LAYOFFS - Merry Christmas, Citi likes to do mass layoffs at the end of the year to avoid bonus payouts in January.  They have reduced their size by over 100,000 employees in the last 1-2 years.  This is not a career company.
VACATION DAYS DO NOT CARRY OVER - You can't carry over more than 5 days, and you'll have to use them by March 31st.
TECHNOLOGY - All the banks they acquired during the getting fat/rich days, created a lot of older technology to be supported.  The recent sell offs the last few years has gotten rid of some of it, but the current technology wasn't able to be maintained and invested in.  Many systems are running 4-5 years behind current releases.

advice: Always have more knowledge of the job duties then your employees.  Never hire friends within your own department and never reward them with better opportunities just because their your friends.  This is a terrible trend within many Dallas Texas base Corporations.  This way of building a large or smal company proves destructive to competitive workers within a company.  Managers should be able to recognize what level of talent they have and know when an employee should reach for more demanding roles within a company.  Managers should recommend and advance candidates for more rewarding roles within their company and in return HR should then reach out to those candidates, not the other way around.  Trying to hold back employees so the Manager can look good on paper is not what Mangers should do.  A Mangers job is to first follow line of business and meet company/ department goals set.  Second, build  employees to make the company as a whole stronger, faster, smarter then competitors.  Third, Mangers should never take the credit for what their team accomplishes; only for the way its organized and how smooth his or her department runs.
pros: Great Company to gain Knowledge and practices.  Will leave the door open for you to learn but at your own risk.  If your great at learning the information yourself this is a great company to work for.  Self taught employees expand really fast here.
cons: Vary High employee turn over here!  Based on my experience with CitiMortgage in Irving Tx, They hire off the street and pay more to the new hires then the employees that have tenure with the company leading to lose of talent and constant turmoil within.  If you want more money or the median pay you have to leave the company and later return in order to gain a couple more dollars for the same position.  Internal hiring will do there best to not reward you for years of service and knowledge.  This seems to be company practice at  Citi.  CitiMortgage has employees that been with the company for 10 plus years making less then new employees off the street in some cases.  CitiMortgage is not a great place to build a career but to gain leading knowledge of the industry.  They still have a "Good ol Boy" way of doing business but if you need a job and your ok with the 80's way of doing business.  This is the place for you.

summary: My experience at Citibank has really helped me grow as a young professional
advice: Stick with one plan and execute it.  Quit changing directions.  Citi has amazing innovative potential as a truly global bank.
pros: The work life balance is a great reason to work at Citibank.  Working remote and having more vacation than my previous employers are my favorite perks.  Hard work is recognized through the citi star program.
cons: The C in Citi stands for change.  The environment is constantly changing.  The worst part is that each re-organization means efficiency through layoffs.

summary: This Bank was my blessing, handpicked & chosen for me.
advice: Don't allow people who don't deliver excellent service, who call-out every-other-day, & who come in late, stay with the company & collect a paycheck. Let them look for employment elsewhere.
pros: Awesome leadership. Could not have asked for a better management team: 3 powerful, truthful women- Regional, BM, & ABM. Teller system was easy to learn & navigate through. Many resources to help meet teller referral goal. Recognized regularly for excellent customer service. Nice location.
cons: The only "con" for me was a few immature, fake, non-customer service co-workers.

advice: At my branch, some tellers and bankers gang up and tried to report every single move managers make to upper managements, I see that it was a tough place. I felt sorry for them. Being firm and getting respect from people who work for you is a key but I understand that it is not easy.
pros: Citibank branch closes at 2PM on Saturdays and 5pm on weekdays. If you work for other banks, end time will be later.
cons: They give you two to three warnings if you don't meet your sales goals and you will be out.

advice: Need to use resources and human talent more effectively and efficiently. Increased talent management could result in more productiveness and/or better processes.
pros: Very engaged with work-life balance and allows work-from-home options and flexible schedules (upon approval and work plans); good compensation packages; good work environment
cons: Some areas have poor leadership. Many managers are chosen by level of Subject Matter Experts and not leadership abilities. Likewise, they do not always use their resources efficiently. (Talented people doing less value added tasks and/or not so talented people not effectively explaining/assigning work.

summary: Global Company, Lots of moving parts
advice: Senior Management should also look two or three levels down when assessing areas.
pros: It is a global company with lots to learn, many different responsibilities and long standing processes. Just before leaving, the senior management was working towards organizing responsibilities and salaries along with ensuring oversight of risk. So depending on what you desired to do or learn, there are plenty of opportunities there.
cons: As with the pros, it is a global company with many different responsibilities. Sometimes it takes longer for changes to occur. Good or bad, some things take a longer (in my opinion) to occur.

advice: Retain talented employees with benefits compensations according to their work.
pros:
In my case, my job responsibilities consist basically in attending calls and discussing topics with people around the globe, so I improved my english and soft skills a lot.
Really talented people work for the company.
cons:
Company processes are very complicated, makes it hard to get things done. 
In terms of technologies used and best practices a bank is not in the cutting edge... So be prepared some long and sometimes boring calls.
Salaries are tied to union agreements meaning there are no raises. Getting a promotion takes 2 years minimum.

pros: Benefits are pretty good. There is not that much opportunity to move up since the branches are so close knitted for the most part. I believe they pay more than the other commercial banks (Chase, Wells) and it is not as hectic. But I think we all know being a teller in general does not pay much.
cons: They can have you work up to 40 hours (full time) but your benefits such as PTO and vacation time would be the amount for a part time worker. So if I took a day off it would only cover a 4 hour day.

advice: Keep up the good work and I am  proud of being working in Citi.  There are lot of technology solutions are implemented in Silo in various regions and should be integrated for cost optimization and to leverage across the region to improve both top line and bottom line growth.
pros: Nice team and part of very big team. Leadership is good at Sr. management level. Good brand name. Variety of technology to work with.
cons: Team is distributed across many places including various offshore places. Communication is difficult but team is good, so one can pull thru.

advice: Continue with recognition programs, providing feedback and encouraging growth opportunities
pros: Great people, great benefits and plenty of opportunities for those that are motivated, ambitious and want to excel. I have been with the company for 8 years and the experience, education and skills I have learned could not have been taught in a classroom. Very positive culture with unique appreciation programs.
cons: Not to many cons, it's what you make of. Insurance cost has increased over the years and annual increases are low, but this is also based on your employment level and monthly/ annual performance reviews.

summary: Great people, closed in slow and very hierarchical structure
advice: Get more flexible. People are your greatest asset, invest in those that want to make company a better place not those that are following what have been good fore years. Risk have to be taken to achieve greatness.
pros: Great people with a lot of knowledge and experience. World wide company, that is recognized in many areas. Great benefits.
cons: Very hierarchical, slowly changing. Closed to even greatest ideas if they didn't come from proper level of hierarchy. Well established and followed rule of "sign door", you can only do what your doors have been assigned to.

advice:
Keep up great momentum on development and innovation. 

Address the known toxic work environment quickly, we have lost too many great people.
pros:
Company has done a great job in product development, marketing strategy, book-balance sheet management and restructuring.

Some of those initiatives have started to show great return on investment, especially with great product suits to cross sell to clients across regions.

Company cultivates self ambition, self enriching, and independence to excel, and to be the only winner.
cons:
Silo and self preservation mentality are not a taboo. 

There are pockets of "old boys" clubs around, and too many old-timer "bullies" with the self enriching attitude.

summary: Customer Service is great but they need to do some major upgrades
advice:
A massive update to your operating system and account opening applications would do absolute wonders.
STREAMLINE!!! The banker should not have to switch between two systems to help customers or search for documents that should print out pre-filled at account opening.
pros:
They really do take care of the customer.
Free trips to Cali for training.
cons:
Their systems are extremely outdated and nothing streamlined.
Still doing wet signatures(were not in the 90's anymore)
So outdated they still use DAS programs.
Business accounts take hours because of all the paperwork you have to search for, fill out manually, and print.

advice: CEO should be more communicative to firm about whats happening in a non formal way. Still have senior MD heads operating in Silos and not working together with partners to bridge that, each business is still out for themselves. Services should be delivered seamlessly to all clients even if they reside in a different business and qualify for a solution - Suggestion, hire an internal global team to go throughout the bank and uncover areas where if the businesses worked together & built partnerships, revenue and client satisfaction will increase by X.  Global bank but no partnership cross business to allow for global account opening for businesses or individuals - each time is a major struggle and poor experience for the client, start paying top performing internal employees! HR will watch a top performer say with 10 yrs experience leave and pay their new replacement 20% more a week later, makes absolutely zero sense - HR needs a total revamp/change from top down to change this mentality. Lastly, allow managers the time to hire quality candidates, headcount allocation comes and a week later pulled or used by another team. Immense pressure to hire in a very short time, often getting the wrong candidate just to have another body on the team. Flawed process and way of thinking.
pros: Global firm allows for mobility, solid pay, change occurring for the better under current leadership, NY Headquarter reno beautiful, smart diverse people, firm trying to come closer together which takes a lot of time but moving in the right direction.
cons: Everyone doing more with much less even as client base grows, middle managers overloaded with work, promotions without pay increase "dry promos", end of year performance rating system needs to be adjusted (forced rankings, bell curve), stale out dated systems where you can still not see say client info in real time. Cost of benefits rising & rising every year with very limited choices compared to other firms.

pros: Overall, great company to work for.  Interesting projects to work on, and the opportunity to work with global teams.
cons: Each time there was a change in upper management, the top priorities would change.  Although, it does make sense to assess potential changes, and definitely cancel certain projects, it does not make sense to kill a project when it is ready to implement and the investment has been made,  just due to the fact a new leader doesn't feel the value in the project.

summary: Citi Bank where people lack common sense
advice: You should all take a course on needs based selling. Vast improvements are needed to streamline the client account opening process. Less paper for consumer and business accounts. Utilize technology to deepen client relationships, systems are poorly built with misinformation. Branch support would give branch staff the run around in working to resolve clients issues. Back office gave me the incorrect information and  negatively impacted the client experience. The left hand doen't know what the right hand does.
pros: You will learn how to file paper and not build relationships with clients
cons:
Poor management
Poor systems
Poor training
Referring to partners is a mission
You get no support and you are on your own trying to resolve branch issues
Too much paperwork for consumer and business accounts
Lack technology to deepen client relationships
Poor commission structure

pros: Talented people are promoted and you can easily move between groups and departments. Quite pleasant corporate culture, people are generally respectful regardless if you are an employee or consultant. Work from home allowed but you are still usually doing 10-12-hour days.
cons: They often pay below market rate. Their benefits are quite poor for a large company (health plan covers only 90% of the costs). Very strict budget, travel not allowed and in most locations that don't even provide decent coffee. Very bureaucratic, like most other banks. No time left for family. You are expected to be on call 24/7.

advice:
When you promote staff to managerial positions please ensure that they get managerial training and her constantly being assessed on their continued ability to lead people.

In some teams,  a situation where a senior staff member simply appoints his crony and clans man/woman to a position of leadership without throwing the position open for team members to vie for, creates leadership by godfatherism, which is the opposite of meritocracy.
pros: Citi is a great company.  They have a strong brand. You can grow your career at Citi.
cons: Some managers lack professionalism and run their teams like an extension of their father's farms.

advice: Trust your employees, at our level, know how to do their job, unless given a reason to look into why they are not performing as expected.
pros: Having a hard time coming up with something. They have decent benefits.
cons: Too much management - I basically have 4 managers. New procedures are implemented as required immediately or even retroactively, without a developed process or introduction to the people who must comply.  It is a regulated business so I get the overkill in process, but I've worked for other businesses that have strict regulatory requirements that have much more streamlined process introduction.

advice: Listen to the employees on the front line and pay them well for their hard work.
pros: Good sales experience, higher base salary if transferring from another firm.
cons: KYC problems cause account closures, directors aren't hired based on merit, but political actions, private bankers are lazy and hurt branch performance, when someone is out bank managers are worked as personal bankers, but don't get paid for overtime. Extensive operations audit and bad (8 out of 10) customer survey scores can take away commission earnings. computers are 15 years old and they still use DOS based programs. Software constantly crashes and systems are slow.

summary: Great company to start your career
advice:
* Improve Infrastructure at each location since Citi is one of the biggest brands globally 
* More employee welfare activities
pros:
* Brand name
* Exposure- interacting with multiple vendors,  organizing and executing events, planning strategies to increase sales at your location,  executing marketing campaigns at local level
* Better work culture compared to companies in financial industry 
* 14 consecutive days mandatory leaves every year
* Good perks
cons:
* Not a very good infrastructure at some locations 
* Targets
* Too many compliance procedures,  though it is necessary,  but makes all the processes longer

summary: Overall a great place to work
pros:
- Pay is at the higher end of the market
- Lots of opportunities to work from home or full remote
- Career progression opportunities are plenty
- A lot of quality training for professional certifications available through udemy.
- 6% 401k match
- 22 days of vacations for VP level and above
cons:
- Work life balance has  not been great the last couple years.
- Company is very large and can be very bureaucratic.
- 401k match lump sum at the end of the first quarter following the performance year in which it is earned.

pros: Overall, the company has a great business in my geography, so it was not a revolving-door sort of workplace, with many colleagues having worked here in the long term. Liked that the firm was overall progressive and strategic in the way their planned their business. Employees are treated well and management sets good personal examples in terms of ethics and behaviour.
cons: There are politics, which I suppose is inescapable in any large organisation. The cost-consciousness practiced is a double-edged sword: rare for layoffs, but this also means bare-bones resources in terms of colleagues, so workload can be pretty heavy.

summary: I worked with some really good people
advice: Yes it is easy to move up if you get someone who likes and believes in you and if you show that you can and will work hard.  I want when an employee speaks, management listens and not try to fire them and shove things under the rug or aside.
pros: I lived working for Citibank. I started out at the 399 Park Avenue Branch as a teller and eventually worked myself up to Personal Banking Officer. I met some great people and I learned a LOT! I had fun and I worked very hard. The branch where I stated out had a daycare below so I was able to leave my son when I did not take him to his regular day care. They give you between 30 to sixty days a year to leave your child which I think is a huge plus. At first I was super nervous but then I got promoted the next year which made me question why I decided to take up a job as a notary public and a customer service officer. the benefits were great and if you get a supervisor to like you you move up very fast. Just be yourself. I had great bosses and some of them were not very nice to other people but they were nice to me. Learn as much as you can from anyone including the source and Citihelp.
cons: You will meet some very mean people and try to avoid them until you find out what is really bothering them. The one problem and greatest problem why I left was when my son got sick, was in the hospital. I had vacation time and I was told by Human resources that I could not get FMLA time off because I had only been there for less than 1 year. I could not believe my ears. I started in 2005 and and this happened in 2012. I could not take time off to take care of my kid and no matter how much I explained and tried to point out the massive mistake/error or deliberate act, they didn't listen. To say I was furious, very anxious and livid would be an understatement. On October 17th 2012, I quietly walked out of 401 west 42nd street, never to return. To add insult to injury, 1 month later I received a UPS letter from the manager, not from Human resources or the Area Director, telling me that because of the few days that I was out, even though I had vacation days, I was being terminated because I did not return or report to work, which was a huge lie. I never received an exit interview. This ladies and gentlemen is what and error or a deliberate act on the part of someone behind a computer can do to you. I say this with no malice because it is only the truth. I guess someone had a vendetta. I liked my job and I liked my coworkers even though they were a pain sometimes. There were things happening that Senior management, those behind the scenes knew about and did not want to speak about it or knew that the only way they could what they wanted was if I specifically moved out of the way. I have not since applied for a job there nor do I think I will ever again because what happened to me should never, ever happen to anyone else.

summary: Great Professional experiences with a world renowned company
pros: The opportunities are vast and wide at Citi.  On a daily basis, one has the privilege of working with people sitting right next to them, and around the globe.  In my experience, I have gotten the opportunity to help set up new call centers, call recording technologies, and manage software development projects for one of Citi's largest strategic programs.
cons: It is difficult at times to see how the scope of your individual assignment plays out in the larger picture of what Citi is doing as a whole.

advice: Re-capture the Citi that John Reed led.
pros: Well balanced matrix organisation.  Great and diverse culture.  I worked here for more than 12 years in various locations and enjoyed every minute of my journey.   Across all these locations I found that this organisation remains consistent in its treatment of staff and actively seeks to be balanced in its inclusiveness of diversity and an environment of non-discrimination.
cons: Ongoing Executive Management changes at the top of this organisation has left Citi vulnerable and caused this iconic brand to be almost destroyed in 2008

summary: Citi has always done right by me
advice: You are now moving in the right direction.  Don't repeat the mistakes of the past
pros:
Great opportunities for growth
Overall, since 2008, very competent senior management
Focus on goals, business objectives and execution
High emphasis on employee development
Global footprint
Very diverse.  A wonderful and interesting blend of cultures from all of the countries we operate in
Not perfect, but always raising the bar and striving to be the best in class
Lots of training available for employees to grow their skill set
cons:
Bureaucratic
Not very nimble
Highly regulated, as you would expect for a global bank

advice: Keep rewarding your team for a job well done, showing appreciation is a wonderful way to keep up worker's moral and motivation to do their job right.
pros:
great benefits
great work environment
Coworkers were amazing, and great support from Management
cons: If you don't like to be micro managed, this might not be the place for you. They watch when you go to the bathroom, when you go to lunch, and monitor every call and give you feedback at the end of the mont.

summary: A great place to experience and gain in depth knowledge about global banking.
advice: Immediate manager have no control or say on the employees performance review.  Corporate message and actual culture is not in sync. Management does not seek and/or value employees feedback
pros: One of the big banks, global presence, plenty of opportunity to move across businesses, portfolios and groups.  You get to work with diverse pool of talent across globe.
cons: No uniform corporate culture across different groups.  Some groups do not promote from within.  No formal training.  Compensation is below industry average.

summary: Big name, global company but SME work environment
advice: Work is not always a bed of roses. And things are not as it seems on the surface.
pros: Met new friends and learnt about processes and systems of a bank. Had a short stay in this company. Unable to provide much pros in this case. Probably a good company to add to the resume.
cons:
A place to stay of you are looking for little growth and minimal career advancement.
Management I had is stuck at looking at improving operation processes and having inefficient meetings. Less strategic and not forward thinking.

summary: A lot to do - Unbalanced Resource Allocation
advice: Make more investment into people.  Recognize the employees in the line who truly add value to the firm (not just their senior managers).
pros: The company will make investments in technology and processes.  Truly global company with opportunities in many different lines of business.  Good to employees in good times.
cons: Good to a handful of inner circle employees in challenging times.  The company tends to focus on the wrong areas for cost cutting.  Large degree of politics (compared to other same sized financial services firms).

advice: Continue to do what you are doing.  Support the employees and provide more training to advance to a high position.  Job well done.
pros: Great work environment.  Coworkers are very nice and all do their job.  Supportive coworkers.  New employee's are trained well and receive support after being placed at a branch.  Branch manager was down to earth and encouraged employees to perform at their best.
cons: No con's the work environment was very supportive.  Had fun working with the customers.  Training program helps new employees succeed at their job.

advice: Be kinder. Understanding. Respectful. Think before you speak. Try to give constructive feedback rather than how terrible everyone is at their job.
pros:
Great people 
Benefits
Salaried (albeit not enough...) 
Vacation (albeit not enough...)
cons:
SALES, SALES, SALES
Never good enough
Weekly, Monthly, Quarterly Coaching which will make you want to curl up under a rock and never come out.
Management that have either A) always worked for the company or B) are on a major power trip and this is all they have in their life.
DRAMA. 

Now, I worked at two different branches in different provinces -- one was awesome the other was so terrible I quit after 3 years without having another job to go to - the stress and hatefulness was too much. Nobody makes enough money to endure that.

pros: Great company to get your foot in the door. Much autonomy and opportunity to network with departments within the building. I had a wonderful experience, I highly recommend.
cons: You think that with bigger companies and internship programs that they would be more structured yet there were definitely times I found myself wanting work- and it all varied on your department and manager. But if you ask for the work you will receive it. Also have an idea what department you would like to be in prior to your interview- this will dictate your experience heavily.

pros: plenty of chances to move up the ladder, Citibank has many opportunities to learn and move to different departments, from the call center to back office research to online banking. I learned a lot in the research department, actually loved it.
cons: the only negative thing in my opinion was the pay, the saying "work hard and you will succeed, well not at Citi, we worked hard, but the pay never went up, out the 12 years I was there the total increase was 4 dollars, so went to Wells.

advice: Please do something about the systems! I know this is out of your control but when you talk to upper management, bring up issues about the outdated system and stop letting tellers with higher seniority get away with everything!
pros:
- Pay is great if you are dependent (not paying rent etc.) when looked at the location—NYC cost of living is ridiculous.
- GREAT coworkers and even a few amazing people in upper management. They become family but even with family comes drama. Managers are usually very caring.
- Healthcare is good.
- If you're part-time, you can work full-time hours especially in branches that operate in NYC since they're only open on week days.
cons:
- THE SYSTEM IS SO OUTDATED! I can bet every Citi teller will put this as the #1 complaint. They are ridiculously slow and from the 90s! Chase has a system that connects and pulls up all info simultaneousl—but with Citi you have to wait ages and take a million and one steps. ALSO, it crashes when it feels like—especially in the middle of the transaction!
- SURVEYS! Basically every branch and area is paid out based on scores from a surveys. Of course, other factors are included as well, but surveys are from teller, service, or sales experience and anything below a 9 is BAD. This is terrible if you work in Manhattan, where people have no patience to listen to you talk about surveys AND if people have issues with Citi as a whole, they give bad scores based on that.
- No work/life balance! If you're a student or have other commitments, forget it! Some managers are compromising but for the most part you have to bend over backwards to cover other tellers (tellers with seniority do whatever they want).
- If you work part-time, you work full-time. This can be a con for people who have other commitments outside of Citi. Obviously if someone is applying for a part-time position, they wish to work part-time hours. If you say no, you never hear the end of it. 
- Sales goals are unrealistic. Sales are also too political. If a banker or CRM is really close with a teller, they always give sales to that teller—even if it wasn't his/her referral. Only booked referrals count.
- Allowing non-customers to cash checks. This is so sketchy and upper management is complaining about fraud every other day. I don't know how they can expect us to properly figure out fraudulent checks and catch fake IDs when the system is crashing all the time. Seriously, get rid of this!

advice: Need a better system for identifying and developing talent at all levels. Different voices will enable you to challenge existing ways of thinking. Invest in external training for employees. Set clear, achievable goals and priorities for teams. Inspire.
pros: Some very talented people. Strong induction and internal training programs and events.
cons:
Sadly, the talented people are more likely to be your colleagues rather than your managers. 
Unnecessarily bureaucratic and political instead of getting on with the job.
Progress is slow.
Inability or lack of want by management to truly challenge the status quo.
Teams are under-resourced and expectations are unrealistic and ever-growing.

advice: Take a look at your people. Turnover is massive and growing - it's imperative to pay attention to your employees and make sure they feel recognized. Decent pay is one thing, but if people don't see opportunity for growth, they're going to keep leaving until you're left with those that don't care about improving.
pros: Job security, pay, and most of the people are great
cons: As most other large companies, everything moves slowly. A lot of people aren't recognized for the work they do and management never makes an effort to keep the people that they need.

advice: People who are very loyal to Citi are losing hope in the compliance department. It is a thankless job and at some point there will not be enough truly talented people to stay in an organization that right now seems to value audit over the skills that people traditionally needed to perform compliance roles.    There is a way to be more nuanced and add more skills but also convey that you very much value staff who have been there before you took over leadership. There needs to be more direct communication and greater focus on developing and retaining internal  talent, rather than just presuming that everyone externally is better than what you will find internally. Compliance is a very small market and if you really know what's going on you will soon find out that the small pockets of deep talent may be right in front of you  but at some point it will be too late because you are losing many of them. Maybe not losing them to other firms, but simply losing their ability to be motivated, energized and feel valued.
pros: Interesting business people, generally a place where they are developing interesting products and business ventures. Some smart people if you can get through the pockets of people who sometimes don't pull their weight.
cons: Compliance is in a complete state of disarray. There is new management constantly and very little focus on retaining talent and developing people. While there is a new chief compliance officer right now the division looks to be moving to become an audit division where compliance skills and experience are simply not even listed as part of the job descriptions.   JDs seem to be irrelevant right now for compliance management and it is unclear where the department is going.

advice: Focus on promoting within the company, and continue to stay ahead of the banks on the street.
pros: Global exposure, different project assignments, flexible work arrangements, visionary management team that truly care about your well being.  Work life is balanced and projects are meaningful.
cons: Visionary management Team without the proper senior management support, projects get completed only for a metric. No clear career progression path - have to wait till an opening is available but ends up being filled with external candidates or no clear upward mobility at all leaving employees feel they are compensated below market rate

advice: Check for teams that might not have a reason to exist, but have been in the company for a long time, having tasks that should belong to the team built for that.
pros:
Big company with a LOT of systems/servers and teams, constantly upgrading to latest technology and hardware.
Many people were able to move horizontally.
cons:
As a bank, IT is not the core of its business, therefore development teams have many junior members, with high rotation.
Tendency to have teams with duplicated tasks, and managers trying to keep that statu quo, just to have more people within them.

summary: good opportunities, depending upon manager and biz are
pros: worked there during financial crisis so part of tenure during turbulent times.  I did have many opportunities to move up, take on new roles, expand my skillset.  If the biz lead or manager were good, all was great. Otherwise, when a bad/toxic manager, you had to just wait it out until they left!  Re-orgs happen frequently, so sometimes waiting it out okay and a new opportunity will be around the corner
cons: Highly matrixed.  Lots of office pollitics. Promote being supportive of women's careers but more talk than action.

summary: Great people, Great benefits, Horrible Pay.
pros: the medical benefits are amazing.
cons:
It's a well known fact that employees that have been with the company for years are paid less than people coming in off the street.  Employees joke about the fact that  you have to quit, go to another company and then come back to get paid a decent salary. 
Many job titles are vanity titles, meaning you may be an "underwriter" at Citi but at another company you wouldn't hold the correct delegations and proper training and thus you can't get hired somewhere else because you aren't qualified.

advice: Value your employees... consider them more than just a number you need to look good for your boss... the manager i worked hardest for was the one who least focused on or berated his employees about how many calls/paymemts you got...
pros: Bonuses, benefits, time off without the guilt... location, there was a pre school for employee children, a bank, ups, good cafeteria, and so on.
cons:
Constantly changing the pay structure making it more and more difficult to get a bonus...
Managers consider you a number and onky your stats matter, not the quality of your work.

advice: Recognize the real stuff. Some people just do nothing but window dressing and still get paid a ton. What is important is to realize your real star and pay him more for his real stuff.
pros: Good recognition. Opportunity to grow, if you want to accept and take risks. Career mobility is a good option. There are a lot of positions that get opened up and you can really use them.
cons: Some politics in promotions. Rest is also luck. Sometimes moving across groups and sectors help you land a promotion faster.

pros:
+ Lots of responsibility and a great place to learn
+ Managers don't micromanage and the role is what you make of it
+ Great brand and some very talented and driven people
+ Generally supportive managers and colleagues
cons:
+ Bank is run by compliance and legal. Difficult to achieve targets in a very heavily regulated environment.
+ In some departments (especially technology driven) there is a lack of diversity
+ Overworked and no work life balance
+ Morale is extremely low in the workplace
+ people come in for a while and jump to the next role or company

summary: Citi...where you go to end your career
advice: Find a way to utilize and acknowledge the talent that has been acquired. There are a lot of good people that could be doing a lot more but they are not given the opportunity.
pros: Bankers' hours. Benefits, holidays a work life balance are great. There is never any pressure to work overtime or weekends. Good experience developing influencing skills in a large organization.
cons: It always seems to be restructuring and refocusing and reprioritizing instead of actually accomplishing goals. It's very slow to adapt to changes. Hard to move up.

advice: - do something please
pros:
- Citi's Brand Name
- Global footprint 
- Leading edge technology 
- Citi's alumni
cons:
- extremely poor work life balance 
- unfortunately folks stay late to 1) utilize the dinner allowance 2) not look like a loser since half/ 3/4 of the department is still hanging around doing ? not much .. 3) on meaningless bureaucratic hoops where a simple task takes 12 signatures of approvals, 24 email chains to cover one's back and aggresive show-down meetings where the one with the loudest voice wins.

summary: Still many years needed to catch up with street
advice: The company is too big to be effective and the strategy to off shore out of NY & London is making us not competitive
pros:
- The good people are really good and want to make it a better company technology wise
- Good base compensation
- Good vacation
cons:

summary: It Came From The Past--And Back It Should Go.
advice: Change your business model. Promising new FAAs that Smith Barney does things differently, then hitting them over the head with "cold call your family" or offering success stories that clearly violate current regulatory requirements isn't the way to stay in business. In fact, at one of the regional meetings, we were regaled with stories of a "successful" FA who literally stalked his prospects, following them around and spying on them. One speaker at their Manhattan headquarters was an ex-NJ cop (who I believe is still in charge of training) that talked about using his skills in the stake out to trail a judge. The judge told him if he wasn't a former cop, he'd have ended up in jail. Is THIS what you want your newest advisors to learn? It's this fast and loose mentality of getting the accounts and assets at all costs that created the mortgage mess, and just isn't what a company with a future needs to do. This whole experience soured my opinion of advisors, and I've permanently left the field.
pros: If you're the kind of person who doesn't mind selling an 85-year-old widow an annuity with a 10-year surrender charge, then this is the job for you.
cons: Management is stuck in the 1970s, crowing about the benefits of their experience in "the Lehman System" of cranking out calls, following the time zones and "gathering the assets." Of course, there's little regard for what happens to clients because you're just supposed to focus on "assets and account." In today's highly competitive market where clients can get many of the services provided by financial advisors on the internet, you need to focus on giving clients the benefits of working with you and only you--that takes time, and it's a relationship that isn't going to start with a dinnertime cold call. Sadly, unless companies like this change, they're going to go the way of the dinosaurs which, by the way, is what many people call management.
