summary: Constant change in deliverables and compensation plan with NO work/LIFE balance as announced by the Regional Manager
advice: Become consistent and place someone in the position of Area/Regional who are people oriented. Current mgmnt are like Wells Fargo churn and burn mgmt.
pros: Salary is higher than most - To much is given Much is expected and much more
cons: Changing goals - every quarter for the last 2.5 years. 3-4 conference calls per day, 4-5 if division wants to add their 2 cents.

summary: In the last seven year's it's been all about cost cutting...
advice: The top sets the tone. By the time it comes down to the end of the pyramid, it's all just a pep-talk.
pros: The best thing about working for a company like Citi is the name recognition. Possibility of transfer between the departments and relocation.
cons: An employee is just as small part of a big machine. It all depends on your immediate manager - he/she is a gatekeeper to your advancement.

pros: The benefits are outstanding! Once paid time off (PTO) is substantial you will enjoy a great paid vacation. Hours are very flexible just pick the right "team" to be on. There's an on site doctors office and also therapy sessions available.
cons: Very precise work ethic, time management is detrimental to working at Citi. If you're not a by the book person with time, this isn't the career for you.  Stuck to a phone with consumers all day

summary: Not a company where you can grow,you just have to follow the process,even when it doesn't makes sense
advice: The top management lay down rules without understanding ground realities and employees concern.In short,communication gap between top level and junior level/mid level
pros:
Good brand in the job market
Salary,incentives and benefits are decent
cons:
Too much process driven,which wastes lot of productive time
Strategies are never well defined
Can't take your own initiative
No trust of employer towards the employees
No flexibility for the employee job rotation/change within the company

advice: Manage more efficiently, utilize your resources
pros: Good vacation time and benefits, everything else was average. Salary may be slightly above average, maybe by $300 or $400.
cons: You are not challenged at work, the work flow is poorly managed. Very inefficiently run, it is hard to find true motivation at the job besides a paycheck. If you are a driven hardworking individual that wants to see a future in your career then avoid Citi, unless it is in NYC.

advice: Better time management.  I and my teammate hardly took our lunch time.  We ate in the office and sometimes we worked passed 10:00 pm to get the project deliver on time.
pros: In general, people are friendly.
cons: Long hours, too many projects at once.  The company lacks of structure.  One department doesn't share their information with the other department.  As a result, I and my team wasting lots of time looking for services from other departments.

advice: There needs to be a better approach to training. There method of training is to sit behind another analyst until you learn how to do it.
pros: This company is great on a resume. It has very good benefits with decent pay. Management really knows how to motivate
cons: The is little to know growth with this company. There are also no raises; and if there are raises they range from 5 to 12 cents.

advice: Mostly a great place.  Integrate contract employees better with existing staff to make more welcome and be part of the organization if possible.
pros: Well structured, interesting work.  Great employees.  Great campus.  Learned lots of skills.  Would recommend to others.  Very professional and great resources.  Excellent opportunities.
cons: Location.  Requires long travel on extremely busy road, I-9 and I-275, making a long commute.  Would have preferred better integration with existing staff.

advice: Stop trying to get everyone to drink the Kool-aid and actually fix the problems.
pros: International organization with fairly strong reputation. Management tries though are far from extraordinary. Can occasionally work from home, etc.
cons: Fairly small player in private banking space compared to other banking goliaths, but they expect you to compete without the staff or same support.  Compliance.....dear God.....compliance. It's terrible and makes the whole organization less effective and is often completely mistargeted. FINRA's fault, but still a major con.

advice: Keep true to your credo of being a "technology company with a banking license." Innovation is key in the technology industry, balance that out with the regulations of finance.
pros: It's a very large company with a lot of resources. They are very patient with new graduates, and provide many useful training sessions.
cons: The compensation for their technical employees compared to other Wall Street Banks is lacking. There is a lot of red tape when trying to get almost anything done.

advice: I don't know what to say. I hope the firm just to keep up with what it is doing right now. Citi in South Korea is very competitive bank which easily outstrips regional banks there.
pros: Immense learning opportunity. You get to work with nice and competent people. Free lunch is sometimes provided.
cons: The working hours are not very good. You are not paid for overworking. The pay is not high compared to the amount of tasks you are given.

summary: Citi is a wonderful call center to work for, I am just looking to get into a new field of work.
advice: It isn't conducive for job satisfaction with employees when you encourage your workers to tattle tale on one another like we are all in elementary school again.
pros: The best reasons to work here are the pay and the excellent benefits.
cons: The work schedule isn't always flexible. Employees are encouraged to "tattle" on one another creating a somewhat hostile work environment.

advice: The intern programme could be better integrated to normal work, so as an intern, I could feel more worthy to the team.
pros: People there are generally nice and helpful, and the culture is quite open. The intern programme is well structured with training and sharing sessions.
cons: People are nice so they will spare time to teach me and hand me things to work on, but I feel what I did and my post is pretty redundant to be honest.

advice: I am not in a position to advise anything to management as the company is performing well and continues to improve its core business and reputation.
pros:
Good career opportunities as the company prefers to hire within the organization.
Good ethical standards.
Thought leadership.
Good policies and procedures in place.
cons:
In some offices the work culture is more focused on long hours and less work/life balance.
The IT systems are very confusing and it is very complicated to request to use a simple program.

advice: KDS needs a major improvement. The nicest employee can still get a 0 just because the customer was in a rush. The employee was just respectfully doing his/her job. Did i mention, half the time the customer doesn't even remember the employee?
pros: Great benefits. I mean you get the whole 9 yards. Paid 10 days vacation, week of sick days,  holidays off, and great insurance!
cons: KDS; a system upper management created that just didn't make sense for any of us.

advice: Not really much to say. They seem to change management frequently there. Overall working environment was decent. Would be nice to have a bigger gym for employees.
pros: Good program and rotation allows one to see different groups before making final decision for associate. Location is a plus thanks to the many restaurants and bars in TriBeCa.
cons: Not as prestigious as other banks. Career trajectory may not be great if stays here. Might be good as a starting point though.

advice: Implement more clearly defined lines of communication between businesses and departments to reduce redundancies. Also, teams should work together and encourage growth in each other, as competition often stunts progress at Citi
pros: Great Benefits, pay in line with industry salaries. Many opportunities for promotion and to switch business areas.
cons: Too much bureaucracy. Lack of communication between business units and working groups, where the same project may be done by 3 or 4 separate groups without their knowledge.

advice: Take a good look at who's running operations day to day.  Some of the worst professionals I've ever met were in these positions; it's costing you business today and even worse, tomorrow's 'bench'.  Fix it.
pros: Firm is truly global, some employees are nice and work can be interesting (depending on where you are).
cons: Pay is terrible-arguably worst on wall street, politics and the personal/financial interests of managers are primary catalyst of business decisions (especially for promotions, bonuses, hiring/firing decisions).

advice: Identify people that are actually doing the job and weed out bad seeds that are collecting paychecks and holding the team back
pros: If you are someone that is happy where you are and can put up with inter office politics then it is a great place to be at . Good benefits, flexible work schedule, decent pay
cons: Not a great place if you are looking to advance in your career at a steady pace

advice: Efficient planning as to the role description is required. No defined roles within the organization currently. Also, skill set matching for roles should be done
pros:
- Compensation is good as compared to industry standard
- Learning potential is good
- Personal Growth and skill set development
cons:
- Organizational Culture
- Manager dependency is high, and it depends how is he to guide you ahead for your future at the company
- Compensation growth is poor, 1 (highest)  rating person gets 6% growth

summary: No work life balance but good benefit
advice:
Fix your policies, follow working hour as per offer. 
Employee comes first.
pros:
Good benefit 
Multi tasking 
Good career and and growth 
Good career start for fresh graduate to be able to work under stressful environment 
Able to demand on salary
cons:
No work life balance, can meet 75 hours per week 
Heavy workload especially on month end. 
Rude customers.
No tolerance for employees  unless work is settled. 
Will be transferred without your consent at anytime, anywhere.

summary: TTS- it’s all about who you know
advice: Take a long hard look at how many people have left TTS in the past few years and how much knowledge has walked out the door.  It’s  time for the management to do some introspection and remove their blinders. The managers who have caused the exodus seem to be thriving while morale is at an all time low. USD clearing and payments/receivables teams are prime examples of this exodus.
pros: Global company offers opportunities to relocate if you  have your managers support
cons: Lacks meritocracy. It’s all about who you know. You have to be part of the “boys club” to have any chance of growth.

summary: Not as good as the hype
advice: Think more about employees outside of NY; we matter too. Add more infinity groups and programs for us. All opportunities seem to be in NY.
pros: Remote work is permitted and some of the people are decent to work with.
cons: Too contractor heavy.  Opportunities slim to none at Wilmington source. Definitely feels like a satellite office. Negotiate salary coming in. Pay increases very small; bonuses are horrible and not as promised. Management focus more in getting out of consent orders than employee development. Many times requiring employees to go well beyond what they were hired to do without providing clear direction. Too many senior management changes.

summary: Good place, wish they paid more
advice: Please pay your employee more and what they are worth. Why are other companys paying their Sr Supervisor 10K more a year. Thats not right and why im looking outside the bank after 11 years
pros: Has great benefits and its very flexible
cons: pay is awful. they need to pay what other banks pay. They have not increase an exempt salary is a very long time. Yet they will keep increasing the no -exempts

pros: Work-life balance is great as a tech employee. Workload is almost always minimal
cons: You won't grow here or be challenged. An old company with old employees, many plan to retire here. Tech is old, clunky, outdated. Management is poor, employee morale is low, the culture is one of apathy and indifference. Promotions are based on time at the company, not performance. Performance reviews are based on your manager's opinions only, not the coworkers you work with daily

advice: Don't play with careers to satisfy egos. Give people the opportunity to choose their path instead of forcing it on them.  Don't give options after they resign. If you value an employee, give them the option to move departments before they leave.
pros: Good perks, depends highly on the team you work for, decent pay and holidays
cons: No direction, too many clashes between seniors, its a cost centre, focus on automation irrespective of whether it brings in that Efficiency or not.

summary: Massive Bureaucracy. Quality of Management is Hit or Miss....
pros: Compensation was very competitive with the market
cons: Citi is massive and complex. Every Business / Function generally works in its own silo, so getting much accomplished is a challenge. Quality of senior management can be hit or miss. For many years, I had great managers. At the end, my manager was more like Napoleon. I was surprised that he wasn't managed out, rather than being given more responsibility....

advice: Get a job you LOVE!! If it’s not helping people to become the best they can at their job, you’re in the wrong field. More passionate managers are needed who genuinely care about the overall success of the employees, the business unit and company as a whole.
pros: Great company, awesome with ensuring work home life balance, upper management very aware of employees needs and accommodating especially during this pandemic
cons: Depending on the department, management is sub par at best.

advice: In Consumer, centralize structure to create executional accountability. Replace business optimizers with people who can grow the business by addressing customer needs and start racking up some organic wins.
pros: Reasonably strong / respected brand among industry participants. Significant resources to tap. Global client services.
cons: Consumer bank is stacked with business optimizers.  Very few business owners who have innovated AND grown revenue post crisis. Slow growth has eliminated personal growth opportunities and created a culture of self preservation among management.

advice: Re-engineer your entire hiring/selection process to be more responsive.
pros: Benefits, flexibility and stability of the organization
cons: The hiring process is extremely long.  You apply and don't know anything after that.  It is as if it goes into a black hole.

summary: Great company overall but terrible retention
advice: Make sure all your employees are being paid market value and that more junior employees don't come in making more than their seniors and mentors.
pros:
Good 401k matching
Bank holidays and 4 weeks paid PTO
work flexibility
Great technology stack
cons: Does not work to retain employees. Prefer to hire from other teams or new grads and pay them more than current senior employees. When confronted with the facts they use the management ladder as excuse for it.

summary: Okay place to work if you have the right team
advice: Be vocal! Communicate with your teams on a real level not just "we need numbers!"
pros: Pay and benefits are decent.
cons: High stress work environment, very sales and numbers driven. They preach they want to do what is best for client but really only care about making money. Lots of meetings that are redundant. High turnover rate. Lots of software issues and glitches. Some back office processes are inefficient causing issues.

summary: It’s just like most Corporate America companies
advice: Put some thought into hiring and layoffs, stop using old tech, pay people what they’re worth, make people feel valued, and stop with the cheesy and pointless trainings.
pros: Benefits, health initiatives, facility is nice, gym is great, I worked for some really great people.
cons: You’re just another number, you always know you’re disposable, mass hirings and layoffs, the company is built to impress shareholders.

summary: Good company until you get a good boss
advice: Minimal training to existing staff would be beneficial instead of hiring outside cheap labor
pros: Great Remote work opportunity (Depending on the boss you get)
cons: Non-technical boss leading technical team in turn encouraging the people who talk their language. No room for growth. Outsourcing and offshoring often leading to layoffs or forcing relocations. Internal positions moves don't happen as they hire contractors and lay off employees, resumes just go into black hole.

pros: Good pay and opportunity for bonuses.
cons: I cannot stress this enough- TERRIBLE management, terrible work hours (often they offer you can switch shifts when you perform well but it is still impossible), discourage employees from actually helping card members but rather focus on metrics, no team work, the list goes on. Anyone reading this, please protect your mental health and run the other way! The only reason this company pays well is because of the excessive stress.

jobTitle: Product Manager, Payments & Liquidity (Treasury & Trade Solutions)
summary: Interesting work, structure and benefits could be better
advice: Make the benefits more competitive
pros: People at regional and country levels are typically very competent and helpful. Also, there is a lot of focus on innovation and digitization, which allows to work in some interesting projects.
cons: Benefits (especially the bonus) in TTS is much lower compared to other departments like coverage and markets. Also, on some issues the ownership is not clear, resulting in a lot of friction with other departments.

pros:
definitely lots of opportunities to find projects that interest you
teams allow ample time for you to learn what you need so don't feel like you have to know everything at once
culture and people great
pay is very good, no complaints
cons:
really depends on the team you're on
some really practice and enforce having work-life balance
some work all day, everyday of the week and the demands for things to be done almost makes you feel like you have to

advice: Culture is very different depending on where you work in company, NY employees getting frustrated with lack of pay increase opportunity, listen to employees more and be more cognizant of burnout based on hours you are asking people to work
pros: Ability to move around company and get different experiences, overall good benefits and 401k match
cons: Ability to make decisions (very bureacratic), long hours are valued, lack of boundaries (work requests coming in all the time frequently interrupting weekends)

summary: Its always best to work with CITI
advice: Be as you are :D
pros: work environment is good also people are friendly and the seniors are approachable. Work is allotted as per the position and seniors make sure that work is done on time with quality
cons: working hours can be hectic at times and can be stressful too but then this is like any other organisation would offer too but CITI is different in lot of ways.

summary: a very large corporation with a lot of employees
advice: have better communication with front-line employees since we are the most likely to recognize problems and suggest solutions.
pros: great benefits and decent pay.  lots of paid time off and pretty flexible hours
cons: can be very stressful especially around tax time (feb through april); customers are often unreasonable and demanding.  also, a lot of red tape and old computer systems which makes it hard to do your job effectively sometimes

summary: Positive overall, make you work, but good benefits
advice: Enhance management capabilities. Make them focus more on people rather always on results - results will follow. Some Managers take advantage of their position against employees by treating them unfairly. Keep checks and balances on management skills. Promote on merit not on buddy system. Internal jobs are generally always settled beforehand.
pros:
Benefits
Employee Surveys
People of all ages
Chance to work in any area
cons:
Bureaucratic
Technical Managers lacking basic management skills but call themselves people managers

summary: Not a bad place to work, but get your money on the way in.
advice: I am grateful to have a job, but there is really no incentive for me to kill myself to get a good rating if there is no payout to accompany it.
pros: Global bank.  Great technology. Great place to learn.
cons: Compensation continually dwindling, even for solid performers.  Facilities shrinking -- SVPs are now sitting in open cubes that used to be for call center personnel.

advice: Please buck up and understand that you can trust the other folks in your circle and just the ones you like.
pros: Lots of Business Communication, Good for Start to Middle management
cons: HR review process and systems are very outdated. Every dept and group have their process, no consistency in review and the top level promotions are locked and the rankings are based on who they want to promote next not who has performed in that year

advice: Spend the money, hire good talent.
pros: It is a more laid-back atmosphere, and in most cases provides good work-life balance.  Working from home remote is on a more widely accepted.
cons: Spends considerable effort defeating itself with excessive bureaucracy, and a simple lack of planning, and good decision making.  Better execution would result with higher quality people, yet Citi seems to look at IT Talent as a commodity and still relies too-heavily on out-sourcing.

summary: Great company in need of some improvement
advice: Focus more on quality of work as opposed to quantity which affects team moral and animosity due to poor service being provided.
pros: Pleasant work experience as a telecommuter in loss mitigation and great benefits.
cons: Very little preparation is given when starting a position and new employees entering our team  had to "learn as you go" and maybe received some help from a co-worker willing to assist you if you are fortunate.

pros: Citi has the best work/life balance I've ever heard of.  Kudos!
cons: If you're an IT professional stay away from Citi.  Morale is low, the pay is uncompetitive with other firms.  Citi is in the process of trying to outsource most of the technology teams.  The teams that not outsourced with mostly be moved outside of the NYC area to places like Texas  where the cost of doing business is cheap.

pros:
- Great Culture, environment
 - Employee friendly / Flexible work policies (2-3 work from home options)
 - Emphasis on Work life balance
 - Wealth of opportunities to work in different areas and location
 - Extremely talented people 
 - Highly competitive environment
cons:
- Work Pressure
-  Highly process driven ( this is at times irritating as for the smallest thing in the world you will have to follow a standard procedure)

summary: Analytics Team - Good place to work!
advice: Year end bonuses should improve - Little more liberty at employees end to choose projects
pros: Good Work - Good Infrastructure - Smart Colleagues - Awesome exposure as a starter in comparison to other companies - Decent pay - Best Leave Policy
cons: Bad training's - Self growth depends largely on your manager - Year end bonuses and increments suck at times - Too much gossiping within the office << Promotes bad work culture >>

advice: policies are very employee unfriendly. management is totally uninvolved whenever an employee is not producing to standards. at other companies, employees are the most valuable asset, not at Citi. Produce or die.
pros: had a 20 year plus career. enjoyed many interesting assignments
cons: one bad year, didn't produce enough sales and I was dismissed. Received no support from management, unlevel playing field, lot's of favortism. management frightened to make any decisions. it's all about the widgets, nothing else.

advice: take better care of your people and customers.   Don't flip in and out of businesses.
pros: brand recognition, global leader, good pay, lots of internal opportunities, bright people, global opportunities.
cons: highly complex organizational structure, in and out of businesses, constant layoffs, no job security, cant make up their mind about strategy.   starts a business, hires a bunch of people, then lays them off.   works on antiquated platforms.

summary: What you would expect of a call center
advice: Be impartial and value your employees
pros: Steady work with reasonable pay
cons: You are a number.  In this office the work you do has little bearing on how you are treated.  Unless you are one of the few favorites how you do on a call will be picked apart and failed while the same call from a favorite will be considered perfection.  Just dont aggravate

summary: Forget your family life.They expect you around the clock and frequently. No appreciation how hard you work
pros: Vacation policy is good, Provided  you can take it.
cons: Too long work hours including working in weekends. Benefits are not at all great. More of the cost is pushed over to the employees. They give work deadline in the evening and expect it to be done that night. Don't hire enough workers Poor management, Always in a put-out fire mode, due to unrealistic deadlines

advice: When filling top level positions internally, don't reorganize to sooth the egos of those who didn't get the job.
pros: Global organization with plenty of opportunities.  Decent work-life balance and very flexible with regard to working remotely when needed.
cons: Still a bit top heavy when it comes to senior management.  Very bureaucratic, but things are starting to improve.  Need a little more organization focus - trying to do too much with too little.

summary: Decent place to work. Smart, dedicated people. Leadership needs some work.
advice: Invest in your employees, weed out the brass that aren't genuinely contributing.
pros: There are quite a few opportunities to be involved in new things - while the culture isn't necessary going to open doors for you, if you ask for new experience and to be involved in new things managers are generally receptive - of course there are always exceptions. Telecommuting is a perk.
cons: Turnover. Staff layoffs. Meager salaries.

advice: Best in class computer systems lead to best in class business.  Citi's are inferior and your customers know it.  Also, the KDS survey scoring system/score card weighting is just a way to take money out of the branch's pockets. You are losing good employees over this.
pros: Better pay than many banks.
cons: Inefficient systems - full of "work-arounds" instead of fixing software - leading to errors, slow service, frustrated employees and customers, missed referral/sales opportunities.

summary: A good place to build a career!
advice: Keep seeking talented people who want to build a career and not just a paycheck. That is why Citi has been in the marketplace since 1912.
pros: Global bank that will allow for you to grow in many different departments within the company. A good work life balance at Citi.
cons: Citi has an opportunity when it comes to pay and pay increase, but in the end everyone feels that way about the job.

advice: Designate only the people that need to be in meetings and allow the team leads to be accessible to the engineers.
pros: It was a very friendly group of engineers. They have a mentorship program setup which helps new employees come up to speed in a fairly short time.
cons: The team leads and management were always in meetings. It was tough to get the approval of the leadership to progress on your workout being that they were constantly absent.

pros: Very large company that hires people at entry level with no experience necessary.  Lots of career options in the world of credit card services.  You can move to other areas of the business if you are motivated, build relationships, and network effectively.
cons: It can become very monotonous and fulfilling if you do not strive to be the best and move into new positions.  Wages are minimal and raises are small

advice: Priority should be on customer service, not sales.
pros: It's an easy job. You sit at a desk and talk to customers. The benefits are good. Training is great, and they do teach you how to sell well. They try to keep the work environment fun and upbeat.  You can make more if you can sell the customers. Good vacation and benefits.
cons: The pay isn't great, pressure is high for sales product add-ons. Heavy on sales pressure, talktimes, hold times, etc.

summary: not bad, but there are better companies out there
pros: good coworkers, it's a huge company so there is room for growth, work-life balance can be achieved if you have a family and need some flexibility around your schedule.
cons: too big and too bureaucratic at times which makes it very difficult to get stuff done being you depend on so many different individuals/team across different functions/locations, compensation (if you have been with the company for a long time, you are probably underpaid)

summary: Unprepared management, laborious unnecessary time-wasting procedures and repetitive unhelpful training.
advice: Promote, retain and adequately compensate mortgage department employees who understand the history of mortgage processes and "get it" as opposed to promoting and tolerating employees who appear to be retained and promoted because they have learned to "play the game".
pros: Benefits and 401k company match
cons: Immediate management, supervisors  over reacting to agency rules, focusing on unnecessary laborious processes and missing the value of combining common sense with guidelines.

pros: Work / life balance if more than perfect. You can take off at 5pm if you do what you are supposed to do and you can get decent salary. very easy to get day-off. the company has good brand image in the region.
cons: The  job is not challenging at all and very routinely. Thus no opportunity for self-growth. Financial products provided are not different from other financial institutions and fees bit more expensive. so it is difficult to sell.

summary: International employee working for Citi International
advice: Promote meritocracy and show more transparency.
pros:
Working in Citi gives you a lot of international visibility. It's multinational environment is quite enriching professionally.
Citi is a value-driven company which facilitates working with integrity and being respected.
cons:
Working in silos is the biggest challenge that Citi needs to fight against.
Work-life balance is difficult to achieve.

Lack of communication on Senior Management decisions to lower levels on strategic decisions and their rationale behind them.

advice: Actually have regular employee engagement meetings and take action.  Usually engagement meetings resulted in no action like 90 percent of the time.
pros: Decent pay.  Flexible benefits and insurance plans, as long as you take the time to read the package thoroughly.
cons: Inconsistent messages and expectations from multiple levels of management.  Remote access available but rarely rarely approved to use.  Workload problems usually have to balloon before management takes action and approves overtime.

summary: Enjoyed the time I spent there.
pros: Work was interesting and challenging. Banking applications present unique challenges in terms of both security and transaction volume, so the work was never boring. Colleagues were in general smart and capable. Was fortunate to work on a talented  team with a great management hierarchy. Compensation and benefits were competitive.
cons: Unfortunately most of our work was moving to Texas, so I decided to seek other opportunities locally rather than relocate. Sometimes the hours were brutal.

advice: Stop thinking of technology as a distinct entity - your very survival depends on having a great technology platform. You are basically a technology company now.
pros: Great in terms of meritocracy and mobility. Citi has some truly talented people. When it gets its act together, Citi can be and is a market leader
cons: Too disjointed at times, people and teams tend to work in silos too often leading to much wasted potential, lack end-to-end coordination

summary: Provided assistance with the Home Depot consumer credit card
advice: Better to be overstaffed than understaffed as we were throughout 2014
pros: Decent pay, no script to follow, work at home position, full benefits and 401k, full 40 hour work week with plenty of overtime
cons: Home Depot customers are completely retarded. The level of stupidity in most THD customers was staggering. The only reason I left the job was the customer base

advice: Keep treating your employees the way you do! Try to give the new junior analysts more encouragement to go above confines of job descriptions
pros: Great Company, Room to move up, decent benefits. The company is well established and the practices within the culture make you proud to work for Citi
cons: Sometimes a lot of tasks, boring, menial work. while its possible to move up, its not easy.  Salaries are not as competitive as other analyst positions in the area

jobTitle: Assistant Vice President of Information Security
summary: Lots of Perks in the Facility
advice: Add more office space and parking in Tampa. Ensure each employee meets his supervisor face to face
pros: Pay was good along with benefits. The campus had great facilities to include an on staff doctor!
cons: Tampa campus was over crowed and we had to share desks or work at home with our own personal computers. The company is very big so I never got to meet my boss face to face.

summary: New snr managers aren't very honorable.
advice: Simplify processes. Focus on things that really matter and be clear and direct with future plans. Cut out the sneaky political agendas at the top and stop creating silos.
pros: Good work / life balance. Great comp and for the most part good direct team leaders.
cons: Individuals running the U.S. CB are new to the segment and shaking things up too much. Need to get back to basics and stop micro managing and changing proven processes.

advice: There should be a better effort to train people as managers, rather than assuming someone who is technically good at their job is therefore going to be successful as a manager.
pros: Many opportunities for career growth both locally and globally. Training and development is emphasized for employees. There is also a great focus on community involvement.
cons: The Buffalo location takes a back seat to New York City, so advancement to the higher levels of management is more restricted there.

advice: talent retention 101

If you are planning to join Citi India (CSIL) and trying to collect information, I would recommend to please read it till end, although it might be bit lengthy.

First thing, what is CSIL. Its one of the two legal entities of Citicorp in India (Citibank & CSIL). The idea of forming this company was plain and simple – Cost Saving. As Citi had outsourced most of its IT business to other IT service companies, So by cost perspective it made sense to top management that what if we start our own IT service firm in a low cost country like India and in-source some of the IT business back to Citi.  So, CSIL was formed as a regular IT service organization which will hire IT people, get the project, deliver it to Citi and get paid by Citi by number of hours their employee spent on execution of that task..like any other service company. Make sense to save cost, but does everyone in Citi on-boarded by this idea... HELL NO. People sitting in US at middle management has their own agenda, Vendors who are in Citi for years and suppose to handover their tasks has their own agenda, people sitting here in CSIL has their own and this has started a mess rather than a place to work.

Let me explain why. Most of the Citi IT employees in US are Indian. They are there for many years and when they started to realize that if things will be started getting delivered from India, ultimately they will be asked to go back. Whats the point of paying a manager in US when his entire or most of the team is in India. This started a triangular fight for survival. Companies which are handling Citi's IT for long are not happily handover their task to CSIL for obvious reasons, IT managers sitting in US are supporting them so that they can see CSIL fail and stay put in US. They started recruiting those vendor resources on Citi's payroll in US and building a team there to justify that some critical tasks are being handled by Citi Employees and the management at CSIL India is fighting to get projects from Citi and show them as delivered to prove their significance. So, when you join CSIL, first you have to fight for good work that is not at all there. Only substandard work that Citi employees in US or their vendors doesn't want to do, comes to CSIL. So after 8-10 years if you was asked to do work that is not going to add anything in your career, its not logical to do just for money. Obviously CSIL is paying better then Indian IT service companies because they are replacing people sitting in US by CSIL so even if they are paying little bit extra, its just a fraction of US pay. But the main thing is 'work and learning' and only thing you can learn is office politics to get some relevant work so that at the end of year you have to show something. 

The worst nightmare (which is the most of the case in CSIL) is if your manager is sitting in US. Since he/she doesn't like the idea of CSIL for the reason I explained above, he might schedule a call at mid-night. If top management is forcing vendors to handover some important project to CSIL, your call might be scheduled at their post lunch hours, so you have to be awake till 2 AM and see call gets canceled at 1.50 AM. Everything is happening here because everyone is trying to survive and save their jobs. You might get a designation which might be so fascinating like AVP or VP but get ready to be dictated by these vendor resources because most of them are in Citi for 8-10 years and god know what they are doing for so long in US. 

Now the management of CSIL, they are already amused and just trying to save their highly paid jobs. In every management call, they have to listen that this center is not performing, attrition rate is always around 30%, so why should not close this center or sell it to some other IT service provider. With the reputation CSIL is building, it will not take long that either CSIL or some of the units that are not performing will be sold off. And for this reason, it seems they are not investing much on this center. Very simple things, like there are no automated HR software..even if you have to declare your investments, it will be just in a homemade portal and after declaring you can't view it ever again!!! People are sitting in meeting rooms as the place is cramped etc etc. Obviously, CSIL is just an experiment and if you are going to join it, please be ready to be a part of that experiment. 

There are lots of other things. If you know anyone there, just pickup the phone and ask how bad it is. And even after going through this review, you are going to join Citi for any reason – Welcome to the mess and please be sure to get an exit plan ready :).

summary: Toxic, arrogant, no controls, puts themselves above customers, poor record keeping, read on . . .
advice: Considering the firm is essentially insolvent (as of the end of 2008--with about $2 trillion of assets and only $131 billion of equity, the firm's equity value would be wiped out with a write-down of about 6.5% of assets, not unheard of in this environment), I think they have worse problems than their employee relations. pros: There are no good reasons to work for this company.  They treat their employees extremely poorly. As an employee, you are just a number.  They expect loyalty, but they give none to employees.  It is highly dysfunctional and business division heads resent one another.  There is no incentive for anyone to work together.   The culture is toxic and bankrupt.
cons:
1) Abusive supervisors and institutional apathy:  I worked for this organization for 4.5 years and was promoted twice.  My supervisor had an extremely hot temper and continually verbally abused his employees.  Despite complaints to HR and notes on his performance review, his behavior did not change.  In fact, he was promoted.

2) Treatment of former employees:  I left my job in the summer to attend graduate school and used my accrued vacation when I quit.  When I left the firm, my supervisor approved my vacation and my official end date was clear (and in the HR system).  Despite this, the firm continued to pay me via direct deposit for two pay periods.  Once they discovered this, they had to ask me when my end date was because their HR systems were in such disarray.  I asked me supervisor for details about how I was to repay the amounts and he passed it off to HR.  I received a letter from HR two months later simply requesting that I pay a flat amount.  I immediately sent a certified letter to Citi's "overpayment coordinator", my old supervisor and HR requesting data on the dates of the payments, the amounts of the payments, a statement that they would correct my W-2 and confirmation that they actually withheld taxes that they claimed they were owed.  No one bothered to reply to my letter.  1.5 months later, I received a call from a bill collector from CitiFinancial on Christmas Eve demanding that I return her call by 2 PM that day.  I called the bill collector and was spoken to quite tersely like I was a criminal or a deadbeat borrower.  I again reiterated my request to the bill collector and she claimed to be sending the data that I requested.  I have yet to see this data.  To date, I have not repaid the company because they cannot provide the data that they would provide an employee on a pay stub.  

3) Immobility:  I was promoted twice, but because of my abusive supervisor, sought work in other departments.  Citi's HR policies required that a supervisor "release" an employee to take a position with another department.  This made it virtually impossible to move to a different department without quitting the firm.

4) Restricted stock lost when returning to school:  I accumulated a substantial amount of unvested restricted stock after working for the firm for 4.5 years (most of my compensation was in the form of bonus, of which 25% was paid in unvested company restricted stock).  When I quit to return to graduate school to upgrade my skills, the firm required me to forfeit the unvested restricted stock that I had earned.  Such a practice is intended to prevent employees from leaving to go to other competitors.  The affect was to punish an employee for wanting to upgrade their skills.  I have no incentive to return to the firm.  I told HR this, but they did not seem to care.  They did not seem to care that they alienated a potential future employee, who would potentially be able to recruit classmates (from a top MBA program).  Clearly, they have no interest in long-term retention of employees.

5) Extremely political:  Relations among business divisions are extremely dysfunctional.  I witnessed this after working in a staff position that dealt with the management of each top division.  They do not talk to one another and approach other business divisions in an adversarial manner.  The resulting culture is extremely toxic.  This system encourages employees not to work together and to develop deep-seated, bitter resentment toward their colleagues in other divisions.  

This list could go on!  I was somewhat annoyed while working for them, but became enraged at them by their treatment after I quit (not responding to simple requests for information and harassing me with an aggressive bill collector).  This is no way to retain talent.  Work here at your own risk.

During our training they stuffed 50 of us in a training room fit for 20 people (only 20 chairs and computers- we squeezed more in creating an obvious fire hazard) we were not allowed to use the restroom or have a bottle of water. They talked down to us as though this job and training were a punishment- like being there was a pun ishment for something we had done wrong. It was a hot mess to say the least. I saw one agent get fired in the middle of the floor, while her manager very dramatically and loudly told everyone she was an 'idiot' and 'she needed to hustle' all while the agent was crying and packing up her desk. I reported this to my manager and was told the agent deserved to be treated like that cause she cheated on her timesheet and what the manager did was citi policy. I took part in a roundtable where I expressed a specific concern about my manager at the time and by the next morning my manager had found out and threatened to put me on a PIP for talking about her in a roundtable and then proceeded to tell other agents she hated me. In addition to these things myself and other agents have been told we cannot use the bathroom, we cannot get water or coffee. summary: Tampa office is hit & miss - I missed. Will never go back & can't recommend.
pros: Beautiful campus in Tampa - outdoor walkways, gym, plenty of outdoor seating. Covered parking. Nice part of town.
cons:
There is literally no on-boarding process. My direct supervisor was useless. Bragged about his 12-hour workdays. Everyone around me, every day, was just grinding it out with minimal vision, minimal strategy (no why/how - just find the nearest problem and start working.) Pay was low from the get-go, but it's my own fault for accepting. I should have seen the writing on the wall. My boss balked at an $11 fee for a new Citi group email (suggested by another employee as a process improvement.) He literally said, "it's $11? Let me think on it." That's how cost-conscious Citi is, so I couldn't wait for year-end raises (not.) No one in my group took lunches. So tied to their desks. Also, AVP/VP is a joke. Title structure is a joke. It isn't nearly as prestigious as one may think, and their pay demonstrates it. After I accepted, my AVP role suddenly showed in the system as AVP Analyst. 

On the day I quit, one of the NYC execs was doing a webinar. No one in my group attended, because no one freaking cares about the big picture, apparently. They just sat there, slumped in their desks, grinding it out. I dialed into the webinar and reviewed the anonymous questions posed by Tampa employees to the NYC exec, for him to answer. 9 of 10, no joke, were about the bad morale, bad pay, and lack of vision in Tampa. It confirmed everything I'd seen. I quit 2 hours later, and walked out with a pep in my step.

Final word: after speaking with several recruiting firms, they all nodded their head when I talked about Citi in Tampa. One recruiter said "Citi sucks, everyone in Tampa knows it." I'm so glad I left, and I pity the people who stay there and grind it out. There's so much else out there. cons:
In one word, it is a sweatshop of Citibank in India.

- There is a concept of DTA (Desktop Tool Analysis), it is a background software which generally runs in every employee desktop and will monitor all the activities which you are doing. Like which websites you are browsing, which software you have opened. The active session you logged-in and the non-active session when you were log-out. In my projects, managers used to send emails to the employee if any team failed to have average DTA of 9 hours. It is like we are working in some cheap start-up company.

- They will enforce you to have a minimum of 9 hours of DTA time and even if you miss by 30 minutes, the manager will escalate this and will pressurize you that it will reduce the overall DTA score of the team, So, we need to keep it minimum 9 hours but there is no bar for maximum as they want to make your work endlessly.

- No work-life balance. Manager will expect you to work all 7 days in a week. They have created several WhatsApp groups in which they will keep messaging you to log-in from home whether it is weekend, public holiday or you just came from office on normal days. 

- Recently, they have closed the facility of WFH by stating that their employee don't do WFH sincerely but still forces many employees to login from home outside of their business hours. This company is the best use case of how to misuse the remote login facility. 

- In the name of the Agile, they will make any changes during the scrum and force you to deliver it on time and will make you pressurized if you don't delivery it on time or raise any concern over delivery

- Due to the above reasons, you will mostly get the negatives to feedback from the Citi employees whether they are former or currently working over there. If you are your vendor to this company then it will be a hell for you.

- During the interview process and pre-joining session, HR will tell you that they care for the employee work-life balance and gives lots of leaves. But in reality, very few lucky ones are able to utilize their leaves completely. 

- Due to this negative working culture, you will see that nowadays most of the employees who are joining them are from mostly service-based or they directly hire their vendor on their permanent role. Because in past most of the new joiners were either absconding them or leaving them within a few months of joining. 

- That is why they are also having a notice period of 90 days from the first day of your joining.

So, my one humble request to anyone who is looking forward to joining this organization, please just have some feedback from an employee or vendor who either worked with or currently working with Citibank. If you found someone who is working in the business unit for which you are also got hired then it will be better. Only then take your decision to join this organization.

summary: Absolute Nightmare - Job Ruined My Life
advice: Don't lie to potential employees about what their job will entail or what the company will do for them just to get them on board. If they knew the truth, they would never come to work for you, but you have a responsibility to be honest.
pros: None. If you only care about the paycheck, it might be acceptable. But there are no other upsides, particularly if you actually want to care about or find fulfillment in what you do.
cons:
This will likely sound like the rantings of a disgruntled employee, but as a human being, I beg you: do not come to work at Citi.

The company perfectly fits the stereotype of a massive decentralized organization characterized by stifling bureaucracy. Employees are almost universally unhappy, save for the paycheck, and there is no management or human resources support when problems arise. Operations at the company work through endless recurring conference calls filled with buzzwords like "leverage," "use cases," and "workstream," but no results are ever achieved and no tasks are actually completed.

Because of the size and global spread of the company and the fact that most employees work from home, managers essentially answer to no one, and it's genuinely possible for employees to completely disappear within the system. Human resources are inaccessible -- if they exist at all -- and getting help with something as simple as a desk to work at and a computer that actually works are left completely up to the individual employee to figure out. There is no ability to advance to a higher role or even a different group: once you're planted in a slot, that's where you're expected to be, for years on end if necessary.

From my experience, no matter what interviewers and hiring coordinators say, job descriptions given to potential employees have no actual relationship to what employees are actually expected to do - in large part because managers operate without any sense of strategic direction, and bodies are just thrown at meaningless projects without any sense of reasoning or applicable skills. Regardless of the nature of the work, everything is done in Excel spreadsheets containing meaningless data, and there is no sense of employee loyalty to the company or to one's co-workers.

Employees refuse to respond to emails or phone messages, and even when meetings are scheduled, individuals completely ignore them, because there is no management penalty or monitoring. Projects are initiated with no sense of timeline or goals - or even a sense of "why are we doing this?" - and frequently discussing the status of projects on conference calls is viewed as a more acceptable substitute than actually getting something done. Individuals frequently ignore deadlines and refuse to collaborate on group projects, because every individual work unit only answers to itself, and upper management has no recourse over individual groups to force results. Meanwhile, even items requiring first-level managers to take the simplest action go completely ignored for months on end - which is actually fine, because no one within the company cares about what others in the company do anyway.

Regardless of the fact that this sounds like a rant, please, as a human being, I beg you to take this seriously: do not come to work at Citi. I have loved every job I ever took before I began working at Citi, and only agreed to come on board to relocate to another area for family reasons. I regret it every day, and regretted it from the very first week. Do not work at Citi. If you care at all about what you do, it will ruin you.

summary: A true example of Mediocrity in action
advice: You need three things to lead people: Trust, Respect, and Like… you don’t’ have to like your boss or employer but you have to Trust and Respect in order for the relationship to thrive.  I know very few people who trust or respect CMI let alone like the company.  Executive management would do well in opening their eyes to the business around them and focusing on changing the culture that has led to such a poor place to work
pros: Large portfolio of more than 4.5 million clients
cons: CMI is a great example of true incompetence in the mortgage industry.  Mortgage professionals who work here after working for other organizations in the industry quickly leave due to the inability of Citi to close a loan adequately and do business the right way.  Many mortgage consultants have no previous mortgage experience so they have difficulty understanding just how badly CMI is when it comes to doing business.  This is also true of the operations staff as well, who are truly clueless when it comes to closing a loan in a reasonable period of time.  The average time to close a loan at CMI is between 60-90 days where the industry average is less than 30.  Typical pipeline pull through is less than 60% from application to closing where the industry average is around 90%.  Instead of simply creating a better process flow for mortgages to close, executive management simply makes all clients pay for a 90 day rate lock which ultimately makes the organization less competitive.  After working for a number of top organizations in the business for the past ten years it is very obvious that there is cowardice of management where no one is willing to step outside their comfort zone and fix the glaring problems that plague the organization.  Moral is VERY low due to two major issues... first, nearly all leaders above a sales manager, which is department heads all the way up to Sanjiv have never originated or closed a loan themselves and are completely clueless on how the business works.  Second, the organization is disinterested in becoming more efficient leaving employees to languish in the mediocrity.  It is truly sad that they are not any more positive things to say about this organization.  Some food for thought, nearly every MC/MLC and middle manager I’ve spoken too would NEVER close a loan with Citimortgage simply because of the organizations inability to offer competent service.  That fact in itself is striking

It's as if they are two completely different companies as there is little to no involvement from one to the other. The building in Brandon is a great place - huge corporate cafeteria, lots of interaction between offices, etc. The building at Hidden River Park is completely isolated. Very stark office. No cubicles, just row-long desks with dividers. No privacy at all and your boss sits at the end of your row to watch your every move. There are often fights between rows over who is making more noise that is preventing people around them from working. (lots of people sing, hum, drum on their desks, etc.) Citi has a policy where they want managers to become involved in an employees private life. My opinion: I have two lives - one at work and one at home. Should they ever intermingle it will be at my discretion, not forced by corporate policy. My ex-boss was more interested in having an after-hours drinking and dinner buddy than a dedicated and knowledgeable employee. Declining invitations (more like demands) to attend after-hours and weekend team events (most often team only, no spouses or family) was frowned upon and caused very hard feelings. So the only way to stay employed and get good reviews was to play the "happy team player" game, even at the expense of causing issues at home. You can learn a lot but there is a common reality at Citi: What you learn at Citi can be used ONLY at Citi. They take packages from vendors like Oracle and modify them to fit Citi's specific needs. Not a problem, but they do sooooo much tweaking and morphing that when they finally get the package to where they want it, it's so far removed from the original package (the one everyone else in the world uses) that it's impossible to take the knowledge you obtain at Citi and use it for any other employer.

summary: OK environment for non-exempt employees. Think twice before becoming a people manager there.
advice: First and foremost, the site leadership needs to be reevaluated. They help to establish the culture there, and what's been allowed to occur under their watch has been exceptionally detrimental. The lack of accountability is seen at all levels, and it actively dissuades both staff and leaders in the business from striving to be the best at what they do. Until that's understood and dealt with, they will continue to miss opportunities to establish the environment that fosters and promotes breakthrough performance results.
pros: The benefits are good, and the schedules offered are varied for employees to balance their work and life. I had the opportunity to work with some bright and talented staff there, but sadly their contributions are eclipsed by the cons that you will read about below.
cons:
During my short time with the organization, I witnessed some of the most appalling examples of poor management decisions I have ever observed in my career. Leadership at the site level holds a philosophy that non exempt employees must be kept happy at any cost, regardless of the negative impact to the business. It is known by the staff all through the department I worked in that employees could get away with performance and conduct that in any other organization would mean dismissal from your job. As a people manager, it is exceptionally difficult to lead your team to perform to the business expectations, as employees saw many examples of peers maintaining their jobs even when they repeatedly failed to meet the business expectations or engaged in poor conduct (In some situations, there have been employees who failed to meet objectives for years, and were allowed to continue their employment). This abject failure of leadership at this site made it extremely difficult to have any meaningful impact on  the job performance of your assigned group. 

Just to highlight some of the examples of these failures:

-Employees who displayed issues with repeated absenteeism are rarely dealt with accordingly. I observed many examples of staff regularly missing time well beyond what's stated as allowable in the employee handbook, yet little is done to dissuade the employees from engaging in this behavior. They may be engaged in a disciplinary action process, but very, very few of those ever result in the employees separation even in light of the behavior continuing. This in turn causes issues with making sure they are appropriately staffed which trickles down to impacting the clients, not to mention allowing for the behavior to perpetuate across the business. 

-There were many, many examples of scenarios where customers were treated very poorly by the front line staff, with the outcome often times being the mildest of disciplinary action. There is a party line in the department about "no tolerance" behaviors, which is completely false. No one was every out right terminated outright for treating customers poorly, regardless of how grievous the situation was. I personally witnessed several examples of this, where individuals engaged the clients in such a rude and condescending manner, that the clients immediately terminated their relationship with the bank. This behavior was met the a simple slap on the wrist, even though that conduct in all of these scenarios cost the bank significant amounts of revenue. 

-The front line leaders of the business are not respected, as the staff knows that they will not held accountable for their behaviors and performance. There were employees who were outright disrespectful and insubordinate to their immediate supervisors, and very little was done to address these types of issues. It wasn't uncommon to hear about interactions where a staff member would outright tell their supervisor they would not follow a directive issued, and have virtually no consequences as a result. H/R representation at the site level has been complicit in this situation as well, often times advocating for the retention of the employee even in the face of this misconduct. Probably the best example of have the how a blind eye was turned to some of the gross misconduct was a leader being called profanity to their face by a staff member (which there was no argument by either side that this incident occurred) and nothing was done beyond a weak attempt at a verbal warning about the employees conduct. 

-Operations leaders spend a majority of their time in their offices, completely removed from observing how the respective area runs. While they spend much of their time looking at the end result (metric performance) they spend virtually no time understanding how those teams are achieving those results. This "head in the sand" approach to leading their departments has led to some rampant impropriety among some of the leaders in their areas in the attempt to achieve the expected performance metrics. Additionally, the operations leaders all seem to fail at making the tough decisions necessary when it's required. I have observed all of them take a softshoe approach to the bad behavior in their respective areas. It's also not uncommon to hear of the Operations managers overturning a decision by the front line supervisor when one of their staff members expresses a concern about a directive. It's been my observation that these leaders wish to avoid confrontation at all costs, and will give in to the employee requests regardless of the short and long term impact to the department. This failure in leadership has resulted in many of the front line supervisors developing an apathy towards their roles and responsibilities, as they feel shackled by a culture that values employee satisfaction over all, even if the employees satisfaction comes at the detriment to the business, and more importantly, the clients.


If you are considering taking a job at Citi, especially as a leader, it's important to understand this is the culture that's in play as of the writing of this review.  Somewhere along the way, striking that balance between the satisfaction of the staff and the needs of the clients and the business has been lost. If you're looking to work in an environment where you are allowed to lead your team in meeting the goals and objectives of the company, I would strongly advise you to look elsewhere. You will be relegated to going through the day to day motions of leading, without actually being able to affect any real change.  It's very likely you will find yourself disappointed and frustrated by the experience.

summary: A lot of lip service but little else

pros: Relatively decent facilities.  Not usually difficult to get time off at short notice. Salaries ok and benefits package quite good.  Looks good on the CV. Some valuable charity work opportunities supported by the company.
cons:
Rigid hierarchical management structure, with a tendency to rule by fear.  Anyone who questions senior management is treated badly.  Some senior staff have too much power and there are no controls over how they use it.  Morale among staff is low - people do not feel respected or valued.  You are simply a disposable commodity.  Employees with problems related to their role or manager have nowhere to turn for support.

People are never sure whether they are at risk of redundancy .  A lot of knowledgable, competent staff have been made redundant with seemingly little forward planning - this has left huge gaps in some areas.  

The appraisal system is supposed to feed into pay/promotion but in reality it does not - ratings on appraisals are in some areas decided solely by a senior manager with no knowledge of individuals' performance.  There are no controls to prevent these decisions being made on personal grounds and there is no way to contest them.

On a day to day basis, the company has many policies and procedures and endless monitoring by different departments - including repeated monitoring of the same things where there is no need for it.  

There are too many layers of management which results in work creation.  

There is a lot of box-ticking and endless different layers of approval are needed for even the tiniest decision, which is frustrating, especially if you are used to having accountability for your own work.  Small tasks take too long and important issues are sidelined.  On the other hand, there is a reluctance at senior level to take accountability for important issues.

Everything that needs support is either outsourced or handled remotely, which means it is difficult to speak to a human about any issues of any kind that arise whether people or IT related.  IT problems, for example, must be logged via a complicated online method, take a long time to resolve and there is no way of discussing them with a human being when they are (invariably) not fully resolved.

Meanwhile, the company talks a lot about how well staff are treated.  Staff are pressured into completing 'voluntary' and 'anonymous' surveys, the results of which are manipulated to play down the negatives.  Some managers are allowed to probe into which employee gave which answer. 

The company claims to value talent but this only seems to apply at senior level.  Below that, staff generally feel that there is no real opportunity for career progression or development, and true ability and expertise is not recognised or valued.
